## VIII. SPECIAL CASE

## 1. Urticarial and Angioedema

Urticarial is commonly encountered in the ED. It is characterized by the presence of wheals, angioedema, or both. Urticarial appears as papules or wheals that consist of central swelling with surrounding reflex erythema and is associated with itching or a burning type sensation. These lesions are a result of mediators (predominately histamine) released from mast cells. They tend to occur on the extremities and are usually transient, with skin often returning to its normal appearance within 24 hours. Urticarial can be classified based on its duration, with acute urticarial lasting less than 6 weeks and chronic episodes lasting longer than 6 weeks. There are also several types of inducible urticarial including cold contact, delayed pressure, heat contact, solar, aquagenic, or cholinergic.

Angioedema is characterized by edema of the subcutaneous or submucosal tissues, commonly involving the face, mouth, lips, tongue, extremities, or genitalia. It is a result of abrupt vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, allowing fluid to move from the vascular to the interstitial space. As the swelling is located in the deeper layers of the skin, the appearance is often normal in color and patients often complain of pain or a pressure sensation, rather than an itch. Of particular concern is when the tongue, posterior pharynx, or larynx is involved, which could progress to airway obstruction and compromise. Angioedema can be mediated by an allergic mechanism in response to exposure to foods, drugs, or physical stimuli or by a nonallergic mechanism such as Hereditary Angioedema (HAE), acquired angioedema, or ACE-inhibitor- induced angioedema.

## 2. Management

Angioedema with urticarial without airway threatening:

- H1-Antihistamine: cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine or Diphenhydramine
- H2-Antihistamine may also beneficial: Famotidine, Ranitidine or Cimetidine.
- Corticosteroids: prednisone as a second-line therapy
- Epinephrine: anaphylactic dosing for severe symptoms and no cardiac risk factors.
- Avoid exposure to potential triggering agents.

Angioedema with airway-threatening:

- Epinephrine at anaphylactic doses.
- Antihistamines
- Intubation if situation required and paralytics should be utilized with caution.
- Prepared for difficult airway algorithm using alternative measures (fiber optic laryngoscopy, surgical airway).

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Biphasic reaction: reoccurrence of anaphylactic symptoms without re-exposure to the triggering agent within 8 hours to 72 hours.
- Prevention by administer corticosteroids but recent studies have failed to show significant effect.
- Risk factor for biphasic reactions include
- Hypotension
- Wide pulse pressure
- Unknown trigger
- Greater than 1 dose of epinephrine
- Cutaneous signs and symptoms, prior anaphylaxis
- And delayed epinephrine administration.

- Patients should be monitored for a minimum of 6 h after resolution of symptoms. This observation period may need to be longer depending on the presence of any of the following high-risk features:
- Extremes of age
- Significant co-morbidity
- Severe reaction with slow onset
- Severe asthma
- Likely continued absorption
- History of significant biphasic reaction
- Evening or night presentation
- Difficulty accessing emergency care
- Hospitalization should be strongly considered for patients who present with protracted anaphylaxis, hypotension, or airway involvement; receive more than two doses of IM epinephrine; or have poor outpatient social support, or inability to acquire an auto-injectable epinephrine device.

## X. COMPLICATION

The main complications which can occur following an anaphylactic reaction include:

- Wheeze
- Stridor
- Hypoxemia
- Hypotension
- End-organ dysfunction
- Death

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening allergic condition which can present with multiple symptoms.

Anaphylaxis should be treated with intramuscular epinephrine, supportive management, and adjunct medications as needed. The mainstay of management is avoidance of triggers and to carry an epinephrine auto-injector.

A prescription for an epinephrine auto-injector should be provided following treatment of anaphylaxis, and training should also be provided regarding its use. Patients should also be assessed and followed by an allergist.

## GENERAL MANAGEMENT OF POISONING

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola , Dr. PHY Sopheak , Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha , Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha , Dr. TES Sovannara , Dr. IM Sothy , Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya

## I. DEFINITION

Poisoning or intoxication is a serious condition that occurs when a person or an animal is exposed to a substance that can harm their health or even kill them.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

An epidemiological Surveillance report 2011 in Thailand found that the incidence of environmental pesticide poisoning is 3.20 per 100.000 person. The incidence of prescribed drugs poisoning is 3.81 and the intentional ingestion of toxic substances is 5.91 per 100.000. In Singapore, the incidence of alcohol consumption-related ED visit was remarkably increased from 48.7 per 100.000 person (in 2007) to 79.1 per 100.000 person (in 2016).

## III. ETIOLOGY

Poisoning may be "acute" (occurs a few hours to few days after exposure) or "Chronic" (problems occur after repeated and long-time exposure). In emergencies most of the intoxication cases was acute poisoning. Intoxication or poisoning may be intentional or nonintentional. Intentional poisoning: suicide attempt, self-harm, abuse, misuse. Non-intentional poisoning: error dose, accidental, environmental toxics (air pollution, arsenic in water...), occupational poisoning, food, drink (methanol poisoning), animal bites. Poison can be a drug that is used in clinic (overdose), food, drink, chemical that use in industrial / agricultural works, or household-use, or biologic (mushroom, some fishes). Exposure route may be inhalation, skin contact, mucous membrane contact, ingestion, or injection. Animals or snakebites were also a kind of poisoning in which the poison or venom were injected into the subcutaneous tissue or muscle during the bite.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

To initiate the poisoning, the organism is exposed to the toxic chemical. When a toxic level of the chemical is accumulated in the cells of the target tissue or organ, the resultant injury to the cells disrupts their normal structure or function. Symptoms and toxic signs then develop, and, if the toxicity is severe enough, death may result. Different groups of substances may have different mechanisms of toxicity to human. It may be a Systemic poisoning (Cyanide, lead, warfarin, pesticides), specific organ poisoning (paracetamol-liver, gentamycin-kidney, snake Viperidae-venom-hematologic / snake Elapidae-venom- neurologic), local poisoning (caustic, acid, snake Viperidae-venom), some substances may cause endocrine disruption (DDT, Bisphenol A, Dioxins), some other may be cancerogenic (arsenic-skin, Asbestos-lung, tobaccolung). Substances belonging to a particular pharmaceutical or chemical class often produce a cluster of symptoms and signs, or

"toxidrome", enabling the identification of potential toxins when a clear history is unavailable.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

The diagnosis of poisoning is based on the meticulous history, physical examination and/or toxidrome found in physical exam.

## 1. Signs &amp; symptoms

The common toxidrome with signs and symptoms are shown in table\_ 1

## 2. Laboratory analysis:

For clinical use, common laboratory tests were order:

- "Basic metabolic panel" for electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, HCO3, Calcium) plus glucose, urea, creatinine) and to determine anion gap;
- ethanol, acetaminophen (paracetamol), and salicylate concentrations (if overdose is suspected)
- transaminases,
- serum osmolarity if toxic alcohol is suspected;
- blood gas for pH

The specific toxicology screens in general, are of limited utility and seldom impact care and outcome. False negative and positive results on urine drug screening may be confusing and potentially distract the clinician. It was indicated in some specific cases e.g., in mass poisoning or empoisoning cases or when the exact cause of poisoning was necessary.

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

In emergency, one should consider a poisoning as a possible cause of unexplained coma / seizure or shock. In practice, patient who was intentionally poisoning usually take more than one drugs or substances. Besides, in intoxication with some products like insecticides, patient may be intoxicated also with the solvent (petroleum, benzene, xylene) of those products. Many compounds medicine has multiple active ingredients, (e.g., Codalgin® = paracetamol + codeine) so overdose of main component may be associated with others.

In the case of Ethanol, sedative hypnotic or opioids, different scenario may happen, patient may enter ED because, experience side-effects / allergic reaction, or present with toxic effects of overdoses, or withdrawal syndrome. In chronic poisoning, it is a challenge to link a clinical feather to a toxic cause, as it may take several years for the symptoms and signs to be uncovered.

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objective of management

- [ ]  Stabilize the vital signs (Resuscitation)

- [ ]  Identify the substances, the amount, the route, the time of exposure or the present toxidrome.

- [ ]  Provide antidote, or antivenom, if available

- [ ]  Decontamination, and/or enhance the elimination.

- [ ]  Supportive treatment (hypotension, respiratory failure, renal failure)

- [ ]  Preventive treatment for recurrence poisoning.

## 2. Critical signs

The severity grading of poisoning depends on whether the poison is stimulant or depressant. Coma and cardiovascular collapse are common in the most severe, grade 4, of stimulant as well as depressant poisoning.

Table 2: Severity grade of poisoning, for stimulant and depressant substances

| Physiologic grading of poisoning severity - Severity                  | Physiologic grading of poisoning severity - Stimulant poisoning                                | Physiologic grading of poisoning severity - Depressant poisoning   |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Agitation, anxiety, diaphoresis, Hyperreflexia, mydriasis, tremors    | Ataxia, confusion, lethargy, weakness, able to follow verbal commands                          | Grade 1                                                            |
| Confusion, fever, hyperactivity, Hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea | Mild coma (non-verbal but responsive to pain); brainstem and deep tendon reflexes intact       | Grade 2                                                            |
| Delirium, hallucinations, hyperpyrexia, tachyarrhythmias              | Moderate coma (respiratory depression, unresponsive to pain); some but not all reflexes absent | Grade 3                                                            |
| Coma, Cardiovascular collapse, seizures                               | Deep coma (apnea, cardiovascular depression); all reflexes absent                              | Grade 4                                                            |

## 3. Mortality risk factor

Multiple factors contributed to the risk of mortality

- Type of poisoning, intentional (suicide, of empoisoning)
- The dose of poison or duration of exposure to the toxic substances
- The degree or intensity of toxicity of the exposed substances or toxin
- Medical background of intoxicated patient, age group
- The delay of management
- Availability of supportive /substitutive treatment (Hemodialysis, mechanical ventilation)
- Some classical procedures may be harmful (gastric lavage-associated aspiration pneumonia)

## 4. Out-patient management

Only people who exposed to a known non-toxic substance and asymptomatic may be observed at home and contact with emergency personal for any abnormality.

## 5. First-line treatment

In all case, consider the supportive treatment first. The shock state, depressed respiration should be the first measure to be taken. If the poison was identified and it has antidote, it should be administered as soon as possible.

## A. Gastrointestinal decontamination

## i. Gastric lavage

If performed because of a potentially life-threatening poison ingestion, an experienced provider should perform the lavage based on the complications that can occur.

Gastric lavage involves a large-bore (36F-40F) orogastric tube passed into the stomach, after which small volumes (200-300 mL) of liquid are alternately administered and aspirated. Comatose patients and those with loss of their protective airway reflexes should have an endotracheal tube placed before this procedure.

Contraindications include loss of protective airway reflexes (unless the patient is endotracheally intubated), ingestion of a corrosive substance or a hydrocarbon, gastrointestinal pathology, and other medical conditions that could be worsened by the use of lavage. Complications of the procedure include aspiration, laryngospasm, hypoxia, hypercapnia, mechanical injury, and fluid and electrolyte imbalances in children.

## ii. Single dose activated charcoal

Administration of activated charcoal may be considered if a patient has ingested a potentially toxic amount of poison that is known to be adsorbed to charcoal not longer than 1 hour before treatment, as its effectiveness decreases over time. There is no evidence that the administration of activated charcoal improves outcome.

The dose is 1 gram/ kilogram in children or 25 to 50 grams in adults. The minimal dose should be no less than a 10:1 ratio of AC to drug Same contraindication as gastric lavage.

## iii. Whole-bowel irrigation

Whole-bowel irrigation consists of administration through a nasogastric tube of an osmotically balanced, polyethylene glycol-based electrolyte solution to decontaminate the entire gastrointestinal tract by physically expelling intraluminal contents. As much as 1500-2000 mL/hr can be administered to an "awake" adult patient.

Whole-bowel irrigation should not be used routinely in the poisoned patient. However, it can be considered for potentially toxic ingestions of sustained-release or enteric-coated drugs and for drugs not likely to be adsorbed to activated charcoal (iron, lithium, potassium) and for the removal of illicit drug packets. Contraindications include bowel pathology, unprotected or compromised airway, hemodynamic instability, and intractable vomiting. Complications are nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.

## iv. Multiple-dose activated charcoal

Multiple-dose activated charcoal decreases the re-absorption blood-enteral, also interrupts the enterohepatic and enterogastric circulation of drugs. Drugs with a prolonged elimination half-life, a small volume of distribution (less than 1 L/kg), and little protein binding are the most amenable to this sort of management. Multiple-dose activated charcoal should be considered if a patient has ingested a life-threatening amount of carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, or theophylline. With all of these drugs, data confirm enhanced elimination, although no controlled studies have demonstrated clinical benefit.

The initial dose of charcoal is 50-100 g, and this treatment is followed every 1, 2, or 4 hours by a dose equivalent to 12.5 g/hr. More frequent, smaller doses may prevent vomiting. Multiple-dose activated charcoal can be continued until the patient improves clinically. Complications include bowel obstruction and vomiting with subsequent aspiration.

## B. Urinary alkalinization

Urinary alkalinization is the administration of intravenous (IV) sodium bicarbonate to produce urine with a pH ≥7.5. The objective of treatment is pH manipulation, not forced diuresis. Hypokalemia is the most common complication. Alkalemia also can occur. Urinary alkalinization should be considered as first-line treatment in patients with moderately severe salicylate poisoning who do not meet the criteria for hemodialysis. Urinary alkalinization is not recommended as first-line treatment for cases of phenobarbital poisoning, because multiple-dose activated charcoal is superior.

## C. Ipecac and emetics

There is no role for syrup of ipecac in the hospital setting.

Not all substances have their antidote. Table 2 shows Common antidotes used in Clinical practice. Outside the poison center, only a few are available.

## F. Supportive / substitution treatment

Supportive treatment is essential; in many situations it was the only feasible measure in poisoning management. Most of the substances do not have their antidote. The decontamination and enhanced elimination process were useful in limited cases only. Even the antidote is available and administered, it takes time for the organ dysfunction to reverse, during this time supportive measures is also needed. E.g., in cobra-snakebites, patient may have respiratory depressed or arrest while antivenom was administered. It takes a few hours for spontaneous respiration to re-appear. The active supportive treatment consists of maintaining the normal water, electrolytes acid-base equilibrium, a good oxygenation and perfusion; sometimes mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis and pharmacologically cardiac support were needed.

## 6. Treatment adjustment

In general, gastric lavage is not recommended when the patient arrived later than 1 hour after ingested the substances, it should be possible to try in case the patient took a large quantity of substance or/and the substance is known to slow the peristaltic. For the corrosive substance or a hydrocarbon, the gastric lavage is not recommended. For patient whose consciousness is altered, intubation and ventilation support should be done prior to lavage.

## 7. Decisional tree (graphic-1)

While taking history and physical examination, the treatment of vital signs disorders is starting. Once a poisoning or overdose has been identified, management can be determined. Management options can include gastrointestinal decontamination, enhancing elimination, and/or use of antidotes. Additionally, some poisonings and overdoses only require supportive care.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASE

## 1. Poisoning during pregnancy

Intoxication during pregnancy can be a serious health concern for both the mother and the baby. Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can cause premature labor, miscarriage, stillbirth, and a range of developmental, physical, mental, and emotional disabilities and disorders in the baby. The effects of intoxication on a developing fetus can vary greatly depending on several factors, including the type of substance used, the amount ingested, and the gestational age of the fetus.

- First trimester of pregnancy: Intoxicants can disrupt organogenesis process, leading to birth defects, developmental delays, and miscarriage.
- Second trimester: \_ growth and development. Exposure to toxins can affect weight, height, and brain development. Risk of cleft palate or other facial malformations
- Third trimester: brain development may interfere by intoxication, risk of premature birth.

Management of acute poisoning in pregnant women follow the same principle.

## 2. Poisoning in children

Children 1-3 years old are prone to acute poisoning. Children's bodies are still developing, and their brains are particularly sensitive to the effects of alcohol and drugs. Even small amounts can cause significant harm. For some substances they are more vulnerable than adult, e.g., lead poisoning. Young children (age 6 months to 7 years) are at the highest risk due to their developing brains and bodies, which readily absorb lead. Effects can range from developmental delays and learning difficulties to behavioral problems, anemia, and even coma in severe cases. Lead poisoning (chronic poisoning) can also affect growth and stature, hearing, and kidney function.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

The evolution and prognosis of patients who are intoxicated can vary widely, depending on the substance involved, the amount ingested, the patient's overall health, and the timeliness and effectiveness of treatment. With proper management, most intoxication patients gradually improve and regain consciousness. Patient who repeatedly intentional intoxicate should be checked and follow up with psychiatric.

## X. COMPLICATION

In acute poisoning, the complications link to intrinsic effect of substances may consist of, seizures, coma, shock, acute respiratory failure, acute kidney failure, acute liver failure and death. Complications may be link to the supportive procedures like mechanical ventilation or hemodialysis. In chronic exposure to toxic substances, long-term complications may be serious e.g., alcohol may lead to liver cirrhosis or/and liver cancer. Chronic exposure to Lead in small children may develop a learning difficulty, behavioral problems, affect growth and kidney function, anemic and hearing problem.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- Store chemicals and medications safely.
- Read and follow instructions carefully
- Dispose of old or unused products and dangerous substances responsibly
- Install childproof safety latches
- Educate children about the dangers of poisoning
- Advocate for proper labeling and packaging
- Do not forcing patient to vomit by any mean; do not try to neutralize the toxic effects by forcing patient to swallow the solution (lemon and sugar) especially when his/her mental status was altered.

## PARACETAMOL POISONING

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola , Dr. PHY Sopheak , Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha , Dr. TES Sovannara , Dr. IM Sothy , Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya

## I. DEFINITION

A disorder characterized by hepatic necrosis following large acetaminophen (or Paracetamol) ingestions.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

In USA, hospitalizations due to acetaminophen toxicity from 1998 to 2011 were 67% due to intentional ingestion, 16% from unintentional ingestion, and 17% unspecified.

Of the hospitalizations related to acetaminophen toxicity, 83% were primarily adults and 69% were female (95% CI 0.68-0.69%). From 2008 to 2012, about 49% of unintentional acetaminophen-related poison-control calls were regarding children aged ≤5 years.

In Thailand, among 184 patients with paracetamol overdosed, had median age 22 (15- 76), 79.9% was female. Most overdoses were intended self-poisoning (90.8%) with a median dose of 10.5g (4.5-50). Overall, 15.6% developed severe hepatotoxicity and 3 patient developed acute liver failure.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Paracetamol preparation has many forms:

- -Rapid-release form\_ onset of action: 10-30min, duration of action: 4-6h; half-life: 2-3h
- -Extend-release form\_ onset of action: 30-60min, duration of action: 8-12h
- -Paracetamol combined formular\_ associated with opioids (e.g., Codalgin®) or caffeine (e.g., Kinal®) to increase its strength. Some flu-medicines may include with paracetamol, pseudoephedrine, antiallergic, dextromethorphane in their constituents.

Mode of poisoning:

- -poisoning from a single large dose, or
- -prolong-repeat of mild overdose or
- -normal therapeutic dose in patients with liver disorders or malnourished alcoholism.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

In a therapeutic dose and normal people, paracetamol is safe. About 2% of administered dose exit unchanged in urine. About 98% is metabolized in the liver. More than 80% by conjugated with glucuronide or sulfate to form a non-toxic fraction that eliminate by urine. About 8% of administered dose metabolized with cytochrome P450 enzymes to produce N-acetyl-pbenzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). NAPQI is a by- product, toxic to the liver. In normal people, this product existed in a very short time without any harm to the liver. It was combined by liver glutathione to form a non-toxic NAPQI and eliminate in urine. In the situation of toxic overdose, the metabolism pathway with glucuronide and sulfate is saturated, the CYP450 pathway increased, more NAPQI was produced; when Glutathione is not enough, NAPQI will damage the liver.

Graphic-1: mechanism of paracetamol intoxication

<!-- image -->

## V. DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis of paracetamol poisoning is based on history, clinical signs with blood-paracetamol concentration assessment.

Signs and symptoms of paracetamol poisoning develop over the first 24 hours following large ingestions. Symptoms may develop gradually in those with a history of long-term ingestion near supratherapeutic doses

A toxic exposure to acetaminophen is suggested when a patient ≥6 years old ingests:

- (1) &gt;10 grams or 200 milligrams/kg as a single ingestion,
- (2) &gt;10 grams or 200 milligrams/kg over a 24-hour period, or
- (3) &gt;6 grams or 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for at least 2 consecutive days.

For children &lt;6 years old,

ingestion of 200 milligrams/kg or more of acetaminophen as a single ingestion or over an 8-hour period, or of 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for the preceding 48 hours is considered a toxic exposure.

These values are empiric and not validated in human trials, but they are widely used as recommendations for emergency evaluation.

## I. Clinic

Presentation of symptoms varies and is divided into four stages:

## Stage 1-first 24 hours after ingestion

- Patients may be asymptomatic in the first 8 hours following ingestion.
- Symptoms may include nausea, emesis, anorexia, and diaphoresis.
- Laboratory results are usually unremarkable at this time.

## Stage 2-days 2 to 3 following ingestion

- Typically, less nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and malaise than in stage 1; right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly may become evident.
- Elevated aminotransferases are usually seen.

## Stage 3-days 3 to 4 following ingestion

- Stage I symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and malaise reappear.
- Severe poisonings may result in jaundice, confusion, somnolence, and coma.
- Marked liver enzyme elevations which usually peak at this point; prolonged prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR); typically, negative acetaminophen levels.
- Multiorgan failure and death most commonly occur in this stage.

## Stage 4-days 5+ after ingestion

- Possible recovery stage in patients with resolving stage 3 symptoms.
- recovery may be prolonged but is typically complete and without long- term sequelae.
- Laboratory abnormalities typically resolve.
- Fulminant hepatic failure occurs in &lt;1% of adults and is very rare in children &lt;6 years of age.

## 2. Investigation

Plasma acetaminophen level is an essential laboratory test that help decide to use antidote early, before the liver injury occurred. Draw plasma acetaminophen levels on all patients ≥ 4 hours after ingestion (levels peak at 4 hours). Draw additional levels at 6 and 8 hours if extended-release form was ingested. Plot the result on the paracetamol nomogram and see if it is above the treatment line? (See Graphic-2) Liver functions test: alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), PT/INR, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is important, but it usually evident after 24h post ingestion.

Additional labs: electrolytes, glucose, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis, serum alcohol, and salicylate

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Consider the presence of co-ingestants, especially alcohol, opiates, and aspirin.

Other ingested toxins that produce severe acute hepatic injury include mushrooms, products containing yellow phosphorus or carbon tetrachloride. Consider other causes of hepatitis: alcoholic, viral, ischemic

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objectives of management
- Stabilized the vital signs
- Check if patient needs antidote &amp; administer NAC as soon as possible
- Supportive treatment
2. Critical Signs

Hepatic encephalopathy, fulminant liver failure,

Hight Transaminase elevation (ALT or SLT) &gt; 1000.

Acute kidney failure, Severe acidosis, bleeding disorders, Coma

3. Mortality risk factor
- Concurrent poisoning with other substances impacting hepatic metabolism
- A psychiatric illness or history of suicide attempts
- Regular ingestion of large amounts of alcohol; chronic malnutrition
4. Outpatient Management
- Behavioral health evaluation for intentional ingestions
- Consider hospitalization for toxic ingestions with vital instability and/or laboratory abnormalities (liver function tests).
- Consider transfer to a psychiatric facility for intentional ingestions when medically stable.

Graphic-2

<!-- image -->

Paracetamol nomogram (the modified Rumack-Matthew nomogram) intent to use for rapid-release form of paracetamol, single oral overdose, in the window of 4-24h post-ingestion.

## 4. First-line treatment

Stabilization of A.B.C is the first priority.

NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is paracetamol antidote. For severe form of paracetamol poisoning (transaminase levels &gt;1,000 mg/L, severe acidosis, coma/hypotension, or renal failure), additional measure like Hemodialysis, or ECMO is needed. Some patients may need liver transplant to survive.

## A. Gastric decontamination:

Ipecac and gastric lavage are no longer recommended for routine use at home or in health care facilities.

Adequate GI decontamination consists of the early administration (&lt; 4h) of active charcoal orally or through a nasogastric tube. More aggressive forms of decontamination, such as gastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation, are unnecessary because of the rapid GI absorption of paracetamol. Patients who arrived later than 4h, and patients whose airway was not well controlled are not the candidate for active charcoal administration.

## B. Active charcoal:

Single dose activated charcoal (1 g/kg PO) may be effective if given within 1 to 4 hours of ingestion. Never delay oral NAC for activated charcoal.

## C. Enhanced elimination: no indication

## D. Antidote treatment

## a. N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC)

N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), detoxify acetaminophen metabolites and replenish glutathione stored in the liver. NAC administration may reduce mortality from 5% to 0.7%. Give NAC when acetaminophen plasma levels measured ≥4 hours after ingestion are at the "treatment line" or higher on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. In most cases, liver enzymes will be elevated only after 24h.

Empirically start NAC within 8 hours for suspect case or even while awaiting lab results. It may be effective up to ≥36 hours after ingestion.

NAC may be given PO or IV, depending on situation and availability. IV NAC has been shown to decrease the length of hospitalization compared to PO NAC.

Begin with a 200 mg/kg IV dose over 4 hours followed by a 100 mg/kg IV dose over 16 hours. A total of 300 mg/kg IV NAC over a 20-hour period.

Oral route: oral loading dose of 140 mg/kg and then 70 mg/kg q4h for 17 additional doses (72-hour regimen).

## b. NAC precautions:

Consider a nasogastric tube, if nausea, vomiting with Oral route. Metoclopramide, 1 to 2 mg/kg IV, or ondansetron, 0.15 mg/kg IV may be effective.

IV NAC may cause anaphylactoid reactions, (3-6%) including rash, bronchospasm, pruritus, angioedema, tachycardia, or hypotension. Reactions usually occur with the loading dose. To prevent this, slow or temporarily stop the infusion; may concurrently treat with antihistamines.

## E. Second Line

In massive ingestions (levels &gt;1,000 mg/L, severe acidosis, coma/hypotension) or when severe renal failure is present, hemodialysis may improve survival.

## Supportive treatment

## 5. Treatment adjustment

Metoclopramide, 1 to 2 mg/kg IV, or ondansetron, 0.15 mg/kg IV for nausea or vomiting.

IV fluids are generally provided for hydration purposes.

E.g., Muclear® 600mg tab; patient 60kg, give 14 tab dissolved in water, drink or via NG tube, then 7 tab every 4h for additional 17 doses. Mucomyst® oral come with 200mg packet. Injectable Acetyl cysteine usually available as 6g/30ml solution (200mg/ml).

6. Algorithm (see Graphic 3)

## VIII. SPECIAL CASE

## 1. Geriatric Considerations

There is an increased risk of hepatic damage in frail, elderly patients due to decreased hepatic metabolism and co-ingestion of other hepatotoxic medications. Keep dose of acetaminophen ≤3,000 mg/day in seniors and in patients with liver disease and/or alcohol abuse disorders.

## 2. Pediatric Considerations

Hepatic damage after ingestion of toxic acetaminophen doses can be less severe in young children, potentially because they have more stores of glutathione.

## 3. Pregnancy Considerations

There is an increased incidence of spontaneous abortion in pregnant patients with acetaminophen poisoning, especially with overdose at an early gestational age. Abortion incidence and possible fetal death is increased if N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment is delayed. IV NAC is generally preferred in pregnancy due to greater bioavailability.

## TREATMENT GUIDELINES FOR PARACETAMOL INGESTION

Graphic\_3\_ Guideline for paracetamol ingestion;

<!-- image -->

(Adapted from Tintinalli, Emergency Medicine. A comprehensive Study Guide, 9th edition)

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Complete recovery with early therapy (with NAC) is possible and more likely in stage 4 of toxicity. 10% of adult patients with severe liver complications develop necrosis, hepatic encephalopathy, or require transplant. Hepatic failure is rare in children &lt;6 years of age.

## X. COMPLICATION

Recovery after acute poisoning is complete, and sequelae are rare.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

In the situation where plasmatic paracetamol level measurement is not available, consider administer NAC early, in the first 8h, based on history and suspect toxic dose.

- 10g in adult, as single dose or in 24h, or &gt; 6g per day for 2 consecutive days.
- For children &lt; 6y, ingestion of ≥ 200 milligrams/kg as a single ingestion or over an 8hour period, or of 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for the preceding 48 hours)
- For people with liver disease (cirrhosis) the maximum dose is lower may be 2-3g/24 depend on the severity of liver disease.

Outpatient management is adequate for nontoxic accidental ingestions.

Transaminase elevation usually occurred from day 2, repeat measurement is necessary to follow up. The elevation of liver enzymes seen on the first few hours after paracetamol ingestion may indicate an anterior liver problem than the paracetamol-acquired one but, in patient with history liver disorders, standard dose of paracetamol can be toxic also. Educate parents/caregivers during well-child visits regarding appropriate OTC dosing and medication storage. Provide anticipatory guidance for caregivers, family, and cohabitants of potentially suicidal patients.

## XII. REFERENCES

## METHAMPHETAMINES POISONING

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya

## I. AMPHETAMINES &amp; METHAMPHETAMINES

Amphetamines were synthesized in 1887 (by Lazãr Edeleanu, a Romanian scientist who was working in Germany), and in 1932, they were marketed medicinally in an inhaler form as a bronchodilator. Methamphetamines (N-methyl amphetamine) were first synthesized in 1883 (Nagai Nagayoshi, a Japanese scientist).

The crystalized form of methamphetamine was first synthesized in 1919 by scientist Akira Ogata. The use of methamphetamine to enhance physical and intellectual performance began in the 1930s.

Amphetamines may be use medically in "attention deficit hyperactivity disorders" (ADHD), and narcolepsy. Some derivatives were used as weight-loss treatment. Nowadays, amphetamines have limited therapeutic roles but are widely used as drugs of abuse. Methamphetamines is purely produced as illicit drugs.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

The use of methamphetamine and amphetamine has increased rapidly throughout the world, with more than 34 million users worldwide. East and Southeast Asia and North America remain the two main subregions for methamphetamine trafficking worldwide.

During the first half of the 2023, Cambodia authorities had arrested 9034 drugs-related suspects. 52% were drug traffickers, manufacturers, possessors, and transporters. A total of 993 kg of illicit drugs, 9kg of dry marijuana and some 326kg of chemical substances used for drug manufacturing were also confiscated. The seized drugs included heroin, ecstasy, cocaine, crystal methamphetamine, methamphetamine pills, cathinone and ketamine, among others*.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Methamphetamines is an illicit street drug with no medical usage. People may expose to it by -smoking, - swallowing, - snorting, - injecting (s/c, IM, IV)- intra rectal, - intravaginal. Methamphetamines enters the brain quicker than other amphetamine drugs, leading to quick and intense effects. When it is used, a chemical, dopamine, is released in the brain, bringing about a sense of well-being. This high is addictive and causes people to crave the drug repeatedly in order to achieve it.

Physiological adaptation occurs through receptor or coupling down-regulation; this tolerance and an accompanying psychological tolerance (need more and more drug to obtain the same effects) can lead to escalating use of the drug and increased toxicity. Some people may expose by misused amphetamine derivatives as weight-loss medicine.

Yama, Yaba, ice (crystal meth.); MDMA (3-4 methylenedioxymethamphetamine, "ecstasy" or "molly") are common name found in Cambodia.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Methamphetamine is an indirect sympathomimetic, it increased arousal and decreased fatigue. On cardiovascular system it induced, tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypertension and/or coronary vasospasm (sympathomimetic toxidrome). Other central effects: movement disorders, schizophrenia, and euphoria, hallucinogenic and anorexic.

## Pharmacokinetic of Methamphetamine

| Route of exposure             | Onset of action   | Peak Action   | Duration of Action   |
|-------------------------------|-------------------|---------------|----------------------|
| IV                            | 15 - 30s          | 30 min        | 10-12h               |
| Nasal insufflation (snorting) | 3 - 5 min         | 1 - 2 h       | 10 -12h              |
| Inhalation (smoking)          | 10 - 30s          | 5 - 10min     | 8 - 12 h             |
| GI                            | 15 - 20min        | 2 - 3h        | 10 - 12h             |

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## 1. Clinic

Clinicians should consider the diagnosis of methamphetamine intoxication in any diaphoretic patient with hypertension, tachycardia, severe agitation, and psychosis.

Acutely intoxicated patients may become extremely agitated and pose a danger to themselves, other patients, and medical staff. Other symptoms include headache, hyperactivity, toxic psychosis, coma, focal neurologic deficits, or seizures. Some abusers develop stereotyped, compulsive behavior such as cleaning or buttoning shirts.

Psychosis from amphetamines can present as paranoid delusions and perceptual disturbances; these may persist long after the drug has been stopped and can result in homicidal or self-destructive behavior.

## 2. Investigation

Many patients who are admitted users of methamphetamine but are clinically well with normal vital signs do not need any lab testing. However, other methamphetamine users with moderate to severe intoxication can develop several dangerous manifestations and complications. The following tests should be obtained:

- Basic serum electrolytes (i.e., sodium, chloride, potassium, bicarbonate)
- Serum lactate
- Creatine phosphokinase (CPK)
- Aminotransferases (ALT, AST)
- Clotting times (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time)
- Renal function studies (creatine, BUN)
- Urinalysis

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Other substances overdoses that produce sympathomimetic toxidromes: Cocaine, cathinone, Ecstasy, amphetamine; the clinical presentation of these different agents is largely indistinguishable, especially initially. The treatment of sympathomimetic intoxication is generally the same across different agents.

Medical conditions in which the present symptoms may be of concerned: Chronic stress, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic-stress- disorders (PTSD), hyperthyroidism, heart disease.

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objective of management
2. o Reduce the toxic effects of the drugs.
3. o Reduce morbidity.
4. o Prevent complications.

## 2. Critical Signs

hypertension, tachycardia, severely agitated delirium, hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis, seizures and coma.

## 3. Mortality risk factors

Prognostic factors for mortality include:

- coma,
- shock,
- body temperature &gt;39°C,
- acute renal failure,
- metabolic acidosis,
- hyperkalemia (K 5.6 to 8.5 mmol/L)

## 4. Outpatient management

Methamphetamines overdose without disturbance of vital signs, without critical signs can be managed supportively at home.

## 5. First line treatment

Follow the standard protocol of "General Management of Poisoned Patients".

· Decontamination Gastrointestinal decontamination - Activated charcoal is rarely indicated due to the route of methamphetamine administration (e.g., intranasal, inhalation, injection, intravaginal). If methamphetamine has been ingested, the greatest benefit of activated charcoal occurs if administered within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion. In case of body packing or stuffing, indication may be a whole bowel irrigation, or immediate laparotomy to prevent bowel ischemia from local vasoconstriction.

- Enhanced elimination- Urine acidification, formerly used to promote the elimination of methamphetamine, is no longer recommended. The administration of acidic intravenous fluids may exacerbate life-threatening metabolic acidosis
- Antidote: not existed
- Supportive treatment: is the main treatment
- o Hyperthermia. Antipyretics have no role in the management of acute methamphetamine intoxication. Aggressive sedation, neuromuscular paralysis, and fluid resuscitation are used to control methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia; these measures can be supplemented with external cooling blankets or evaporative cooling techniques. Paralyzed patients at risk for seizures should receive continuous bedside electroencephalography.
- o Rhabdomyolysis: (muscle pain or weakness, dark red or brown urine, abdominal pain) Aggressive IV hydration is the primary treatment for rhabdomyolysis. One method is rapid correction of the fluid deficit with IV

- crystalloids followed by infusion of 4 mL/kg/h, with the goal of maintaining a minimum urine output of 3 to 4 mL/kg/h (1-2ml/kg/h). Another method is a goal of 200 to 300 mL of urine output each hour. Any isotonic fluids can be used (attention: patient may have hyperkaliemia).
- o Seizures are initially treated with benzodiazepines, status epilepticus requires aggressive treatment, propofol or thiopental may be used. Attention of blood pressure falling and / or respiratory depression that necessitate supportive ventilation. Obtain a head CT to identify intracranial pathology as the cause of seizures. Phenytoin should be avoided.
- o Agitation: Lorazepam, 2 milligrams IV, or diazepam 5 milligrams, midazolam 2.5mg IV, can be administered and titrated with repeated doses after 8-10min. May start by double the dose and give IM, then about 10min later, give IV dose (up to 30-50mg with appropriate airway monitoring). If it was not effective enough, use antipsychotics: Haloperidol (5-10mg IM / IV), droperidol or chlorpromazine. Ziprasidone 10mg IM (check ECG for long QT first). Physical restraints should be avoided if possible. Patients who struggle against physical restraints undergo isometric muscle contractions that can be associated with lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, sudden cardiac collapse, and death.
- o Chest pain: Cocaine users with suspected acute coronary syndrome are managed with aspirin and nitroglycerin and IV Diltiazem 5-20mg IV if STsegment elevation or depression was observed.
- o Dysrhythmia: may response to sedation, cooling and IV fluid rehydration; other anti-dysrhythmia used is a calcium channel blocker, blood alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (to pH 7.50-7.55), and Lidocaine. If beta-blocker is necessary, use labetalol (alfa and beta-adrenergic antagonist).
- o Hypertension: Severe hypertension not response to sedation should be treated with phentolamine (initial dose, 2.5 to 5.0 mg IV), or nitroglycerine, nicardipine, or sodium nitroprusside, but do not use beta blockers except labetalol.

## 6. Treatment adjustment

ACUTE WITHDRAWAL\_ After heavy or prolonged use, abrupt discontinuation of methamphetamine can cause a withdrawal syndrome. Symptoms may develop within hours, typically peak within 1 to 2 days, and most often decrease within two weeks. Symptoms of withdrawal are strongest during the first 48 hours, but milder symptoms can last up to 2 weeks.

During the acute withdrawal phase ("the crash"), patients may have dysphoria, anhedonia, fatigue, increased sleep, vivid dreams, insomnia, agitation, anxiety, drug craving, and increased appetite.

A subacute withdrawal phase: may persist for up to three weeks with insomnia, hypersomnia, appetite changes, depression, and possibly suicidal thoughts.

Treatments: There is no specific methamphetamine withdrawal medication approved. The combinations of the following drugs, have been used with variable efficacy: benzodiazepines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, riluzole, naltrexone, and behavioral therapy. Some studies found that injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion was safe and effective.

## 7. Algorithm

Graphic-1\_ management of methamphetamines poisoning

Initial emergent control of psychomotor agitation and hyperthermia is of the highest priority to limit life-threatening sequelae.

Aggressive supportive care with supplemental oxygen, sedation, fluid administration, prevention and treatment of hyperthermia, and close monitoring while addressing the specific myriad complications that can occur.

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 133 -->
- Methamphetamines poisoning
  - Venous access & fluid, give oxygen support
    - Rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain, weakness, brown urine, abdominal pain)
      - Initial ttt
        - Fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia. Use RL bolus 1.5-2L in 60min then continue with 4ml/kg/h to get urine 1-2ml/kg/h (Attention to kele mia and heart overload)
          - If failed (oliguria, pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, severe acidosis)
            - Hemodialysis
    - Agitation
      - Initial ttt
        - Diazepam 5mg IV, or start 10mg IM, then IV repeat every 8-10min titrate to sedation or Lorazepam 4mg or Midazolam 2.5mg IV repeat every 8-10min (if seizures may add propofol or thiopental. Phenytoin had minim effects.)

    - Hypertension
      - Initial ttt
        - Nicardipine, Phentolamine Nitroprusside (use betablocker cautiously) Labetalol
          - If failed (End organ damage + Hyperthermia)
            - Myorelaxant + intubated + ventilated (no succinyl choline)
    - Hyperthermia
      - Initial ttt
        - (No antipyretic) Evaporative cooling Cooling blanket
          - If failed (> 38.3°C)
            - Myorelaxant + intubated + ventilated (no succinyl choline)
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Pregnancy and lactation - In utero exposure to methamphetamine is associated with low birth weight and decreased head circumference, among several abnormalities, and may produce withdrawal symptoms in the perinatal period.

Amphetamines, including methamphetamine, are excreted into breast milk.

Pediatric\_ Although sympathomimetic and neuropsychiatric manifestations of methamphetamine exposure should be similar in a pediatric patient, inadvertent exposure may be difficult to diagnose. The most frequent signs and symptoms noted in pediatric patients exposed to methamphetamine are nonspecific.

Asymptomatic children taken from clandestine production sites may also have been exposed to methamphetamine and other chemicals (eg, ephedrine) used to synthesize methamphetamine. These children are particularly vulnerable to child abuse, neglect, serious injury, exposure to toxic chemicals, and malnutrition. The hypersexuality and drug-seeking behaviors of adult methamphetamine users may lead to sexual abuse of such children, or they may be prostituted for money or drugs.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Methamphetamine user rapidly became addicted. Addicted people show the "methamphetamine-use disorders" symptoms:

- A compulsive use of the drug despite harmful consequences.
- Taking larger amounts of meth or using it for a longer period than planned
- Unsuccessful attempts to cut down or quit
- Giving up activities due to meth use
- Inability to keep up with responsibilities at home, work.

The physiologic tolerance process makes the user use higher and higher dose to get the same effects, increase the risk of intoxication.

It is a chronic brain disease.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

Long-term use of the drugs can lead to myonecrosis and dilated cardiomyopathy or myocardial infarction. Use of methamphetamine during pregnancy has been associated with intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth. Incidental injuries from blunt and penetrating trauma are common.

Complications of methamphetamine use include (substance-induced disorders):

- Rhabdomyolysis
- Acute kidney injury
- Seizures
- Stroke with permanent deficits
- Coma
- Acute coronary ischemia or infarction
- Congestive heart failure (CHF)
- Ventricular arrhythmias
- Psychosis (paranoid delusion, may be dangerous to surrounding)
- Addiction (substance-use disorders)
- Death
- HIV and viral hepatitis
- Periodontal disease
- Skin infections

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMANDATION

Early to have consultation (better, is in the Emergency room, when the vital signs were stable) with psychiatric specialist for continue the treatment. Be aware that Methamphetamine addiction is notoriously difficult to treat successfully.

## ORGANOPHOSPHATE AND CARBAMATE INSECTICIDES POISONING

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola,

Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha

## I. DEFINITION

Organophosphate insecticides are a class of chemical compounds that are derived from phosphoric acid. They work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which is responsible for breaking down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. This leads to a buildup of acetylcholine in the nervous system, which can cause a variety of symptoms, including muscle weakness, tremors, convulsions, and even death.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

There are approximately 385 million cases of acute pesticide poisoning each year globally, resulting in around 11,000 deaths. A significant proportion of these cases are due to intentional self-poisoning, particularly in low- and middle-income countries 1 .

Agricultural workers and individuals in areas with heavy pesticide use are at higher risk of accidental poisoning.

Older pesticides like DDT and lindane, though banned in many developed countries, are still in use in some developing regions, contributing to ongoing health risks

## III. ETIOLOGY

In Cambodia, Organophosphates is one group of chemical compounds commonly use as insecticides among other group like pyrazole, thiazole, neonicotinoid, pyrethroids, organochlorines. Organophosphate can be further categorized into several subgroups based on their chemical structure and mode of action:

- Phosphates: These include compounds like malathion and parathion, which are commonly used in agriculture
- Phosphorothioates: ex. diazinon and chlorpyrifos, metamidophos, (commonly use in Cambodia)
- Thiophosphates: phosmet, which is used in both agricultural and residential settings
- Dithiophosphates: dicrotophos.

Example of tradename of metamidophos (OP) available in Cambodia market:

- Bamate
- Bent 600
- Filitox 50EC
- Filitax 60DD
- Filitax 70SC
- Glant 50% WW EC
- Giant 70DD
- L. Talon
- Marathon
- Methamidophos 70SL
- Methamidophos 60
- Methamidophos 70%
- Methaphos 70SC
- Monitor 50EC
- Monitor 50SC
- Monitor 60SC
- Monitor 70DD
- Methon
- Morris
- Ovansu
- Sigtifos
- Siter-Nissan
- Tom 50EC
- Tom 60EC
- Tom 70EC
- U-T 70
- U-T 80
- Vindo

Carbamate insecticide is another chemical group classified into two main subgroups based on their chemical structure:

- o Phenolic Carbamates: ex. Carbaryl, pirimicarb, Propoxur, Bendiocarb
- o Oxime Carbamates: Examples of this subgroup include aldicarb and methomyl,

The most use carbamate in Cambodia is Propoxur, and Bendiocarb, commonly used to control pests like cockroaches, flies, mosquitoes, and lawn insects.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

## Organophosphates (OPs)

- Primary toxic mechanism is inactivating acetylcholinesterase (AChE)
- OPs cause alkyl phosphorylation of the AChE enzyme. The phosphorylated AChE is inactive. AChE is thereby unable to degrade and hydrolyze acetylcholine into choline and acetic acid. Resulting accumulation of acetylcholine at the synaptic junction throughout the nervous system causes overstimulation of receptors.
- Potential locations where cholinergic synaptic transmission can be paralyzed----
- o Central nervous system
- o Autonomic ganglia
- o Parasympathetic nerve endings
- o Some sympathetic nerve endings (such as sweat glands)
- o Somatic nerves
- Direct myocardial injury can occur during the acute, early phase in severe OP poisoning

## Carbamates

- When a carbamate binds to AChE the enzyme undergoes an allosteric change which prevents breakdown of acetylcholine. Carbamates undergo carbamylation of the serine hydroxyl group. The carbamylated AChE is inactive. AChE activity can be spontaneously regenerated.
- Clinical signs of toxicity often occur more rapidly than Ops

Organophosphates (OPs) and carbamates are highly lipophilic, and therefore readily absorbed across the skin, respiratory, and gastrointestinal mucosa.

Onset and severity of symptoms depends on the specific compound, amount, route of exposure, and rate of metabolic degradation. Symptoms are proportional to the decrease in cholinesterase activity

## V. DIAGNOSIS (ACUTE POISONING)

- History
- o Substance(s) involved or suspected (including specific product name when available)
- o Timing, duration, and mode of exposure (such as inhalation, ingestion, or cutaneous)

## · Classic symptoms of cholinergic toxicity

## Muscarinic effects

- o SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhea, Gastrointestinal upset, Emesis (literature meaning: Sludge = soft, wet soil, muddy deposit)
- o "3 Killer Bees" Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Bronchorrhea,

## Nicotinic effects

- o Nausea, vomiting, increased salivation, muscle cramping and weakness, headache, dizziness
- o Can also produce opposing symptoms to muscarinic effects, including mydriasis, tachycardia, and hypertension

## Central nervous system

- o Headache, insomnia, giddiness, confusion, dizziness, ataxia, emotional lability, slurred speech, drowsiness, seizures, unconsciousness, coma

## Laboratory

- RBC and plasma cholinesterase levels to confirm diagnosis:
- o RBC (true) cholinesterase level is best for synaptic inhibition
- o Plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase level not as reliable but more timely:
- These are markers for poisoning
- Depending on the agent and the patient, these levels may vary
- o Cholinesterase levels:
- Latent exposure: &gt;50% of normal value
- Mild exposure: 20-50% of normal value
- Moderate exposure: 10-20% of normal value
- Severe exposure: &lt;10% of normal value
- o Do not wait for cholinesterase results before administering treatment
- o CBC, electrolytes, glucose, BUN, creatinine
- o ABG when respiratory symptoms are present

## Imaging

- CXR if respiratory difficulty is present or suspect pulmonary edema:
- o Pneumonitis from hydrocarbon aspiration
- ECG
- o Dysrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes, QT prolongation)
- o Bradycardia
- o Heart block
- o ST-T-wave abnormalities
- CT scan of head for altered mental status when diagnosis is uncertain Definitive diagnosis: There is no specific assay readily available to screen for individual agents.

Suspecting the diagnosis:

- History of exposure to/contact with a cholinergic agent
- Clinical signs and symptoms of cholinergic toxicity
- Decreased red blood cell cholinesterase activity
- Symptom improvement following atropine or oxime administration

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- Mild to moderate exposure:
- o Gastroenteritis
- o Asthma
- o Venomous arthropod bite (black widow, scorpion)
- o Progressive peripheral neuropathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome)
- o Carbon monoxide
- Severe exposure:
- o Narcotic overdose
- o Coma and miosis:
- PCP, meprobamate, phenothiazine, clonidine
- Muscarinic-containing mushrooms - cholinergic crisis without nicotinic symptoms
- Nicotine poisoning
- Metabolic and infectious:
- o Ketoacidosis, sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis
- o Hypoglycemia
- o Reye syndrome
- Neurologic:
- o Cerebrovascular accident
- o Subdural or epidural hematoma
- o Postictal state

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objectives
- Maintain stability of vital signs
- Neutralize the toxic effects (on muscarinic, nicotinic and central receptors)
- Prevent or minimize the treatment-related disorders
- Prevent the recurrence intoxication
2. Critical signs
- Shock, seizures or coma, difficult breathing or respiratory failure
3. Mortality risk factors
9. o Advanced age
10. o OP poisoning: elevated lactate, low blood pH, and poor lactate clearance
11. o Hypoglycemia
12. o The insecticide of group Ia (Parathion, Methyl parathion, Aldicarb, Metamidophos)
13. o Delay from accident to emergency care

4. Outpatient management

Pre-Hospital (if patient have normal vital signs, and cooperated)

- Decontamination is initial priority:
- o Decontaminate, airway, breathing, circulation (DABC)
- o Remove all clothes (in spillover accident) and store as toxic waste (double bagged)
- o Protection of health care workers of utmost importance:
- Impenetrable gloves (neoprene, nitrile), gowns, eye protection
- o Decontaminate skin with soap and water:
- o Shower or gentle scrubbing ideal if done before entrance into the ED
- Maintain airway and oxygenate
- IV access and place on cardiac monitor
5. First line treatment

Initial Stabilization/Therapy

- Decontaminate and ABCs:
- o Decontamination and protection of staff
- o Maintain airway and oxygenate
- o For unstable airway, intubate, and ventilate (caution: succinylcholine may produce a long myorelaxant time)
- o IV access with D5W 0.9% NS
- Altered mental status: Administer thiamine, glucose, or naloxone if suspect alcoholic overdose, hypoglycemia or overdose opioids respectively.

## ED Treatment/Procedures

## Atropine:

- Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptor sites
- No effect on nicotinic receptors
- Onset of action is 1-4 min, peaks at 8 min
- Goal of therapy/end point:
- o Drying secretions of tracheobronchial tree
- Administer test dose 1-2 mg IV/IM:
- o No clinical response: Double dose q5min until muscarinic findings subside
- Dose: 1-4 mg IV q5min (peds: 0.05-0.2 mg/kg)
- Common pitfalls in therapy:

- o Not giving enough atropine
- o Using pupillary findings (mydriasis) as end point of treatment
- o Dilated pupils or tachycardia are not contraindications to atropine

## Pralidoxime (2-PAM):

- Regenerates cholinesterase by reversing the phosphorylation of the enzyme
- Synergistic with atropine - muscarinic signs/symptoms will start to resolve in 10-40 min
- 1-2 g (peds: 25-50 mg/kg) dissolved in 0.9% NS over 30 min IV; repeat in 1 hr if necessary, then q6h as needed:
- o Some propose continuous infusion (500 mg/hr) for serum concentration of 4 mg/L
- Side effects: Neuromuscular blockade with rapid infusion, respiratory arrest, HTN, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, blurred vision
- End point is resolution of muscle weakness and fasciculations
- Effective before enzyme aging occurs (permanent inactivation of cholinesterase)
- Onset of aging varies among products
- No restriction to its use even if 24-48 hr have passed

## Supportive care:

- Dermal decontamination: Remove clothes and flush skin with water
- Gastric lavage (early presentation of severe ingestion):
- o Gastric emptying with continuous suction via a nasogastric tube
- o Handle contents with care - avoid direct contact to prevent personal exposure
- Respiratory difficulty:
- o Frequent oropharyngeal suction
- o Treat bronchospasm with atropine, not bronchodilators
- o Tachycardia may result from hypoxia (pulmonary secretions and bronchospasm)
- o Atropine will dry secretions and paradoxically lower the heart rate
- o Intubate and ventilate if necessary
- o Avoid succinylcholine; may have prolonged duration as it is metabolized by cholinesterase
6. Treatment adjustment
- In case of carbamate intoxication, Pralidoxime was usually no need.
- Treat hypovolemia (from gastrointestinal losses) with IV crystalloid
- Treat vomiting with antiemetics such as ondansetron
- Vasopressors: Can be used as an adjunct to treat hypotension
- Diazepam recommended for seizure control. Phenitoine was not effective.
- Prophylaxis with diazepam has been shown to decrease neurocognitive dysfunction after OP poisoning

## 7. Algorithm (next page)

The management of organophosphate and Carbamate insecticides poisoning

<!-- image -->

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

## Pediatric Considerations

- Symptoms are difficult to differentiate in toddlers
- Common symptoms: Miosis, salivation, and muscle weakness
- Seizure activity in 25% of pediatric cases. Only 3% in adults

## Pregnancy Consideration

- Organophosphate poisoning during pregnancy can be particularly dangerous due to the potential for both maternal and fetal toxicity.
- These toxic effects can be exacerbated in pregnant women due to physiological changes during pregnancy, such as increased cardiac output and decreased plasma cholinesterase levels. Additionally, there is concern that organophosphate exposure may have adverse effects on fetal development, including birth defects and neurodevelopmental problems.
- The management of organophosphate poisoning in pregnant patients follows similar principles as in non-pregnant individuals.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Mortality rate from acute organophosphate (OP) poisoning varies between 10% and 20% and is generally due to respiratory failure.

- X. Complications
2. o Intermediate syndrome
- Symptom onset typically 1-4 days after OP poisoning
4. o Delayed polyneuropathy--
- Referred to as organophosphate-induced delay peripheral neuropathy (OPIDN)
- Onset 7-14 days after large exposures to OP
7. o Long-term effects

- Pulmonary: aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia, respiratory failure
- Cardiovascular: arrhythmias, hypotension
- Neurological: seizures, muscle fasciculations, paralysis
- Delayed sequelae

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

- Consult with psychologists for mental disorders.

Preventing accidental insecticide poisoning involves several essential measures:

- Read Labels Carefully: Always read and follow the instructions on the pesticide label. This includes proper application methods, protective equipment, and first aid measures.
- Use Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Wear appropriate PPE such as gloves, masks, goggles, and long-sleeved clothing when handling or applying insecticides.
- Store Safely: Keep insecticides in their original containers, tightly sealed, and stored in a locked cabinet out of reach of children and pets
- Avoid Mixing Chemicals: Never mix insecticides with other chemicals, as this can create toxic reactions
- Proper Disposal: Dispose of empty pesticide containers and unused chemicals according to local regulations to prevent accidental exposure.

- Ventilation: Ensure good ventilation when using insecticides indoors to avoid inhaling harmful fumes.
- In case of accidental exposure or suicidal encounter, early contact with Emergency service.

## METHANOL AND ETHYLENE GLYCOL INTOXICATION

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha

## I. INTRODUCTION

Methanol is considered toxic alcohol, due to its metabolite\_ the formic acid. It is not intended for ingestion. Methanol poisoning typically occurs from ingestion of methanol-containing substances that may include denatured alcohol, homemade or illegally produced alcohol, or commercial products. More rarely methanol poisoning may be caused by inhalation or dermal absorption.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Methanol poisoning outbreaks occur when illegally produced or homemade grain spirits are fortified with methanol due to its low cost.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), outbreaks of methanol poisoning have occurred in various countries, including Cambodia, Czech Republic, Ecuador, Estonia, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Libya, Nicaragua, Norway, Pakistan, Turkey, and Uganda. These outbreaks often result from methanol being added to these drinks, either accidentally or deliberately.

In Cambodia, methanol intoxication is a sporadic accident, from time to time the outbreaks of methanol poisoning have occurred with a few to many dozens of deaths and many more hospitalized. One of the largest outbreaks was in 2012 involving 49 deaths and 318 persons hospitalized. Many events happened after funeral ceremony in rural area when people often consume illegally produced alcohol.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Common sources of methanol:

- Wood alcohol
- Paint solvents
- Windshield washer fluid
- Inhalational abuse of carburetor cleaners
- Fuel antifreeze solutions
- Formalin (10-12% of it volume is methanol)
- Gasoline (racing car)
- Household cleaners
- Sterno® cans (cooking fuel)
- Moonshine
- Photocopying fluid
- Perfumes

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

Dose toxic

- lethal doses are not well-established and vary from person to person, generally estimated at 1-2 mL/kg of pure methanol. Doses as low as 0.1 mL/kg (6-10 mL in adults) have been reported to cause permanent blindness and death.

Toxicodynamic

- Methanol has low toxicity on its own, but is metabolized into toxic products (formic acid)
- First metabolized in liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to produce formaldehyde (slowly) which is then oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to produce formic acid (1- to 2-minute half-life) and does not accumulate most formic acid dissociates into hydrogen cation and formate anion hydrogen cation reduces pH of body fluids, resulting in acidemia.
- Formate accumulates and inhibits cellular functions by disrupting oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and decreasing production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Decrease in ATP produces effects similar to hypoxia, although tissue oxygenation may be increased with reduced cellular oxygen uptake.
- Formate is toxic to:
- o central nervous system
- o basal ganglia and subcortical white matter in untreated patients.
- o retinal and optic nerves.
- Retinal dysfunction occurs at lower formic acid concentrations than optical neuropathy
- Acidosis enhances toxicity by increasing diffusion of undissociated formic acid into cells, especially optic disc and retrolaminar section of optic nerve.
- Estimated formate elimination half-life is 1-3 hours for low concentrations and 24 hours for high concentrations.
- small amounts of methanol are excreted in urine and eliminated by lungs (due to high vapor pressure)

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## A. Clinic

- Clinical presentation is characterized by early, latent, and delayed stages.
- o Early stage of methanol intoxication usually presents with similar symptoms as ethanol inebriation, including mild euphoria, drowsiness, gastric symptoms, sedation and central nervous system (CNS) depression, and faint alcoholic odor on breath.
- o Latent period occurs after inebriation subsides and methanol is slowly metabolized to formic acid, lasting from 6-30 hours. Patients may be asymptomatic or have blurred vision during this period.
- o Delayed period begins after significant amounts of methanol have been metabolized, formate accumulates, and acidosis worsens. Serious effects of methanol poisoning begin to present. Visual disturbances and central nervous system symptoms (such as seizures) predominate.
- Gastrointestinal symptoms may include hemorrhagic gastritis or pancreatitis.
- Hyperpnea (Kussmaul respirations) may be present with severe metabolic acidosis.

## B. Investigation

- Confirmed ingestion of methanol-containing substances from patient or witness may facilitate diagnosis.
- Positive serum methanol concentrations can offer definitive diagnosis, but methanol concentrations below limit of detection cannot rule out methanol poisoning. Coingestion of ethanol or other substances may affect methanol metabolism and serum methanol levels.
- Routine toxicity evaluations are especially important in patients with incomplete or unknown histories.
- o Measure arterial pH in all patients.

- o Severe metabolic acidosis with increased osmolar or anion gaps suggests methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.
- o Arterial blood gases suggest methanol poisoning if metabolic acidosis is severe.
- o Low total carbon dioxide measurements may suggest metabolic acidosis.
- Brain imaging indicated in patients presenting with altered mental status, seizures, coma, or focal neurological abnormalities. Computed tomography is often normal within the first 24 hours of exposure.
- Nonenhanced head computed tomography findings in patients with severe methanol poisoning may include putamen hypodensity or caudate nucleus.
- Calculate anion gap = (Na+) - (Cl- + HCO3-): Normal = 8-12
- Determine serum osmol gap: Osmol gap = measured osmolality - calculated osmolarity
- Calculated osmolarity = 2(Na+) + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 + ethanol (in mg/dL)/4.6

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Few conditions other than methanol and ethylene glycol intoxication present with a profound metabolic acidosis (serum bicarbonate less than 8 mEq/L), and most of these conditions present in a characteristic fashion (e.g., status epilepticus, profound shock, ischemic bowel). other causes of elevated serum osmolar gap or anion gap, including

- diabetic ketoacidosis
- alcoholic ketoacidosis
- multiple organ failure
- chronic kidney failure
- critical illness
- spurious hyponatremia secondary to hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia
- endogenous solutes (such as amino acids during end-stage organ failure)
- exposure to some other substances.

Methanol and Ethylene glycol poisoning have some similarity as cause of severe metabolic acidosis, neurologic symptoms. Ocular toxicity from methanol is more frequent than from Ethylene glycol. The antidote treatment is the same for the two: Fomepizole or ethanol. The difference is on the toxic metabolite that is formic acid from methanol, and Glycolic acid from ethylene glycol. The onset of symptom of ethylene glycol poisoning is sooner than methanol, and ethylene glycol causes acute renal failure (from calcium depot), more frequent than methanol poisoning.

Clinical poisoning of Ethyle glycol has historically been divided into three stages, although timing may vary, and stages may overlap:

- o The first or "neurologic" stage typically begins 30 minutes to 12 hours after ingestion due to the intoxicating effects of the ethylene glycol parent compound
- o The second or "cardiopulmonary" stage begins 12 to 24 hours after ingestion. Arrythmia, multiorgan dysfunction, hypocalcemia. Most deaths occur during this stage.
- o The third or "renal" stage is often delayed 24 to 72 hours after ingestion. Renal failure, delay neuropathy

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objectives
- Block or delay methanol and ethylene glycol metabolism,
- Treat the toxic effects of formic acid glycolic acid
- Facilitate the elimination of formic acid and methanol

- Prevent and early treatment of acute kidney injury (ethylene glycol)
2. Critical signs
- Rapid and deep respiration (Kussmaul respiration)
- Blurred vision
- seizures
3. Mortality risk factors
- Severe metabolic acidosis, pH&lt; 7.2
- Coma
- Acute kidney failure
- High concentration of methanol
4. Out-patient treatment
- Transport all possibly ingested substances
- Dermal decontamination of a methanol spill by clothing removal, irrigation with soap and water
- Monitor airway and CNS depression
5. First line treatment
- Initial Stabilization/Therapy

Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs)

Dextrose, naloxone, and thiamine for altered mental status and known hypoglycemia, suspect opioids overdose or alcoholism respectively.

Prevent further methanol absorption:

- ❖ Gastric lavage with nasogastric tube: no indication
- ❖ Activated charcoal: may be use for co-ingestants.
- Ed Treatment/Procedures
- ❖ Prevent methanol conversion to toxic metabolites with fomepizole (preferable) or ethanol infusion
- ❖ Fomepizole (4-MP, Antizol®):
- o Competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
- o Indications:
- Intentional methanol ingestion OR
- Accidental methanol ingestion of more than a sip OR
- Altered mental status or visual symptoms associated with unexplained osmol gap &gt;10 mmol/L and/or elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L, serum pH &lt;7.3
- o Initiate before serum methanol level returns if intentional ingestion or more than a sip OR if serum methanol concentration is &gt;20 mg/dL
- Fomepizole Loading dose: 15 mg/kg slow infusion over 30 min
- Maintenance dose: 10 mg/kg q12h for 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h until methanol levels reduced &lt;20 mg/dL
- Dosing related to hemodialysis:
- Do not administer dose at beginning of dialysis if last dose was &lt;6 hr previously
- Administer next dose if last dose was &gt;6 hr previously
- Dose q4h during dialysis
- If time between last dose and end of dialysis was &lt;1 hr from last dose, do not administer new dose
- If time between last dose and end of dialysis was 1-3 hr from last dose, administer 1/2 of next scheduled dose

- If time between last dose and end of dialysis was &gt;3 hr from last dose, administer next scheduled dose
- o Continue until methanol level is &lt;20 mg/dL
- o Advantages:
- No need for continuous infusion
- No inebriation/CNS depression
- Ease of dosing
- No hypoglycemia, no hyponatremia, no hyperosmolality
- No checking serum concentrations
- Reduced nursing care and monitoring
- Occult methanol exposure can often be ruled out before 2nd dose is needed
- o Disadvantages:
- Blurry vision
- Transient elevation of liver function tests
- Ethanol therapy
- o Not FDA approved for treatment of methanol
- o Ethanol has greater affinity than methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase:
- Slows metabolism to formaldehyde and formic acid by competitive inhibition
- o Ethanol is the 2nd-choice antidote if fomepizole is not available
- o Initiate before methanol level returns if potentially toxic ingestion is highly suspected or confirmed by history:
- Therapeutic range is 100 mg/dL
- Oral: 50% ethanol solution (100-proof liquor) via nasogastric tube:
- Loading dose 2 mL/kg
- Maintenance dose 0.5 mL/kg/hr
- Maintenance dose during hemodialysis 1 mL/kg/hr
- IV: 10% ethanol in D5W:
- Loading dose 8 mL/kg over 30-60 min
- Maintenance infusion 2 mL/kg/hr
- Maintenance infusion during hemodialysis 4 mL/kg/hr
- o Continue until methanol level is &lt;20 mg/dL
- o Indications for ethanol therapy:
- Intentional methanol ingestion
- Accidental methanol ingestion of more than a sip OR
- Altered mental status or visual symptoms associated with unexplained osmol gap &gt; 10 mmol/L and or elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L and serum pH &lt;7.3 OR
- Serum methanol concentration &gt;20 mg/dL
- o Advantages:
- Easily accessible
- Oral and IV routes
- o Disadvantages:
- CNS depression especially in children
- Respiratory depression
- Hyponatremia or hypernatremia
- Hypoglycemia
- Hyperosmolarity
- Continuous infusion

- Frequent lab testing
- Contraindicated in pregnancy
- Pancreatitis
- Gastritis
- Folic acid and folinic acid (leucovorin):
- o Folic acid: Cofactor required for conversion of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water
- o Folic acid: 50 mg (or 1-2 mg/kg) IV q4h for 24 hr
- o Supplemental folate important in malnourished individuals (alcoholics)
- Correct acid-base abnormalities:
- o Sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis (pH &lt;7.3)
- o Sodium bicarbonate: 1-2 mEq/kg in 1 L of D5W with 40 mEq KCl at 250 mL/hr
- o The goal of the sodium bicarbonate drip is to maintain a normal serum pH
- o Full compensation (mmol) = 0.3 x body weigh x Base deficit
- Hemodialysis:
- o Decreases elimination half-life of methanol
- o Removes formaldehyde and formic acid
- o Indications:
- Ingestion of &gt;1 mL/kg of 100% methanol OR
- Ophthalmologic manifestations OR
- Severe metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L and serum pH &lt;7.3 OR
- Serum methanol level &gt;50 mg/dL alone without above criteria
- Continue hemodialysis until methanol level approaches &lt;20 mg/dL and the metabolic acidosis has resolved
6. Treatment adjustment
- Not all patients will have an elevated osmol and anion gap. Early presenters will have an osmol gap only, because methanol is osmotically active, and there are no toxic metabolites yet. Late presenters may have an anion gap only, because the osmotically active parent compound has metabolized to the toxic acidotic metabolites. Patients who are present in between will have a combination of an anion gap and an osmol gap.
- supportive therapy for methanol poisoning includes treatment with
- o IV fluids
- o sodium bicarbonate in patients with severe metabolic acidosis. Dose to give (mmol) = 0.3 x body weight (kg) x base deficit
- o antiseizure medications in patients with seizures
- o Cofactors
- In a methanol-poisoned patient, administer either leucovorin 50 mg IV or folic acid 50mg IV every six hours.
- In an ethylene glycol-poisoned patient, administer thiamine 100 mg IV and pyridoxine 100 mg IV daily.
- If toxic alcohol poisoning is possible or suspected but the exact alcohol is unknown, especially in the presence of a metabolic acidosis, it is reasonable to empirically administer all three cofactors
7. Algorithm

Approach to possible methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning when confirmatory

## toxicologic testing is not available.

Note that Fomepizole an intravenous ethanol is not available in most hospital in Cambodia, as well as measurement of blood methanol level, at least until this day (end of 2024).
