## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Unavailability of antidotes (Fomepizole, or ethanol for injection), consider ethanol oral

(usually not practical), and hemodialysis. Check the alcohol content (%) of spirit to use if medical product 50% was not available. Mind also the ingredients used in that spirit.

Severe patients (pH&lt;7.2, visual disturbance, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L) should be transferred to institution where Hemodialysis is available, and early indication should be considered.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

The prognosis in methanol poisoning correlates with the amount of methanol consumed and the subsequent degree of metabolic acidosis; more severe acidosis confers a poorer prognosis. The prognosis is further dependent on the amount of formic acid that has accumulated in the blood, with a direct correlation existing between the formic acid concentration and morbidity and mortality. Little long-term improvement can be expected in patients with neurologic complications.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- visual dysfunction (33%-40% of patients reported to have permanent visual sequelae)
- acute pancreatitis
- Parkinson-like extrapyramidal syndrome
- rare neurological complications include
- o transverse myelitis
- o pseudobulbar palsy
- o cognitive defects
- o brain hemorrhage
- myoglobinuria is rare but may lead to acute kidney injury
- fatal intracranial hemorrhage reported 46 hours after methanol poisoning from ingesting windshield wiper fluid.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- Increase public awareness about the dangers of methanol poisoning and the importance of consuming safe alcoholic beverages
- Strengthen regulations and enforcement to prevent the sale of illicit or adulterated alcohol.
- Ensure healthcare facilities are equipped to diagnose and treat methanol poisoning promptly.

## CARDIOPULMONARY ARREST BASIC AND ADVANCE CARDIAC LIFE SUPPORT

Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha , Dr. TES Sovannara , Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya

## I. DEFINITION

Cardiac arrest is the cessation of cardiac mechanical activity resulting in the absence of circulating blood flow, confirmed by the absence of a pulse, apnea or agonal breathing ("gasping") and unconsciousness. Cardiac arrest stops blood from flowing to vital organs, depriving them of oxygen, and, if left untreated, results in death.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Cardiac arrest (or cardiocirculatory arrest) in adults is a common syndrome and constitutes an absolute life-threatening emergency. It occurs most often outside the hospital and affects twice as many men as women with an average age of 60 years. The main cause is coronary ischemia through a mechanism of ventricular rhythm disturbance (ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia).

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Acute coronary syndrome (40%-77% depending on the study)
- Other cardiac and vascular etiologies
- o Rhythm disorder in ancient ischemic heart disease.
- o Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or dilated cardiomyopathy.
- o Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia.
- o Arrhythmia-conduction disorder
- Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (VF)
- Brugada syndrome
- Paroxysmal auriculoventricular (AV) block (elderly +)
- Congenital or drug-induced long QT syndromes
- Congenital short QT syndromes.
- Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
- o Congenital cardiopathy (Tetralogy of Fallot)
- o Acute myocarditis
- o Tamponade.
- o Aortic dissection
- o Massive pulmonary embolism
- o Aneurysm rupture.
- o Non-cardiovascular origins (5 to 25%): The most common are toxic, traumatic causes, acute respiratory failure or drowning.
- Risk factors associate with atherosclerotic coronary artery disease.
- o Smoking
- o Hypercholesterolemia
- o High blood pressure
- o Diabetes
- o Familial histories of coronary artery disease

- In infants and children, cardiac causes of cardiac arrest are less common than in adults. The predominant cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children is respiratory failure due to various respiratory disorders (eg, airway obstruction, drowning, infection, sudden infant death syndrome [SIDS], smoke inhalation).

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

We divide in two sections depending on whether respiratory arrest or cardiac arrest occurs first. Respiratory arrest (blood circulation continues, there is no cardiac arrest yet) lead to hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis (muscular hypoxia produces lactic acid) and then, these three conditions cause secondary cardiac arrest.

A victim may be in cardiac arrest (absence of pulse) and continue to breathe (agonal breathing).

## V. DIAGNOSIS

The diagnosis of cardiopulmonary arrest should be rapid (&lt;10 seconds), confirmed by loss of consciousness (coma), apnea or agonal breathing ("gasping"), absence of arterial pulse either in the carotid or femoral artery.

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 155 -->
[Image: illustration of a person performing rescue breathing on an unconscious individual lying on their back]
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

At the moment of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), blood and radiological investigation may be needed; like blood sugar; serum potassium; EKG (Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT); Ventricular fibrillation; Asystole; Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)), Heart ultrasound.

It is essential to diagnose the signs of aspirations of a foreign body in the respiratory tract, which includes severe stridor, dyspnea, suprasternal and intercostal retractions. It is recommended to do the Heimlich maneuver if we are suspecting aspiration.

## VI. DIFFERENCIAL DIAGNOSIS

- Coma
- Syncope
- Seizure
- opiate overdose

## VII. MANAGEMENT

## 1. Objective

- o To maintain an open and clear airway (A).
- o To maintain breathing by external ventilation (B).
- o To maintain blood circulation by external cardiac massage (C).

## 2. Warning signs of sudden cardiac arrest (But often has no warning)

- o Chest pain,
- o Sweating,
- o Shortness of breath,
- o Palpitation or Dizziness

## 3- Mortality risk factors of cardiac arrest

- o History of cerebrovascular disease
- o Higher lactate and presence of PEA or asystole.
- o Being aged 45-60 years old.

## Basic life support (BLS) for adult

BLS for adults focuses on doing several tasks simultaneously. In many situations, more than one person is available to do CPR. This choreographed method includes performing chest compressions, managing the airway, delivering rescue breaths, and using the automatic external defibrillation (AED), all as a team. By coordinating efforts, a team of rescuers can save valuable seconds when time lost equals damage to the heart and brain.

## B) Defibrillation

## i. Patient selection

- Shockable rhythms: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and Pulseless Ventricular tachycardia (VT)
- Unshockable rhythms: Asystole or PEA

Defibrillation is contraindicated for sinus rhythm, conscious patient with a pulse, or when there is danger to the operator or other (e.g., from a wet patient or wet surroundings).

## ii. Equipment

There are two types of defibrillation's waveforms: monophasic and biphasic. The amount of energy required for successful defibrillation is typically lower with biphasic waveforms.

Manual defibrillators require a manual analysis of the patient's cardiac rhythm, as well as manual delivery of the shock through paddles or self-adhesive pads by the operator.

Automated external defibrillators (AED) may be fully or semi-automated. Fully automated external defibrillators will analyze the rhythm automatically, and if indicated, charge and deliver the shock, whereas semi-automated external defibrillators will require an operator to manually deliver the shock after analysis and charging.

## iii. Patient positioning and skin preparation

Ensure that scene is safe for performing defibrillation including water and environmental scene dangers such as traffic. The patient should be in the supine position with ongoing CPR. To avoid skin burns, remove all metallic objects, jewelry, or medication patches (wipe off any residue). If there is excessive chest hair over the areas where the pads or paddles are to be placed, quickly shave the hair off to ensure a good contact with skin. Remove all direct sources of oxygen to avoid fire.

## a) Placement of pads/paddles

There are several possible positions for the placement of the pads or paddles:

- Antero apical position: place one paddle/pad to the right of the upper half of the sternum, just below the patient's right clavicle, and place the other pad just below and to the left of the left nipple. With a female patient, place the

paddle/pad just below and to the left side of the breast. Do not place it over the breast.

- Anteroposterior position: Place one pad/paddle at the left lower sternal border and the posterior pad/paddle below the left scapula
- Pacemakers automated implantable cardiac defibrillators, and other implants: such devices are implanted under the skin and palpable on examination. Ensure that the placement of the pads is at least four fingerbreadths away from such devices.

## iv. Step-by-step technique

- ❖ Manual defibrillation
- a. Prepare the patient and equipment as described earlier. CPR should be ongoing.
- b. If using paddles, attach the rhythm monitoring electrodes. Alternatively, the paddles may be applied to the chest directly in "quick look" mode to read the rhythm.
- c. If pads are used, the rhythm will be read by the pads, and additional rhythm electrodes are not necessary.
- d. Interrupt chest compressions only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) to analyze the rhythm manually.
- e. Confirm that the rhythm is ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, then resume CPR immediately.
- f. Select the appropriate energy level. For biphasic defibrillators, select according to the manufacturer's recommendation (150 to 200 J for biphasic truncated exponential waveforms and 120 to 200 J for rectilinear biphasic waveforms). If the recommendation is unknown use the maximum energy available. For monophasic defibrillators, begin with an initial 360-J shock. If starting with less than the maximum energy, consider escalation of shock energy for failed shocks or recurrence of fibrillation.
- g. Ensure that the defibrillator is in unsynchronized mode.
- h. If using paddles, apply the paddles and charge. CPR should NOT be interrupted during charging. All other personnel may begin to stand clear at this point.
- i. Call out, "Stand clear," and ensure that no one is in contact with the patient or trolley. CPR is interrupted only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) at this point.
- j. With the CPR interrupted, quickly confirm the rhythm remains shockable, then deliver the shock. The operator's eyes should be back on the patient at the time of shock delivery, to ensure safety.
- k. Resume CPR immediately once the shock has been delivered. Do NOT pause to check the pulse or reanalyze the rhythm at this time.
- l. Continue management according to the local resuscitation protocol.
- ❖ Automated external defibrillation (AED)
- a. Prepare the patient and equipment as described earlier. CPR should be ongoing.
- b. Turn on the automated external defibrillator (follow the voice prompts according to your device).

- c. Open the package containing the defibrillation pads with the attached cable and connector. With the chest prepared, carefully pull off the protective backing from the pads and apply the pads to the chest, taking care to avoid air pockets. The pads should be placed at least 2 inches away from any automated implantable cardiac defibrillators.
- d. Initiate analysis of the rhythm. This may be automatic or require pressing a button to activate analysis. Ensure that there is no movement of the patient during analysis, including a brief interruption of CPR.
- e. If a shock is advised, the device will automatically charge to a preset energy level. If a semi-automated external defibrillator is used, CPR should immediately resume while charging. All other personnel may begin to stand clear at this point. Note that fully automated defibrillators do not require the operator's input to discharge a shock, and all rescuers should stay clear at the time of charging. Follow the voice prompts of the device.
- f. Call out, "Stand clear," and ensure that no one is in contact with the patient or trolley. CPR is interrupted only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) at this point.
- g. Deliver the shock.
- h. Resume CPR immediately once the shock has been delivered. Do NOT pause to check the pulse or reanalyze the rhythm at this time.
- i. Continue management according to the local resuscitation protocol.
- j. There are increasing numbers of automated external defibrillators that provide CPR "guidance" in the form of metronome beats or active feedback on the correct rate and depth of chest compressions in real time. Achieving optimal CPR quality increases the likelihood of successful defibrillation.

## v. Risks and precautions

Electrical energy can terminate an abnormal rhythm, but if inappropriately delivered, it may also induce ventricular fibrillation. This can happen if the electric shock is delivered during the relative refractory period of the cardiac electrical cycle. Movement artifacts or loose leads may resemble ventricular fibrillation and result in an inappropriate shock. New defibrillator technology is available that can filter compression or movement artifacts to "see through" the artifacts to reveal underlying rhythm. However, when using automated external defibrillators, all manufacturers currently still recommend stopping all compressions and patient movement (e.g., during transport) before initiating rhythm analysis.

## H: HYPOVOLEMIA OR HEMORRHAGE

History of fluid or blood loss may be available. Rectal examination can identify massive lower GI bleeding; nasogastric intubation can identify massive upper GI bleeding; and bedside FASTcan diagnose massive intraperitoneal bleeding. Treat with fluids and blood products.

## H:HYPOXIA

Hypoxia occurs with lack of oxygen and alveolar ventilation. Make sure that the airway adjunct is placed correctly. Check breath sounds at intervals to ensure that the endotracheal tube has not slipped out of the trachea or to identify pneumothorax. Verify the source of oxygen—an oxygen cylinder or the piped oxygen supply.

## H:HYPOTHERMIA

Trymn nw   nn n wrm IV fluids. If there is no recovery of consciousness in the hypothermic patient following ROSC, maintain a body core temperature of 33°C until further assessment and decisions can be made.

## H: HYDROGEN ION (ACIDOSIS)

The acidosis of cardiac arrest is a combination of respiratory and metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis is addressed by early endotracheal intubation and alveolar ventilation. Metabolic acidosis can be somewhat addressed by good-quality CPR. Sodium bicarbonate can be administered for severe metabolic acidosis from prolonged or poor initial resuscitation, at a dose of 1 to 1.5 mEq/kg. Half the initial dose can be readministered after10 to 15 minutes, depending on pH. However, data currently do not support routine administration of sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, with no controlled studies demonstrating improved hemodynamics with sodium bicarbonate.62 If administered, ventilatory rate should be increased to counteract the increased CO₂ produced by sodium bicarbonate. Continuous venovenous hemodialysis may be required for severe acidosis.62

## H: HYPER-OR HYPOKALEMIA, OTHER METABOLIC DISORDERS

Suspect hyperkalemia in patients on hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis (look for presence of arteriovenous fistula or dialysis catheter). Other metabolic disorders are extremely difficult to confidently identify in cardiac arrest. If hyperkalemia is suspected, administer calcium chloride, os   oi,   s  ss psi  is ucit i in  si cic Fab fragments (Digibind®).

## T: THROMBOSIS (PULMONARY EMBOLISM)

## T: CORONARY THROMBOSIS

Pulmonary embolism causing cardiac arrest requires fibrinolysis or embolectomy. However, the diagnosis is rarely made at time of collapse, and even then, most systems are not geared to make such prompt diagnosis and initiate the necessary procedures for embolectomy. Fibrinolytic agents could be considered during cardiac arrest from suspected pulmonary embolism on a case-by-case basis.7² A single-center case series of patients with diagnosed pulmonary embolism suffering PEA arrest found that rapid administration of alteplase 50 milligrams IV to be safe and effective, with 20 of 23 patients demonstrating ROSC.73-75 High-quality compressions should be continued after thrombolytic therapy is administered, with several studies recommending 60 to 90 seconds of compression after the drug is given. Factors suggestive of pulmonary embolism causing cardiac arrest include two of three signs or symptoms (prearrest respiratory distress, altered mental status, or shock); arrest witnessed by a physician or emergency medical technician; and PEA as the first or primary arrest rhythm.

## T: "TABLETS" (DRUG OVERDOSE)

Drug overdose is rarely identified as a cause of cardiac arrest during the resuscitation process. In the event of antidepressant overdose, administer IV sodium bicarbonate. Lipid emulsion infusion may be useful in cardiac arrest associated with cyclic antidepressants or local anesthetics. β-Blocker or calcium channel-blocker overdose may require high-dose insulin therapy and lipid emulsion infusion.

## T: CARDIAC TAMPONADE

Cardiac tamponade is best identified during resuscitation by bedside transthoracic US. This requires brief interruption of chest compressions. Treatment of tamponade causing cardiac arrest is bedside pericardiocentesis.

Acute coronary thrombosis or acute myocardial infarction is one of the most common causes of cardiac arrest. Risk factors are a history of coronary artery disease and initial rhythm of VF/VT.63-67 Cardiac catheterization after resuscitation is an underused procedure.67A 12-lead ECG in the immediate post-cardiac arrest state can identify an ST-segment elevation acute myocardial infarction and allow arrangements for immediate corona oo  og s o o  trr percutaneous coronary intervention following cardiac arrest.68 The 2015 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines1 provide a class I recommendation to activate the cardiac catheterization laboratory in patients with OHCA with ST-segment elevation acute myocardial infarction on ECG. Thus, after ROSC, especially in the face of post-ROSC ECG evidence of acute myocardial infarction, advocate for cardiac catheterization and percutaneous coronary revascularization if available and appropriate. A few case reports describe fibrinolysis during CPR with resultant ROSC and good neurologic outcome.69 Coronary angiography is reasonable in select patients with suspected cardiac origin of arrest but without ST elevation or in those electrically unstable patients without ST-segment elevation with suspected cardiovascular lesions. The absence of ST-segment elevation on postarrest ECG does not exclude acute coronary thrombus, as approximately one third of patients without ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction on postarrest ECG demonstrate a culprit lesion on angiography.7º Reports are too few to determine whether thrombolysis together with CPR results in more severe bleeding than thrombolysis without CPR.71

## T: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX

Suspect tension pneumothorax duringcardiac resuscitation if breath sounds are unequal on chest auscultation after verifying correct endotracheal tube placement. Treatment is immediate needle decompression.

## VIII. Special case

## 1- BLS for children (Age 1 to puberty) and Infant (Newborn to age of 12 months

## Children/ Infant

- For Child: Use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum in the middle of the chest. Put your other hand on top of the first hand. Straighten your arms and press straight down. Compressions should be about two inches (5 cm) into the child's chest and at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

For infant: Place 2 or 3 fingers of one hand on the sternum in the middle of the nipple line. Press straight down. Compressions should be 1.5 inches (4 cm) into the infant's chest (or about 1/3 the diameter of the chest) and at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

- Be sure that between each compression you completely stop pressing on the chest and allow the chest wall to return to its natural position to make CPR less effective.
- After 15 compressions, stop compressions and open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin or jaw thrust (neck injury is suspect)
- Give a breath while watching the chest rise. Repeat while giving a second breath. Breaths should be delivered over one second.
- Resume chest compressions. Switch quickly between compressions and rescue breaths to minimize interruptions in chest compressions.
- Attach the AED when it becomes available. Use pediatric pads for infant and children under the age of 8 and less than 55 pounds (25 kg). place the pads in an anteriorposterior position if they would overlap on the front of the chest.
- Listen to the AED and perform the steps as directed.

In the event of ventricular fibrillation, use a weight-based energy dose of 2 to 4 J/kg body weight for monophasic or biphasic devices. ## 2- Resuscitation in pregnancy

## a. Resuscitation step

The best maternal care provides the best fetal care, so follow general principle of resuscitation when treating the pregnant woman.

- To accommodate the increase in blood and plasma volume that develops during the pregnancy, make sure that the volume of resuscitation fluids increases by 50% above that required by the non-pregnant patient.
- Place 2 large-bore IVs above the diaphragm level and provide rapid infusion of isotonic saline or ringer lactate. Volume must be adequately replaced before considering vasopressor, especially in pregnancy. Select the vasopressor by desired effects in the mother and least harmful effects on the fetus.
- Place the patient to full left tilt position.

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 168 -->
[Image: A pregnant woman lying on her back on a hospital bed, with her legs slightly bent and feet bare, covered with a light blue blanket. She has an IV line in her left arm and is connected to medical equipment, including monitors and an oxygen tank. The room appears to be an intensive care unit or emergency department, with various medical devices and supplies visible in the background.]
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

## b. Airways changes affecting intubation.

In the pregnant patient, the incidence of Mallampati class III airways increase making intubation more difficult associated with weight gain in pregnancy, this contributes to the likelihood of a difficult airways.

## Adjunctive airways equipment and patient preparation:

- Smaller sized endotracheal tubes
- A gum elastic bougie
- A short laryngoscope handle, and a stylet readily available.
- Pre-oxygenation (&gt;95%)
- Pace the patient to supine position manually displace the uterus to the left. Elevate the head and the shoulder with a pillow.

## c. CPR and defibrillation in pregnancy

Cardiopulmonary arrest in pregnancy is broken down in 2 categories: Before and after fetal viability. Typically, the onset of fetal viability varies between 22 and 26 weeks. By 20 weeks the uterus fundus is palpable at the umbilicus; Then from the 20 weeks to 32 weeks, the fundus height (in centimeters) approximates the gestation age. If the fundus height is at or below the umbilicus, resuscitation effort should focus on the mother with no modification of CPR. If the uterus fundus is palpable above the umbilicus, one person should provide manual left lateral displacement of the uterus while another is performing CPR.

According to current advance life support guidelines, Perform defibrillation at recommended adult dose.

| Ephedrine                                                          | Hypotension related to spinal anesthesia or unresponsive to fluids                                                                                    | Class C. Multiple reports of use during anesthesia-related hypotension in pregnancy. Maintains uterine blood flow. May cause dose-dependent increase in fetal acidosis, tachycardia, and abnor- mal variability in fetal heart rate (indicative of fetal stress), or an increase in metabolic activity. |
| Phenylephrine                                                      | Hypotension related to spinal anesthesia or unresponsive to fluids                                                                                    | Class C. Superior to ephedrine for management of hypotension after spinal anesthesia with a decrease in fetal acidosis.14                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Vasopressin                                                        | No longer recommended for cardiac arrest                                                                                                              | Class C. There are no controlled data in human pregnancy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

## IX. Evolution and prognosis

Survival rates vary significantly; favorable factors include:

- Early and effective bystander-initiated CPR. The American Heart Association (AHA) estimates that the survival rate for cardiac arrest is estimated to be around 50% in cases, where the CPR is administered within 3-5 min. However, this survival decreases by 7-10% with each minute that defibrillation is delayed.
- Witnessed arrest.
- In-hospital location (particularly a monitored unit)
- Initial rhythm of ventricular fibrillation (VF) or ventricular tachycardia (VT)
- Early defibrillation of VF or VT
- Post resuscitative care, including circulatory support and access to cardiac catheterization.
- **** Out hospital cardiac arrest (60%-80%)

## X. Complications

- Neurologic dysfunction
- Brain injury
- Disorder of consciousness
- Neurocognitive deficits
- Changes in quality of life

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

## Lifestyle Changes to Prevent a Heart Attack

- Stop smoking and limit alcohol.
- Choose good nutrition: Vitamin, mineral, fiber, low calories.
- Control LDL cholesterol level (&lt;70 mg/dL) and Triglyceride level at the normal value is considered good for your heart health.
- Control your blood pressure regularly.
- Manage diabetes.
- Exercise regularly and weight control
- Get enough sleep and reduce stress.

## ACUTE METABOLIC COMPLICATION OF DIABETES MELLITUS, HYPEROSMOLAR HYPERGLYCEMIA STATE

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya,

Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha

## I. DEFINITION

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS, also known as hyperosmotic hyperglycemic nonketotic state [HHNK]) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia but no ketoacidosis. Each represents an extreme in the spectrum of hyperglycemia.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Diabetes prevalence has increased significantly worldwide, leading to a higher incidence of diabetes-related complications. This trend is observed across all regions, with low- and middleincome countries experiencing the most rapid rise. Common acute complications include diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). These conditions are more prevalent in type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes under certain conditions.

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Hyperosmolar state precipitated by factors that:
- o Impair peripheral insulin action
- o Increase endogenous or exogenous glucose
- o Decrease patient's ability to replace fluid loss
- Infection (esp. pneumonia and UTI) most common precipitating factor
- Other precipitating causes include:
- o Inadequate therapy/medication omission
- o Sepsis
- o Medications/drugs:
- Diuretics
- β-blockers
- Calcium channel blockers
- Atypical antipsychotics
- Corticosteroids
- Sympathomimetics
- Phenytoin
- Cimetidine
- Amphetamines
- Ethanol
- o Myocardial infarction
- o CVA
- o Renal failure

- o Heat stroke
- o Pancreatitis
- o Appendicitis
- o Intestinal obstruction
- o Endocrine disorders
- o Pregnancy
- o Trauma
- o Burns

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The pathophysiology that gives rise to HHS requires that three interrelated elements be present: insulin deficiency, renal impairment, and cognitive impairment.

- Relative insulin deficiency is the fundamental defect in HHS. Patients have sufficient insulin to inhibit ketone body formation but not enough to prevent hyperglucagonemia, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis. The resulting hyperglycemia induces osmotic diuresis, with resultant fluid and electrolyte losses.
- typical patients with HHS are old. Their renal blood flow and GFR are reduced, and they cannot readily excrete a glucose load. When they become hyperglycemic, the glucose is neither metabolized nor excreted. It remains in the extracellular fluid space. The resulting increase in osmolality, together with the decreased GFR, causes still less glucose to be excreted.
- Hyperglycemia leading to hyperosmolality normally activates thirst. The combination of mild diabetes and azotemia does not lead to HHS unless the affected individual does not drink sufficient water to prevent hyperosmolality.

Together, these three factors produce dehydration and the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. The severe dehydration that occurs is due to the osmotic diuresis of glucose in the absence of compensatory free water intake. Dehydration, in turn, leads to hemoconcentration, setting the stage for severe prerenal azotemia, thrombosis, and shock.

Moreover, hyperglycemic crises are proinflammatory states that lead to generation of reactive oxygen species and oxidative stress. Proinflammatory factors returned to near-normal levels within 24 hours of insulin therapy and resolution of hyperglycemia.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

- 1) Clinic
- History
3. o Progression of signs and symptoms typically occur over days to weeks
4. o Polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss
5. o Dizziness/weakness/fatigue
6. o Decline in mental state
7. o Blurred vision
8. o Leg cramps
- Physical Exam
10. o Dehydration
11. o Tachycardia
12. o Sunken eyes
13. o Hypotension

- o Orthostasis
- o Dry mucous membranes
- o Decreased skin turgor
- o Collapsed neck veins
- o Coma/lethargy/drowsiness
- o Decreased urinary output - late finding
- o Seizures/focal neurologic deficits
- o Concurrent precipitating medical illness

## 2) Investigation

- Diagnostic criteria:
- o Serum glucose ≥600 mg/dL (usually &gt;1,000 mg/dL)
- o Minimal ketosis
- o pH ≥7.30, HCO3 ≥15 mEq/L
- o Effective serum osmolality &gt;320 mOsm/kg:

## Serum osmolality = 2 × Na + + glucose in mg/dL/18

BUN not included because it is freely permeable between fluid compartments

- Lab
- o Broad testing indicated to evaluate hyperosmolar syndrome and identify precipitating causes
- o Electrolytes:
- o K+ may be elevated even in the presence of total body deficit owing to shift from intracellular space to extracellular space
- o Mild anion gap metabolic acidosis owing to lactic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid, or renal insufficiency

Sodium corrected for hyperglycemia:

## Corrected [Na+] = [Na+] + 0.016 × [(glucose in mg/dL) - 100]

- o BUN, creatinine:
- o Venous blood gas (VBG) or arterial blood gas (ABG
- o Serum ketones, β-hydroxybutyrate, and lactate level if pH &lt;7.3 or significantly elevated anion gap to evaluate mixed acid-base disorder
- o Serum osmolarity
- o CBC, blood culture
- o Lipase: 3× upper limit of normal is diagnostic for pancreatitis
- o Urinalysis: Check for ketones/glucose, UTI
- o Magnesium, calcium, phosphate

## · Imaging

- o CXR to evaluate for possible underlying pneumonia
- o Head CT: When indicated for altered mental status or with focal neurologic deficit

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- If acidosis or significant anion gap present, must determine cause (i.e., ketosis, DKA, lactic acidosis, [hypoperfusion, sepsis, or postictal], or other causes of metabolic acidosis)
- Alcoholic and fasting ketoacidosis
- Anion gap acidosis

- Metabolic encephalopathy
- Mixed disorder of HHS and DKA present in up to 33% of patients
- Differentiate HHS from DKA

| DKA                                                   | HHS                                          |
|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Precipitant factors                                   | Precipitant factors                          |
| Noncompliance with insulin treatment                  | Noncompliance with treatment                 |
| Infection                                             | Infection                                    |
| New -onset (type1) diabetes                           | New-onset (type2) diabetes                   |
| other                                                 | Other (corticoids, excess diuretics, etc..)  |
| Course of illness                                     | Course of illness                            |
| Rapid (in general < 24hs)                             | Insidious (days)                             |
| Clinical finding                                      | Clinical finding                             |
| Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, hypovolemia        | Polyuria, dehydration, hypovolemia           |
| Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain                      | Depressed mental status up to coma           |
| Fruity odor of breath, Kussmaul respiration           | Fruity odor of breath, Kussmaul respiration  |
| Diagnostic laboratory Criteria                        | Diagnostic laboratory Criteria               |
| Blood glucose > 200-500 mg/dL*                        | Blood glucose > 540-600 mg/dL*               |
| AND elevated ketones in blood or urine                | AND serum osmolality > 320mmol/kg            |
| AND metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and HCO3 < 18 mmol/L) | No significant ketosis No metabolic acidosis |
| Concomitant Laboratory Abnormalities                  | Concomitant Laboratory Abnormalities         |
| Elevated anion gap                                    | Variable anion gap                           |
| Low C-peptide                                         | Normal C-peptide                             |
|                                                       | Acute kidney injury                          |

* For conversion of blood glucose concentrations in mg/dL to mmol/L, divide by 18. The numbers are the highest reported blood glucose cutoff for both diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. In patients at risk-taking sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, pregnancy, excessive alcohol use, decreased caloric intake, chronic liver disease-ketoacidosis may develop in the absence of elevated blood glucose concentrations (euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis).

## VII. MANAGEMENT

The best treatment for HHS is prevention.

- 1) Objectives
- correction of the fluid and electrolyte abnormalities that are typically present and
- the administration of insulin
- find and treat the triggering cause
- 2) Critical Signs
- Shock
- Coma
- Hypokalemia
- Very high serum osmolarity

- 3) Mortality Risk factors
- Prognosis is worse for elderly patients and
- patients in whom coma and hypotension are found.
- 4) Outpatient management
- Check glycemia, give water to drink if possible.
- HHS is an acute condition and may be life threatening, patient should be checked and treat in hospital.
- 5) First-line treatment
8. o Secure airway in comatose patients
9. o Cardiac monitor and 18G IV
10. o Naloxone, thiamine, and blood glucose for Altered mental status, when suspect the corresponding cause.
11. o Restore hemodynamic stability with IV fluids 0.9% NS 1-2 L over the first hour.
- Frequent reassessment of volume and mental status Serum levels of Na + , K + , PO4 - do not accurately reflect the total body solute deficits or the

Initial Stabilization/Therapy: ABCs:

intracellular environment. Repeat electrolyte and glucose levels hourly.

- Search for a precipitating event. Mortality/morbidity of HHS usually secondary to inciting cause
- Fluids:
- o Begin resuscitation with 0.9% NS 1-2 L over 1-2 hr to restore intravascular volume and achieve hemodynamic stability
- o Fluid loss avg 20-25% body weight or 100-200 mL/kg
- o Calculate total body water (TBW) deficit using corrected serum sodium:

## Total Body Water deficit = 0.6 × weight (kg) × (1 - 140/corrected Na + )

- o Average fluid deficit is 8-10 L
- o Replace 50% of the fluid deficit over the next 12 hr
- o After initial resuscitation use NSS if serum sodium is low, 1/2 NS if serum sodium is elevated/normal or patient is hyperosmolar.
- o Add D5 to fluid to when serum glucose is &lt; 250 mg/dL
- Potassium:
- o Anticipate hypokalemia:

## Total body deficit of ∼5-10 mEq/kg body weight (replace over 3 d)

- o Begin potassium repletion after urine output is established. Do not start in anuric patients or if initial K + level is &gt;5 mEq/L
- o 1g Kcl = 13.4 mEq K + 13.4mEqCl = 27mEq
- o If the initial K + is normal (4-5 mEq/L), give 20-30 mEq KCl in the first L of fluids, then give 20 mEq/hr
- o If the initial K + is low (3-4 mEq/L), give 40 mEq in first L
- o If serum K + is &lt;3 mEq/L hold insulin and give 10-20 mEq/hr until K + &gt;3.3, then add 40 mEq to each liter
- o Follow repeat serum K + levels q1-2h and adjust treatment accordingly
- Insulin:
- o No role in the early resuscitation

- o Earlier use of insulin may cause rapid correction of hyperglycemia with collapse of the intravascular space, hypotension, and shock or hypokalemia precipitating dysrhythmias
- o Some patients will not require insulin
- o Use insulin as sole therapy in patients with fluid overload (i.e., acute renal failure)
- o Begin only after achieving hemodynamic stability and evaluating for hypokalemia:
- o Do not use unless serum K+ &gt;3.3 mEq/L
- o SC/IM insulin not recommended due to erratic absorption
- o Titrate drip to optimally decrease serum glucose by 50-90 mg/dL/hr. More rapid correction places the patient at risk for developing cerebral edema
- o Decrease drip rate by 1/2 when serum glucose &lt; 250 mg/dL
- o Adjust insulin drip to maintain serum glucose between 150-200 mg/dL
- o Insulin: Begin with 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr; modify after assessing clinical response
- Phosphate:
- o Routine replacement not recommended
- o If serum levels &lt;1 mg/dL, give 20-30 mmol potassium phosphate over 24 hr
- o Monitor serum calcium levels closely
- o Potassium phosphate IV:
- Phosphorous serum level &lt;0.5 mg/dL: 0.5 mmol/kg IV infused over 4-6 h
- phosphorous serum level 0.5-1 mg/dL: 0.25 mmol/kg IV infused over 4-6 h
- o Potassium phosphate PO:
- Phosphorus 250 mg per tablet and potassium 1.1 mEq per tablet
- Magnesium:
- o 0.35 mEq/kg magnesium in fluids for first 3-4 hr (2.5-3 g MgSO4 in 70 kg patient). Caution in ARF.
- o MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate): 50% (5 g/10 mL; dilute to at least 20% before IV use)
- Anticoagulation:
- o Arterial thrombosis may complicate hyperosmolar state: Consider SC heparin as prophylaxis
- o Remain vigilant to detect thrombotic complications (e.g., MI, pulmonary embolus, mesenteric ischemia).

## 6) Treatment adjustments

Insulin used without concomitant vigorous fluid replacement increases the risk of shock.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- Geriatric Considerations: Most commonly seen in elderly type II diabetics who experience a stressful illness that precipitates worsening hyperglycemia and reduced renal function
- In the elderly, 30-40% of cases are associated with the initial presentation of diabetes
- Pediatric Considerations: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic states (HHS) rare in pediatric patients.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Overall mortality for HHS is estimated at 5-20% [7] and is usually due to the underlying illness that caused the hyperglycemic crisis. The prognosis is worse for elderly patients and patients in whom coma and hypotension are found. This is in contrast to the mortality rate of DKA, which is estimated to be about 1-5%.

## X. Complications

- Hypotension (insulin shifts glucose from interstitial compartment to intracellular accompanied by water may precipitate hypotension and shock)
- Cerebral edema (Rapid reduction of glucose concentration is a major contributor to the development of cerebral edema.
- Non cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- For diabetic patient, the elderly, the chronically ill, and institutionalized populations are at increased risk for HHS. Any living situation or comorbidity that prevents adequate hydration, including for example immobility, advanced age, debility, dementia, agitation, impaired thirst response, restricted access to water, and restraint use, place these patients at risk.
- Patient education focused on encouraging adherence to blood glucose monitoring and compliance with prescribed medications coupled with adequate follow-up to establish a durable diabetes management regimen.
- Sick days management (many factors lead to hypoglycemia, or hyperglycemia)
- Review with nursing home staff the importance of adequate fluid intake and close monitoring of hydration status in patients with diabetes.
- Avoid medications that interfere with effectiveness of insulin

## TRAUMATISM IN ADULT

Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya

## I. DEFINITION

Traumatism = A morbid condition of a system owing to an injury or a wound.

Traumatic injuries can range from minor isolated wounds to complex injuries involving multiple organ systems. All trauma patients require a systematic evaluation to maximize outcomes and reduce the risk of undiscovered injuries. Life-threatening injuries must be immediately stabilized before moving along the primary survey. A primary survey should be repeated whenever the patients' status deteriorates.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), road traffic injuries accounted for 1.25 million deaths in 2014, and trauma is expected to rise to the third leading cause of disability worldwide by 2030 1 . Over 45 million people globally sustain moderate to severe disability each year due to trauma 2 . Outside areas of armed conflict, penetrating injuries are responsible for fewer than 15 percent of traumatic deaths worldwide. Approximately half of traumatic deaths result from central nervous system (CNS) injury, while a third result from exsanguination.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Variety of causes including:

- Penetrating trauma
- Motor vehicle and motorcycle accidents
- Falls from height.
- Assault (including domestic violence)
- Mass-casualty events (including terrorism)
- Burns

High-risk patients: Extremes of age, pregnancy, bleeding disorders (including potent antiplatelet or anticoagulant use), GCS &lt;14, abnormal vital signs, dangerous mechanism.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Particular mechanisms predispose patients to specific injuries.

Certain high-risk blunt mechanisms, have been associated with greater morbidity and mortality including:

- pedestrians struck by automobiles,
- motorcycle accident.
- severe motor vehicle accidents, and

1 Global Status on Road Safety 2015, World Health Organization, http://www.who.int/violence\_injury\_prevention/road\_safety\_status/2015/ (Accessed on April 04, 2016)

[2 World Health Organization. Global burden of disease. www.who.int/healthinfo/global\_burden\_disease/en/](http://www.who.int/healthinfo/global_burden_disease/en/)

(Accessed on May 01, 2010)

- falls greater than 6m.

Any hypotensive trauma patient is at risk for development of hemorrhagic shock, a common cause of postinjury death.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

In general, severely injured patients (especially those with unstable vital signs) with a potential need for acute surgical intervention should be transported immediately to the nearest major trauma center.

Triage to major trauma center per EMS/SAMU protocol.

A primary survey should be performed at the scene and upon ED arrival.

- a. Clinic and investigations

The protocol Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) provides a standardized approach to trauma including rapid assessment and treatment. This protocol consists of following steps:

- Preparation
- Triage
- Primary survey (ABCDEs)
- o Resuscitation
- o Adjuncts to primary survey &amp; resuscitation (eFAST, blood type, Ht…)
- Secondary survey (Head to toe Evaluation)
- o Adjuncts to secondary survey (Xray, CT scan.)
- Continued post resuscitation monitoring and reevaluation
- Definitive care (to OR, or ICU.)

The primary and secondary surveys should be repeated frequently.

In the actual clinical situation, many of these activities occur in parallel or simultaneously.

## Signs and Symptoms

## Primary survey (ABCDE):

Airway (with cervical spine precautions):

- o Assess and stabilize the airway before moving to the next step in the primary survey.
- o Maintain C-spine precautions throughout
- o Indicators of airway patency: Clear speech or effectively/silently moving air
- o Indicators of airway obstruction: Gurgling, stridor, snoring, choking, or no air movement

## Breathing:

- o Assess and stabilize breathing before moving to the next step in the primary survey.
- o Indicators of effective breathing: Symmetric chest wall rise/fall, equal bilateral breath sounds, normal resp rate, and O2 saturation.
- o Indicators of ineffective breathing: Asymmetric or minimal chest movement, unequal breath sounds, abnormal resp rate or O2 saturation
- o Tension pneumothorax: Suggested by unilateral decreased breath sounds, tracheal shift (to opposite side), hyper expansion, hyperresonance to percussion, subcutaneous air, hypoxia, and/or hemodynamic compromise
- o Hemothorax: Suggested by decreased breath sounds and/or dullness to percussion Circulation:
- o Assess and stabilize circulation before moving to the next step in the primary survey.
- o Assess HR, BP, pulse quality, and end-organ (e.g., mentation, capillary refill, urine output); when abnormal, assume internal hemorrhage.

## Disability:

- o Assess and stabilize disability before moving to the next step in the primary survey.
- o Assess level of consciousness, gross motor and sensory function, pupillary size/reactivity
- o Glasgow Coma Scale is commonly used; score of ≤8 indicates severe head injury/coma.
- o Spinal cord injuries: Grossly assess for lateralization of motor/sensory deficits.
- o Assess brainstem function via pupillary size and reactivity to light.

## Exposure:

- o Undress completely, then warm passively

## Secondary survey:

- Performed after the primary survey.
- Complete physical exam from head to toe
- "Finger in every orifice"

## History

Key features: Initial clinical presentation, mechanism of injury, suspected injuries, and treatment rendered should be elicited from EMS/SAMU personnel, family, and bystanders. Motor vehicles collision (MVCs): Note approximate speed of all vehicles, impact point, location of patient in vehicle, seatbelt use, passenger space intrusion, steering column damage, or extrication by EMS/SAMU.

AMPLE history: Allergies, medical/surgical issues, past medical, last oral, events leading up to trauma. (Discuss tetanus status if stable)

## Physical Exam

- See Signs and Symptoms
- Stabilize simultaneously during assessment.

## Essential Workup

- Primary and secondary surveys
- Critically ill patients: Activate trauma team, rapid transfusion and lab/imaging standby.
- Point of care (POC) US (e-FAST)

- Portable radiographs include AP chest, AP pelvis, and lateral cervical spine.
- Computed tomography: Only when hemodynamically stable or adequately stabilized.
- Use evidence-based clinical decision rules (e.g., NEXUS, Canadian) to avoid unnecessary imaging.

## Diagnostic Tests and Interpretation

Lab

- POC Hgb serially if hemorrhagic shock
- POC glucose if altered mental status.
- Blood type, CBC, coagulations, blood gas, lactate, renal function, lipase, and Urine analysis for major trauma patients
- Pregnancy test in all females of childbearing age
- Consider cardiac enzymes to rule out cardiac injury.

## Imaging

- Significant chest trauma requires objective evaluation of the lungs, heart, and great vessels with e-FAST, CXR, CT, angiography, and/or thoracotomy.
- Blunt abdominal trauma requires objective evaluation using e-FAST followed by abdominal CT or exploratory-laparotomy:
- o If free fluid on e-FAST
- o Hemodynamically stable: CT with IV contrast
- o Hemodynamically unstable: Exploratory lap

For head trauma, CT is recommended if prolonged loss of consciousness, amnesia, persistent altered level of consciousness, or severe head ach or vomiting.

For cervical spine fractures: CT is highly sensitive.

Pan CT scan, (head, neck, chest, abdomen/pelvis in a single pass with IV contrast) lower missed injury rate but significant radiation exposure

- Suspected spine injuries (with neuro deficits): emergent MRI
- Extremity injuries:
- o Plain films identify most fractures (aside from scaphoid, hip, tibial plateau, talus, etc.)
- o Suspected vascular injury: Duplex US or CT angiography.

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Consider medical conditions leading to trauma (e.g., stroke, seizures, dysrhythmias, and suicide attempt)

## VII. MANAGEMENT

## 1- Objectives

Rapid assessment, rapid treatment to maintain vital signs. Treat as early as possible the derangement that may threaten the victim life. Not left behind or overlook any lesion incurred by trauma. Get the definitive treatment early.

- 2- Critical signs

Trauma with unstable vital signs, altered mental status, combined head-chest trauma, head trauma plus other bleeding lesion. Spinal trauma with neurological signs or cervical spinal lesion.

## 3- Mortality risk factor

Mechanism of trauma (pedestrian hit by car, high speed motor vehicle accident, fallen from height &gt; 6m, blast injury, penetrating wound, high velocity projectile or fragments etc) Multiple lesions, age extremities, victims were under anticoagulant treatment, medical condition of victims.

## 4- Out-patient management

Any patient of remarkable trauma or accidents should be assessed in ER. A presumed minor head injury or minor chest trauma may overlook a progressively develop severe lesions.

- 5- First line treatment

## a. Initial Stabilization/Therapy

- Primary survey: Immediately stabilize any serious injuries once identified:
- o Airway (with cervical spine precautions):
- Use jaw thrust, suction, oropharyngeal vs. nasopharyngeal airways, and/or McGill forceps.
- Rapid sequence intubation: the preferred technique in major trauma; consider ketamine or etomidate to minimize peri-intubation hypotension.
- Video laryngoscopy may allow endotracheal intubation with minimal impact on traumatic brain or unstable cervical spine injuries.
- Failed airway: Extra glottic device (e.g., laryngeal mask airway) or cricothyroidotomy.
- o Breathing:
- 100% oxygen and respiratory monitoring
- Pre-oxygenation: 8 deep breaths or 3 min of tidal volume
- Tension pneumothorax: (Diagnosed clinically) emergently decompress with needle thoracostomy followed by tube thoracostomy.
- Hemothorax: Tube thoracostomy (28F) is usually indicated, if massive hemothorax consider autotransfusion and thoracotomy in the OR.
- Open chest wounds: Cover with a 3-sided adherent dressing and consider tube thoracostomy.
- Flail segment, pulmonary contusion, burns: Treat respiratory distress with mechanical ventilation (use low tidal volume + PEEP for lung protection)
- o Circulation:
- Place on a cardiac monitor.
- Obtain IV access (ideally 2 large-bore peripheral IVs; alternatives include intraosseous lines, central lines, or venous cut down)
- Control external bleeding with direct pressure or tourniquets temporarily.
- Crystalloid fluid bolus (10-20 cc/kg) is controversial (e.g., allow permissive hypotension)
- Replace lost blood with blood products in 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC, FFP, and platelets. (CE, plasma frais congelé, plaquette)
- Treat unstable pelvic fractures with pelvic binding.
- Consider giving tranexamic acid (TXA) to all patients with hemorrhagic shock, as part of a massive transfusion protocol.
- Pericardial tamponade:

- Stable: Emergent pericardiocentesis window

- Unstable; thoracotomy
- Penetrating chest trauma and witnessed arrest: Consider thoracotomy (if an available surgeon); see "algorithm" below.
- o Disability:
- If Glasgow Coma Scale score of ≤ 8 + head injury: Treat elevated intracranial pressure with mannitol or hypertonic saline, controlled ventilation (ideal PCO2 30-35 mm Hg), and elevating head to 30 degrees (while maintaining spine immobilization)
- Intracranial bleeding or spinal cord injury: Obtain neurosurgical consultation; high-dose steroids are generally not recommended.

## b. Emergency department Treatment/Procedures

Emergency department Treatment/Procedures

- Definitive treatment may require emergent surgery or interventional radiology.
- Prompt stabilization, early recognition of the need for operative intervention, and appropriate surgical consultation are paramount.
- Re-evaluation is key to identify occult/delayed injuries.

## Medication

- Dictated by need for specific interventions.
- TXA (Tranexamic acid) must be given before transfer/arrival to a trauma center in order to meet the time requirement of early administration. The dose is 1 gram of tranexamic acid IV bolus over 10 minutes, followed by 1 gram IV over 8 hours.
- Consider short-acting, hemodynamically neutral medications.
- Consider prophylactic antibiotics in penetrating trauma.
- Ensure an updated tetanus status.

## c. Disposition

Admission Criteria

- Many major trauma patients are routinely admitted for observation, monitoring, and reevaluation.
- Patients with significant injuries or hemodynamic instability should be admitted to the OR/ICU.
- Patients requiring frequent assessments should be admitted to a monitored setting.
- 6- Treatment adjustment \_Pearls and pitfalls
- In general, severely injured patients (especially those with unstable vital signs) with a potential need for acute surgical intervention should be transported immediately to the nearest major trauma center.
- The ABCs of trauma remain the standard approach to the initial assessment and treatment in major trauma.
- Life-threatening injuries must be immediately stabilized before moving along the primary survey.
- A primary survey should be repeated whenever the patients' status deteriorates.
- A high level of suspicion for occult injuries should be maintained, with a low threshold for observation and/or advanced imaging.
- Ensure an updated tetanus status.

## 7- Algorithm

Unless obvious signs of death are present in the field, providers in most emergency medical systems continue to transport patients without pulse or respiration to a hospital once cardiopulmonary resuscitation has been initiated.

For patients in traumatic arrest upon arrival to the ED, a critical decision must be made regarding the appropriate level of intervention and, specifically, the use of emergent thoracotomy.

The strongest recommendation for performing ED thoracotomy can be made for patients with penetrating chest trauma with witnessed signs of life during transport to or in the ED and at least cardiac electrical activity upon arrival. There were no survivors among patients with blunt trauma and no respiration or pulse in the field. ED thoracotomy for this group is not indicated (including in the presence of myocardial electrical activity).

ALS= advanced life support

Adapted from Truhlar AJ, Deakin, CD, Soae J, et al: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines for Resuscitation 2015. Section 4. Cardiac arrest in special circumstances. Resuscitation 95: 148-201, 2015.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

## · Elder patients

Assume that older patients involved in trauma have sustained a significant injury, even if they appear well. The paradox of elder trauma patients is that their physiology and medical interventions can both mask and exacerbate the severity of injuries. Medications are but one example: beta blockers may mask the effects of shock by suppressing tachycardia, while warfarin and other anticoagulants increase the risk of severe hemorrhage.

## · Victims of crime

Clinical evaluation and treatment of injuries is the foremost responsibility of the clinician caring for a trauma patient. When possible, caretakers should consider and act on the need to preserve potential evidence if the trauma may be connected to a crime. As examples, placing removed clothing into paper bags, avoiding cutting through holes in clothing created by penetrating injuries, and careful documentation of injuries may all be significant.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

There are notable disparities in mortality rates for injured patients around the world. For example, one study looked at the mortality rates for all seriously injured adults (injury severity score of 9 or more) in three cities, in countries at different economic levels. The mortality rate (including both pre-hospital and in hospital deaths) rose from 35% in a highincome setting to 55% in a middle-income setting, to 63% in a low-income setting. Considering only patients who survive to reach the hospital, a similar study demonstrated a sixfold increase in mortality for patients with injuries of moderate severity (injury severity score of 15-24). Such mortality increased from 6% in a hospital in a high-income country to 36% in a rural area of a low-income country.

In addition to an excess mortality, there is a tremendous burden of disability from extremity injuries in many developing countries. By comparison, head and spinal cord injuries contribute a greater percentage of disability in high income countries. Much of the disability from extremity injuries in developing countries should be eminently preventable through inexpensive improvements in orthopedic care and rehabilitation.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

Complications of trauma management may arise from some special situations.

Common pitfalls and ways to avoid them:

Esophageal intubations -

Between 0.5 and 6 percent of prehospital intubations are esophageal due to airway difficulty or displacement during transport. Verify the position of all endotracheal tubes either by direct visualization or use of an end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) detector.

Hemorrhagic shock -

Approximately 30 percent of the circulating blood volume may be lost before the onset of hypotension. A transient response to one or more fluid boluses means the patient likely has ongoing hemorrhage and is in a persistent state of shock. A high index of suspicion should be maintained and an aggressive search for the source of ongoing hemorrhage is warranted.

Cardiac tamponade -

Assume that elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) in a trauma patient is caused by pericardial tamponade. However, hypovolemic patients with tamponade may not have elevated JVP. Perform the FAST exam early in the circulation evaluation of the unstable patient and begin by looking at the heart.

Thoracoabdominal injury -

Assume that any penetrating wound of the thorax or abdomen involves both compartments until proven otherwise.

Penetrating bowel injury -

During the initial resuscitation, injuries caused by low velocity penetrating wounds (typically stab wounds) are easily missed by ultrasound, because there is too little intraperitoneal blood to be detected, and by CT, because there is inadequate tissue destruction. For stab wounds, high clinical suspicion may warrant further evaluation by laparoscopy, laparotomy, or diagnostic peritoneal tap despite initially negative imaging studies. Alternatively, a trauma surgeon may opt to perform serial observations of patients with abdominal stab wounds (and some extraperitoneal gunshot wounds) over a 12- to 24-hour period.

Gunshot wounds typically require therapeutic laparotomy and should be distinguished from the aforementioned stab wounds - these high velocity injuries are associated with a much greater morbidity and mortality than their low velocity counterparts.

Open book pelvic fractures -

The unstable pelvis should not be manipulated multiple times; additional manipulation exacerbates hemorrhage. Once suspected, open or unstable pelvic fractures should be stabilized using a pelvic binder, or a sheet if no binder is available. If the patient is hemodynamically stable, computed tomography (CT) imaging is obtained. The unstable patient requires either surgery or angiography.

Ocular injuries -

Periorbital swelling and ecchymosis do not preclude performing an ocular examination. Patients with such findings are at higher risk of ocular injury. In addition, injuries such as a globe rupture or retro-orbital hematoma must be diagnosed quickly in order to maximize the opportunity to salvage vision.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

Improved safety standards and programs to minimize injury from vehicular-related events (motor vehicle, motorcycle, bicycle, pedestrian), working places, falls, violence, sports, and recreation provide best prevention against Traumatic injuries.

Wear helmet while riding two wheelers.

Do have access to seat belts and air bags while driving. Take good care of children to avoid injuries.

Do not drive under the influence of alcohol and drugs.

Maintain safe living areas for seniors.

## INITIAL MANAGEMENT OF HEAD TRAUMA

Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. Kruoch Sophallida, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak

## I. DEFINITION

Head trauma is a broad term describing an external trauma to the craniofacial area of the body from blunt, penetrating, blast, rotational, or acceleration-deceleration forces. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is often categorized into mild (Glasgow Coma Scale score, 1315), moderate (GCS score, 9-12), and severe (GCS score, 3-8), but this actually represents a spectrum of injury. Patients with a presentation GCS score of 13-15 who are stable or improving are unlikely to have CT scan findings that warrant intervention

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

The most common principal mechanisms of injury for all age groups includes falls, being struck by or against an object, and motor-vehicle crashes in the civilian population. Gunshot wounds (GSWs) to the head are particularly lethal; the overall mortality rate is estimated to be 90%, with 70% of deaths occurring at the scene. TBIs in Cambodia are on the rise, 34% occur during 5-9pm and 40% during the weekend; while the vast majority is 74% occur as the result of road traffic accidents of which 81% are motorcycle related. Skull fracture is the most common diagnosis, where frontal lobe hematomas most commonly involved, resulting the ratio of subdural to epidural is 1:1.05 1 .

## III. ETIOLOGY

Direct injury. Direct head trauma occurs when the head is struck, or its motion is suddenly arrested, by an object. The resulting damage to the skull and brain depends on the consistency, mass, surface area, and velocity of the object striking the head. Direct injury can also be caused by compression of the head.

Indirect injury. In indirect brain injury, the cranial contents are set into motion by forces other than the direct contact of the skull with an object. A common example is an acceleration- deceleration injury in which no direct mechanical impact is sustained, but the cranial contents are set into vigorous motion. As the bridging subdural vessels are strained, subdural hematomas (SDHs) may result.

Besides these two patterns of head injuries, there are more causes such as: penetrant head trauma, scalp wounds, skull fracture (linear fractures, depressed fractures and basilar fractures), extra-axial injury (epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, subdural hygroma) and intra-axial injury (diffuse axonal injury, cerebral contusion, intracerebral hematoma and intracerebellar hematoma).

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Cerebral hemodynamics and increased intracranial pressure The brain has an extremely high metabolic rate, accounting for approximately 20% of the entire oxygen consumption of the body and requiring approximately 15% of total cardiac output. Hypertension, alkalosis, and hypocarbia promote cerebral vasoconstriction, whereas hypotension, acidosis, and hypercarbia cause cerebral vasodilation. Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) defines by: CCP = MAP - ICP

1 Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30790736/

If CPP falls below 40 mm Hg, autoregulation is lost and cerebral blood flow (CBF) declines, resulting in tissue ischemia and altered cerebral metabolism. Avoidance of hypotension or elevation in ICP in the head- injured patient helps ensure that CPP can be maintained. The recommended target CPP value is between 60 and 70 mm Hg. Cushing reflex

Progressive hypertension associated with bradycardia and diminished respiratory effort is a specific response to acute, potentially lethal increases in ICP. This response is called Cushing reflex or Cushing phenomenon, and its occurrence indicates that the ICP has reached life- threatening levels. However, only one- third of cases of life- threatening increased ICP manifest the full triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## Physical examination:

In the setting of head trauma and suspected brain injury, management should be guided by the principles of trauma resuscitation. A primary survey focusing on airway, breathing, and hemorrhage control should be performed expeditiously. After immediate life threats are adequately addressed, a secondary survey should evaluate for underlying head injury, brain injury, and neurologic compromise.

Acute Neurologic Examination:

The goals of the acute neurologic assessment of head trauma patients include detection of life- threatening injuries and identification of neurologic changes in the immediate posttrauma period. An efficient neurologic examination in the emergency setting includes evaluation of mental status, GCS score, pupillary size and responsiveness, and motor strength and symmetry.

## Investigations

Laboratory tests: Routine laboratory tests are generally not needed for patients with isolated mild TBI in the acute setting, except for a bedside glucose test in patients with altered mental status and determination of the blood alcohol level in patients suspected of alcohol intoxication and head trauma. Suspicion of systemic pathology as the cause of the head trauma, such as when a diabetic patient sustains an moto vehicle collision (MVC) after losing consciousness from hypoglycemia, warrants directed testing for culprit conditions. Coagulation studies are indicated in patients with coagulopathies (e.g., hemophilia, Von Willebrand disease), suspected liver disease, and those on anticoagulants.

## Neuroimaging

Skull radiography: skull radiography after head trauma has long been replaced by cranial CT, which is the cornerstone of imaging for acute head trauma. Skull radiographs for adults with either mild or severe TBI are not recommended.

Computed tomography: Noncontrast CT of the head is the diagnostic standard for identifying intracranial injury in the ED. This scan delineates acute intra- axial and extraaxial bleeding, cerebral swelling, ischemic infarction caused by hypoxia after trauma, evidence of increased ICP, and pneumocephalus. It is sensitive for demonstrating mass effect, ventricular size and configuration, bone injuries, and acute hemorrhage, regardless of location (i.e., parenchymal, subarachnoid, subdural, or epidural spaces).

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

In the context of trauma, conditions presenting with an altered loss of consciousness (LOC) include seizures, intoxication with alcohol or drugs, and systemic trauma resulting in hypoxemia or hypoperfusion. Sedatives or motor function may be altered by neuromuscular blocking agents administered prior to ED arrival. Head trauma may result in confounding injuries to other parts of the head or neck, including skull or facial bone fractures, cervical spine or spinal cord injuries, eye injuries, otolaryngeal injuries, and damage to blood vessels within the neck. LOC can be also caused by stroke, spontaneous acute subdural hematoma, cerebral aneurysms, brain metastasis, hydrocephalus, or Alzheimer disease.

With age, the brain atrophies and creates more space within the cranial vault for blood to accumulate, so older adults can have significant hemorrhage and not show signs of deterioration.

## VII. MANAGEMENT

## Out- of- Hospital Care

The out- of- hospital management of the head- injured patient should focus on preventing or minimizing secondary brain injury specifically on the major systemic insults of hypotension, hypoxia and hypocarbia. Interventions should be aimed at maintenance of oxygenation and prevention of hypocarbia through appropriate airway management, supplemental oxygen as needed, and controlled ventilation. Hypotension should be avoided through directed fluid resuscitation and control of hemorrhage.

## Emergency Department Management

Airway: The airway should be secured early to protect against aspiration and prevent secondary brain injury as a result of hypoxia or hypercarbia.

Hypotension: Systemic hypotension has profound implications for neurologic outcomes. As such, fluids or blood transfusion should be delivered to maintain a blood pressure as close to normal as possible, with a SBP of at least 110 mm Hg for those 15 to 49 and over 70 years of age, and at least 100 mm Hg for those 50 to 69 years old.

Brain- directed osmotic therapies should be reserved for patients with signs of transtentorial herniation or progressive neurologic deterioration not attributable to extracranial causes. If there are signs of impending herniation syndrome, such as deepening coma, a newly asymmetric pupil, or other substantially diminishing neurologic parameters, osmotic diuretics, such as mannitol is recommended.

Hyperventilation: hyperventilation was recommended as a method to reduce ICP. However, this reduction in ICP is accomplished by reducing CBF, which is important in meeting the brain's metabolic demands. A low Paco2, and the resulting lower CBF, may result in cerebral ischemia, whereas high Paco2 levels can result in cerebral hyperemia and high ICP. Normal ventilation is currently the goal for severe TBI patients in the absence of cerebral herniation, and Paco2 should be maintained in the normal range of 35 to 45 mm Hg.

Cranial decompression: In patients with impending herniation who do not respond to firstline therapies, cranial decompression may temporarily reverse or arrest the herniation syndrome.

## (*) Risk factors:

- Severe headache
- Persistent altered mental status/acting abnormally
- Abnormal neurology
- Suspected child abuse
- Palpable skull fracture
- Signs of base of skull fracture
- Non-frontal scalp hematoma (occipital, parietal or temporal) in child &lt;2 years
- Severe mechanism
- Post-traumatic seizure
- Loss of consciousness
- Persistent vomiting
- Known bleeding disorder/anticoagulation
- Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
- Neurodevelopmental disability

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Mild Traumatic Brain Injury and Sports- Related Concussion: Athletes with a concussive head injury should be immediately removed from play and not return until they have been evaluated by a health care provider with expertise in concussion management. There should be a gradual stepwise increase in physical activity. Anticoagulated patients: there is a higher incidence of intracranial bleeding in TBI patients on anticoagulants following head trauma, with an incidence of up to 22% in patients. patients taking anticoagulation with intracranial lesions should be managed with reversal of anticoagulation like vitamin K or fresh frozen plasma, where patient with a negative initial head CT scan do not need to have their anticoagulation reversed.

Head trauma in older adult: older patients have increased morbidity and mortality from TBI and have higher rates of intracranial injuries following head trauma The presence of comorbid medical conditions, use of anticoagulants, preexisting cognitive deficits, polypharmacy, alcohol consumption, and unique physiology of the aging brain make it challenging for the emergency clinician to detect brain injury.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

The ultimate survival and neurologic outcome of the brain-injured patient depends on the extent of TBI occurring at the time of injury (primary injury) and the subsequent effects of systemic insults (secondary injuries), such as those caused by hypotension and hypoxia. Thus, clinical care of patients with TBI emphasizes early management to minimize the occurrence of secondary brain injury. Emergency clinicians can influence the incidence and severity of primary brain injury through injury prevention programs.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

The complications of head trauma are divided into two main outcomes: Central Nervous System Infections: meningitis after basilar fractures (caused by variety of microbes but early meningitis within 3 days injury of CSF usually caused by Pneumococci), brain abscess (after penetrant injury) and cranial osteomyelitis.

Medical complications: Disseminated intravascular coagulation, respiratory complication and cardiac dysfunction.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

All patients with moderate to severe head trauma require imaging to determine the extent and nature of the brain injury and necessity of neurosurgical intervention. Neurosurgical consultation should be obtained as soon as possible to help direct the patient's subsequent management.

In patients with persistent symptoms of headache, confusion, or memory difficulties, delayed MRI may define lesions in the regions related to cognition that cannot be seen on CT. Although not useful in the emergency setting, MRI has prognostic value during subsequent care and assists in directing the future rehabilitation of these patients
