DIC: disseminated intravascular coagulation; FFP: Fresh Frozen Plasma; PCC: prothrombin complex concentrate; RBCs: red blood cells; TTP: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; VWF: von Willebrand factor.

* 450 mL blood and 63 mL citrate-phosphate-dextrose (CPD) anticoagulant-preservative solution.

## IV. EFFECTS OF MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE (OTHER THAN HYPOVOLEMIA)

Changes Occurring as a Result of Massive Hemorrhage

- the lethal triad in trauma includes coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia
- acute coagulopathy of trauma-shock
- o also known as trauma-induced coagulopathy, acute traumatic coagulopathy, acute coagulopathy of trauma, trauma-associated coagulopathy.
- o may occur within 30 minutes of severe injury - prior to red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and fluid resuscitation
- o tissue injury from trauma or surgery leads to local and subsequent systemic release of tissue factor leading to initiation of coagulation pathway and massive disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
- o hypoperfusion due to massive hemorrhage leads to expression of thrombomodulin in endothelial cells and formation of thrombin-thrombomodulin complex, resulting in
- activation of protein C, leading to inactivation of factor Va and VIIIa, and enhancement of fibrinolysis by consumption of plasminogen activator inhibitor and increase in plasmin formation
- inactivation of thrombin-activatable inhibitor (TAFI), leading to further hyperfibrinolysis
- o The acute coagulopathy of trauma shock is a disease entity similar to or same as DIC with fibrinolytic phenotype, with possible exception that trauma-shock uniquely activates the thrombomodulin and protein C pathway.
- acidosis
- o initial appearance may indicate tissue hypoperfusion further contributes to coagulopathy due to:
- change in platelet shape at pH &lt; 7.4
- inhibition of thrombin generation at pH &lt; 7.1
- acceleration of fibrinolysis
- hypothermia
- o defined as core body temperature &lt; 35 degrees C

- o may occur in patients having trauma or elective surgery as a result of abnormal thermoregulatory control due to general anesthesia and opening of body cavities
- o effects include abnormal platelet function and coagulopathy, enzyme inhibition, and fibrinolysis
- Exacerbation of Coagulopathy as a Result of Massive Transfusion
- dilution of clotting factors and platelets due to transfusion of red blood cell (RBC) units
- acidosis may occur due to normal saline administration and toxicity from citrate present as anticoagulant in stored blood products
- hypothermia as a result of administration of fluids below body temperature
- hypocalcemia from citrate in storage solution that contributes to decrease in plateletrelated activities
- severity of coagulopathy is modified by patient-related factors including
- o age
- o comorbidities
- o inflammation
- o genetic background
- o premedication (especially oral anticoagulants)
- o pre-hospital admission fluid administration

## V. EVALUATION

Findings commonly associated with bleeding patients requiring future massive transfusions include ≥ 1 or more of the following:

- INR &gt; 1.5
- systolic blood pressure &lt; 90 mm Hg
- hemoglobin (Hb) &lt; 11 g/dL (&lt; 110 g/L)
- Base deficit (BD) ≥ 6 mEq/L (≥ 6 mmol/L)
- positive focused assessment for the sonography (FAST) of trauma
- heart rate ≥ 120 beats/minute

Routine assays include hematocrit (Hct), Hb, platelet count, and assays for coagulopathy (including prothrombin time [PT], activated thromboplastin time [aPTT], INR, and fibrinogen measurement).

Viscoelastical hemostatic assays, including thromboelastography and rotational thromboelastometry, are emergency room or bedside point-of-care assays that use whole blood within minutes of collection, and therefore have shorter turn-around time compared to routine assays.

Complications of massive transfusion include transfusion-related lung injury (TRALI), transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), transfusion reactions, and electrolyte abnormalities

## VI. MANAGEMENT

- The ultimate goal of massive transfusion is to maintain sufficient circulation and hemostasis in patients with massive hemorrhage.
- In an emergency, provide group O red blood cell (RBC) and AB plasma until patient blood type is determined and patients can receive crossmatched RBC and AB-compatible plasma.
- Massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should be implemented to optimize management and delivery of blood products.

## VII. MASSIVE BLOOD TRANSFUSION (MBT) PROTOCOL

MTPs may involve predetermined ratio-driven transfusion or goal-directed transfusion protocols or combination of both, but most current MTPs use ratio-driven transfusion protocol followed by goal-directed strategy as laboratory information becomes available.

## General Concepts

- massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should facilitate communication between departments and services to deliver rapid clinical care
- MTPs may involve ratio-driven transfusion or goal-directed transfusion protocols or combination of both, but most current MTPs use ratio-driven transfusion protocol
- MTPs should include
- o timing and personnel involved in the activation of MTP notification of start and stop of protocol to transfusion service and laboratory
- o definition of laboratory testing parameters used to predict need for massive transfusion blood product preparation and delivery, including predetermined transfusion packages
- o patient identification protocol to avoid ABO incompatible transfusion errors
- o other patient care needs (for example, blood warmers)
- American College of Surgeons Trauma Improvement Program (ACS TQIP) recommendations
- o during early stages of resuscitation, transfuse universal red blood cell (RBC) and plasma in a ratio between 1:1 and 2:1
- o once laboratory data are available, use goal-directed resuscitation
- o transfusion may be discontinued or downgraded to goal-oriented transfusion if bleeding is under control
- Task Force of Advanced Bleeding Care in Trauma recommendations
- o for initial management of patients with expected massive hemorrhage 1 of 2 following
- o strategies should be considered
- fresh frozen plasma (FFP) in a plasma:RBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed
- Fibrinogen concentrate and RBC
- o switch to goal-directed strategy as laboratory information becomes available; goals for various blood components
- transfuse RBC to maintain Hb &gt; 7-9 g/dL (70-90 g/L) (ABC-T Grade 1C)
- FFP
- transfuse FFP to maintain prothrombin time (PT) and activated thromboplastin time (aPTT) &lt; 1.5 × normal control or if viscoelastic hemostatic assay results suggest coagulation factor deficiency
- avoid use of FFP in patients without major bleeding or for treatment of hypofibrinogenemia
- administer fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate if significant bleeding associated with viscoelastic signs of functional fibrinogen deficiency or plasma fibrinogen level &lt; 150 mg/dL (1.5 g/L)
- transfuse platelets to maintain platelet count &gt; 50 × 10 9 /L or &gt; 100 ×10 9 /L in patients with ongoing bleeding or traumatic brain injury.
- coagulation factor concentrates

- if used, treat based on routine laboratory coagulation testing and/or viscoelastic evidence of functional coagulation factor deficiency.
- prothrombin complex concentrate may be indicated for bleeding patients with delayed initiation of coagulation as evidenced by viscoelastic monitoring.
- consider monitoring factor FXIII activity and if deficient, supplement in patients who are bleeding

## Ratio-driven Transfusion

- uses predetermined ratio of red blood cells (RBCs), plasma, and platelets
- administration of fixed ratio of RBC to plasma to platelets at 1:1:1 (initially proposed by the United State military and subsequently used in both military and civilian settings, with rationale that is more closely resembles whole blood)
- more commonly incorporated in MTPs than goal-directed transfusion
- treats coagulopathy early in resuscitation (&lt; 6 hours of admission) while decreasing use of crystalloids and RBCs
- no delay in preparation and delivery of blood products
- may be discontinued or downgraded to goal-oriented transfusion if bleeding is under control

## Goal-directed Transfusion

- uses laboratory results and clinical findings to guide blood product administration choices, volumes, and timing until target test values are achieved.
- requires use of laboratory tests that are timely and provide enough information on patient coagulation profile.
- viscoelastical hemostatic assays such as thromboelastography (TEG) or rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) results may be helpful in guiding transfusion

## Special Populations

Obstetric Hemorrhage

- for patients with major obstetric hemorrhage, consider ratio-driven transfusion (for example, 6:4:1 ratio of RBC to plasma to platelet units)
- hyperfibrinolysis is common; monitor closely for fibrinogen level and consider early transfusion of fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate
- tranexamic acid administration may decrease blood loss at the time of cesarean section and risk of progression to severe obstetric hemorrhage
- fibrinogen level &lt; 200 mg/dL independently associated with severe bleeding Pediatric Patients
- having pediatric patient-specific MTP may be beneficial but could be logistically difficult to create in institutions without free-standing children's hospital
- data on successful management of massive transfusion in children and neonates is limited, and optimal transfusion protocol is not clear.

## Patients in Surgical Settings

- American Society of Anesthesiologists suggests use of MTP implemented by individual institution.

- consider that patients having cardiac surgery may have had preoperative administration of anticoagulants or antiplatelets, and on-pump heparin that may also contribute to impaired hemostasis.

## Patients in Combat Settings

- administration of fixed ratio of RBC to plasma to platelet at 1:1:1 initially proposed by the United States military and continues to be used in both military and civilian settings
- administration of fresh whole blood is used in cases when apheresis platelet products are not available
- o transfusion-transmitted infections and transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease may be a concern

## Monitoring

- termination of transfusion with blood products if further transfusion is futile
- discontinuation of ratio-driven massive transfusion or downgrade to goal-oriented transfusion if either
- o surgical bleeding has been controlled
- o radiographic or physiologic indication of bleeding control after angioembolization
- discontinuation of goal-oriented blood product transfusions based on laboratory test values (including routine laboratory tests and/or viscoelastical hemostatic assays) if patient is not actively bleeding and still in the acute resuscitation phase.

Guide to Laboratory Target Values for Goal-Directed Transfusion*

| Test                                  | ABC-T target Value                                   | ACS TQIP Target Values   | Case transfusion                          |
|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Hemoglobin level                      | ≥7-9g/dL                                             | ≥ 10g/dL                 | RBCs                                      |
| Prothrombin time                      | <1.5xNormal                                          | < 18seconds              | Plasma                                    |
| Activated partial thromboplastin time | <1.5xNormal                                          | < 35seconds              | Plasma                                    |
| Platelet count                        | >50x10 9 or >100x10 9 if ongoing bleeding and/or TBI | >150x10 9 /L             | Platelets                                 |
| Fibrinogen level                      | ≥150 mg/dL                                           | > 180 mg/dL              | Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate |

* ACS TQIP: American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program,

ABC-T, Task force for Advanced Bleeding Cared in Trauma

## VIII. COMPLICATIONS OF MBT

1. complications arising from rapid transfusion of large volume of fluids during massive transfusion include:
- exacerbation of coagulopathy
- metabolic complications--
4. o complications due to citrate in blood product storage solution include
- hypocalcemia - neonates and patients with liver disease may be at higher risk
- acidosis\_may be more sever and difficult to treat in patients with liver failure who cannot metabolize citrate to bicarbonate or process lactate
- metabolic alkalosis occurs as a result of increase in blood pH as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate.

- hypomagnesemia - due to transfusion of magnesium poor solutions in addition to citrate overload
- o hyperkalemia
- due to increase in potassium concentration as a result of red blood cell (RBC) membrane (adenosine triphosphatase) ATPase pump inactivation and hemolysis of RBCs in storage and/or irradiation
- neonates, patients with cardiac and renal insufficiency and tissue injury at higher risk
- o hypokalemia due to
- restoration of RBC membrane ATPase pump and potassium uptake by RBCs
- release of aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, and catecholamines
- co-transfusion of low potassium solutions such as platelets, plasma, and crystalloids
- o hypothermia
- due to rapid infusion of blood products in cold storage
- infants and neonates at higher risk
- o transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) - acute lung injury that occurs within 6 hours of transfusion and not related to other causes of acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome
- o transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)
- hydrostatic pulmonary edema
- patients with cardiac disease and infants at higher risk
2. Other complications arising from transfusion of blood products include
- allergic reaction
- hemolytic transfusion reaction (acute and delayed)
- febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction
- transfusion-related immunomodulation
- transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease
- posttransfusion purpura
- infection
- air embolism

## IX. PROGNOSIS

- Mortality reported in
- o 39% of patients having ≥ 10 red blood cell (RBC) units during hospital stay (2.6% of all patients with trauma)
- o 57% of patients having ≥ 50 units of blood products in first 24 hours (0.6% of all patients with trauma)

## I. DEFINITION

ACS is the clinical spectrum of unstable ischemic heart disease ranging from unstable angina (UA), Non-ST segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) to STEMI depending upon the degree and acuteness of coronary occlusion.

STEMI is ACS with persistent ST-segment elevation or new left bundle-branch block.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- Most recent data from WHO in 2019, ischemic heart disease (IHD) was the principal cause of death (62,22 per 100 000 population) in Cambodia.
- In Cambodia:
- o Primary PCI rate: 78%

- o Mean age: 59,71 years
- o Female: 26,3%
- o In-hospital mortality: 11,14% (PCI: 4,7% vs non-PCI: 15,73%)

## III. ETIOLOGY

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) cause by the rupture or erosion of atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries, leading to the formation of blood clots that block blood flow partially or completely.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

STEMI reflects transmural necrosis caused by acute thrombotic occlusion and longer duration of a coronary artery.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## 1. Clinical

- Symptom:
- o Chest pain Ischemic-type (Angina): retro-sternal, intense, at rest, longer (&gt;30min), irradiate to jaw and neck, trinitro-resistant.
- Physical finding:
- o Vital sings: BP, HR, SpO2
- o Heart sounds: Third heart sound (LV dysfunction), Systolic murmur (mechanical complication)
- o Lung: rales (heart failure)

## 2. Investigation

- ECG: ST segment elevation &gt; 2mm in 2 contiguous leads or a new onset LBBB in the resting ECG
- Cardiac Biomarkers- should not delay to wait for results for reperfusion therapy
- Echocardiography-if available

## VII. MANAGEMENT

## 1. Objectives

- "Time is muscle"- Every patient with STEMI should have the occluded artery reopened (reperfusion therapy) as soon as possible after the onset of symptoms.

Primary goal of STEMI management is to reduce the risk of death and the extent of permanent cardiac injury associated with MI.

## 2. Critical sign

- Shock (cool extremities, altered mental status, moist skin, weak pulse)
- Heart failure (orthopnea, jugular venous distension, pulmonary edema)
- Cardiac arrhythmia (sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, bradyarrhythmia)
- High bleeding risk patient (elderly, CKD with eGFR&lt;30ml/min, cirrhosis, cancer, previous stroke, previous bleeding transfusion &lt;6months, long-term oral anticoagulation)

## 3. Mortality risk factor

- Killip classification: Using physical examination and the development of heart failure to predict and stratify risk of mortality
- TIMI risk Score for STEMI: to evaluate strategy risk, in-hospital adverse events and outcome of STEMI patient. It shows strong predicted with mortality at 30 days

All STEMI patient is recommended to hospitalization. 5.First-

## line treatment

## A. STEMI &lt; 12hours:

## i. Pre-hospital:

- Antalgic: Morphine 5-10mg SC or IV
- On-going chest pain: Nitroglycerine sublingually or oral spay
- Transfer with Emergency medical services (EMS) by full monitoring: oximeter, scope vital signs monitor
- Aspirin 250mg-500mg IV or PO (absence contraindicated)
- Thrombolysis: (see details in iii.a)

## ii. Arrival Cardiac Care Unit (CCU):

- Strictly bed rest
- Monitoring with ECG 18 derivations
- G5% 500ml + 2gKCL/24h
- Blood test: CBC, groupage rhesus, electrolytes, glycemia, cardiac enzyme (CK-MB &amp; Troponin T or I), Creatinine, BUN, PT, cholesterol, triglyceride
- Chest x-ray and echocardiography on bedside
- Clopidogrel 75mg: 6cp PO then 1cp daily after PCI
- o Or Ticagrelor 90mg: 2 cp then 1cp twice daily after PCI
- o Or Prasugrel 10mg: 6 cp then 1 cp daily after PCI
- Anticoagulant:
- o Heparin: 60IU/kg (max. 4000 IU) i.v bolus then continues infusion: 400IU/kg/24H (max. 24.000IU). ACT monitoring 4 after with target treatment &gt;250ms or ACT 2 times upper normal value.
- o Or LWMH: Enoxaparin: 1mg(100IU)/Kg s.c, 2 times/day
- Nitroglycerine: if present LV dysfunction signs (stop if SBP &lt; 100mmHg)
- Betablocker: for all patient if no contraindication
- ACE-Is/ARBs: for all patient if no contraindication
- High dose Statins: for all patient if no contraindication

## c.3. Contrindication to Thrombolysis:

## Absolute

- Previous intracranial hemorrhage or stroke of unknown origin at any time
- Ischemic stroke in the preceding 6 months
- Central nervous system damage or neoplasms, or arteriovenous malformation
- Recent major trauma/ surgery/head injury (within the preceding month)
- Gastrointestinal bleeding within the past month
- Known bleeding disorder (excluding menstrual)
- Aortic dissection
- Non-compressible punctures in the past 24h (e.g. liver biopsy, lumbar puncture)

## Relative

- Transient ischemic attack in the preceding 6 months
- Oral anticoagulant therapy
- Pregnancy or within 1-week post-partum
- Refractory hypertension (systolic blood pressure &gt; 180mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure &gt;110mmHg)
- Advanced liver disease
- Infective endocarditis
- Active peptic ulcer
- Prolonged or traumatic resuscitation

| - hemodynamic +/- electrical stability                                                                  | - Hemodynamic and electrical instability                             |
| Pharmaco-invasive therapy- Elective PCI (3-24hours)                                                     | Rescue PCI-Very early(1-2hours)                                      |

- o Or LWMH: Enoxaparin: 1mg(100IU)/Kg s.c, 2 times/day
- Nitroglycerine: if present LV dysfunction signs (stop if SBP &lt; 100mmHg)
- Betablocker: for all patient if no contraindication
- ACE-Is: for all patient if no contraindication

## ii. Reperfusion indication:

- Delayed PCI indicated:
- o Ongoing symptoms suggestive of ischemia
- o Hemodynamic instability
- o Life-threatening arrhythmia
- STEMI &gt; 12hours with asymptomatic and stable, PCI (Delayed selective PCI) is indicated depend on age, risk strategy and viable myocardium via non-invasive ischemia test.

- Nitroglycerine can't use in case: inferior AMI +/- RV infarction, Low SBP &lt; 90mmHg, severe bradycardia &lt;50bpm, tachycardia &gt;100bpm
- Pulmonary edema: Furosemide
- Malaise: Atropine + vascular filling
- Shock: Norepinephrine, Dobutamine or Dopamine

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- STEMI in elderly: may have atypical symptoms or may present with confusion or altered mental status. Special consideration in managing STEMI in elderly include careful assessment of symptoms, monitoring complication and adjusting treatment plans base on individual patient factors.
- STEMI in Women: may present with atypical symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. They may have higher risk of complication and worse outcomes compared to men.
- STEMI in diabetic patients: may have more extensive coronary artery disease and higher risk of complication. Special in managing include aggressive blood sugar control, close monitoring for complications and individualized treatment.
- STEMI with cardiogenic shock: is life-threatening co-condition. Special in managing include immediate revascularization with PCI, aggressive hemodynamic support with medications and mechanical devices and close monitoring in an intensive care unit.
- STEMI with concurrent conditions: STEMI can occur in patients with other conditions such as renal failure, liver disease, or bleeding disorders. Special in managing include careful assessment of risks and benefits of reperfusion therapy, close monitoring for complications, and coordination with specialists in managing the underlying conditions.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Early reperfusion of STEMI gives good outcome for short and longtime prognosis.
- Without reperfusion treatment, survivors of STEMI face a substantial excess risk of further cardiovascular events, including death, recurrent MI, heart failure, arrhythmia, angina and stroke.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- Arrhythmia: ventricular arrhythmia, Atrial fibrillation, heart block
- Heart failure
- Cardiogenic shock
- Mechanical complications: ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture
- Thrombo-embolic events
- Post-infarction angina
- Post-infarction syndrome (pericarditis post infarction)

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- All high-risk cardiovascular patient shall be screen for coronary artery disease (CAD) annually.
- Lifestyle modification and managing risk factors can help prevent CAD and reduce risk of STEMI.
- Cardiac rehabilitation after STEMI can help improve cardiovascular health, manage risk factors, and promote lifestyle modification.
- Regular follow-up with a specialist provider is crucial for ongoing management and assessment of cardiovascular health.

## ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME (ACS)

## NON-ST ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (NSTEMI)

Dr. KHUON Rithy Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay,

Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) encompass a spectrum of conditions that include patients presenting with recent changes in clinical symptoms or signs, with or without changes on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and with or without acute elevations in cardiac troponin (cTn) concentrations.

NSTEMI is one type of ACS with characterize by acute chest pain (or chest pain-equivalent signs/symptoms) but without persistent ST-segment elevation (or ST-segment elevation equivalents) on ECG. The majority of patients in this category who subsequently display a typical rise and fall in cardiac troponin levels

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most common cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, with a substantial portion of this burden borne by low- and middle-income countries. ACS is often the first clinical manifestation of CVD.

In 2019, there were an estimated 5.8 million new cases of ischemic heart disease in the 57 countries. The median age-standardized incidence estimate per 100 000 people was 293.3 (interquartile ratio 195.8-529.5). Ischemic heart disease is the most common cause of CVD death, accounting for 38% of all CVD deaths in females and 44% in males.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) cause by the rupture or erosion of atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries, leading to the formation of blood clots that block blood flow partially or completely

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The underlying pathology of ACS is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. UA, NSTEMI, and STEMI all represent consequences of thrombotic vessel occlusion and varying degrees of this mismatch. Plaque rupture is the most common underlying source of thrombotic occlusion in ACS. Plaque erosion with an intact fibrous cap is the etiology in up to one-third of patients with ACS, typically, women, younger patients, and smokers. Additionally, vasoconstriction at the level of the culprit plaque or of the microcirculation may also cause ACS.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## 1. Clinical presentation

- Chest pain Ischemic-type (Angina): retro-sternal, intense, at rest, longer (&gt;30min), irradiate to jaw and neck, trinitro-resistant.
- Acute chest discomfort: Pain, Pressure, tightness, Heaviness or burning. It can radiate from the chest to the neck, jaw, back and sometime both arms. Other symptoms include:
- Shortness of breath
- Nausea or vomiting
- Feeling faint
- Sweating, weakness and fatigue.

## 2. Physical examination and history taking

- It is crucial to take a focused medical history and accurately characterize the presenting symptoms in order to manage the patient via the appropriate care pathway as soon as possible. Vital sign and EKG are recommended at first medical contact (FMC)
- Focused physical examination should include checking for the presence of all major pulses, measurement of blood pressure in both arms, auscultation of the heart and lungs, and assessing for signs of HF or circulatory compromise

## 3. Investigation and risk stratification

- It is recommended to base the diagnosis and initial short-term risk stratification of ACS on a combination of clinical history, symptoms, vital signs, other physical findings, EKG and hs-cTn.
- 12 lead EKG with in 10mn at FMC:
- o These patients may exhibit other ECG alterations, including transient ST-segment elevation, persistent or transient ST-segment depression, and T wave abnormalities, including hyperacute T waves, T wave inversion, biphasic T waves, flat T waves, and pseudo- normalization of T waves. Alternatively, the ECG may be normal
- High sensitive cardiac troponine ( hs-cTn): is recommended in all patients with suspected ACS
- o European Society of Cardiology 0 h/1 h and 0 h/2 h algorithms
- Echocardiography:
- o should not result in relevant delays in transfer to the cardiac catheterization laboratory if there is suspicion of an acute coronary artery occlusion
- o can be useful to identify signs suggestive of ongoing ischaemia or prior MI.
- o can also be useful to suggest alternative etiologies associated with chest pain.
- Coronary CT angiography:
- o Routine, early CCTA in patients with suspected ACS is not recommended.
- o Diagnostic tool of choice for ruling out alternative potentially life-threatening differential diagnoses of ACS, like PE or aortic dissection.

Normal, Inverted T waves,or ST depression

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- ACS in elderly: may have atypical symptoms or may present with confusion or altered mental status.

Special consideration in managing STEMI in elderly include careful assessment of symptoms, monitoring complication and adjusting treatment plans base on individual patient factors.

- CS in Women: may present with atypical symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. They may have higher risk of complication and worse outcomes compared to men.
- ACS in diabetic patients: may have more extensive coronary artery disease and higher risk of complication. Special in managing include aggressive blood sugar control, close monitoring for complications and individualized treatment.
- ACS with cardiogenic shock: is life-threatening co-condition. Special in managing include immediate revascularization with PCI, aggressive hemodynamic support with medications and mechanical devices and close monitoring in an intensive care unit.
- ACS with concurrent conditions: STEMI can occur in patients with other conditions such as renal failure, liver disease, or bleeding disorders. Special in managing include careful assessment of risks and benefits of reperfusion therapy, close monitoring for complications, and coordination with specialists in managing the underlying conditions.

## IX. VOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Short term prognosis can be vary significantly based on risk factors, age, comorbidities, and the initial clinical response. In general, NSTEMI has a better immediate outcome than STEMI, but It can still result in complications.
- The long-term prognosis can be influenced by various factors, including the severity of coronary artery disease, the presence of left ventricular dysfunction and adherence to medical therapy post-discharge.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- Arrhythmia: ventricular arrhythmia, Atrial fibrillation, heart block
- Heart failure
- Cardiogenic shock
- Mechanical complications: ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture
- Thrombo-embolic events
- Post-infarction angina
- Post-infarction syndrome (pericarditis post infarction)

## XI. REVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- All high-risk cardiovascular patient shall be screen for coronary artery disease (CAD) annually.
- Lifestyle modification and managing risk factors can help prevent CAD and reduce risk of STEMI.
- Cardiac rehabilitation after STEMI can help improve cardiovascular health, manage risk factors, and promote lifestyle modification.
- Regular follow-up with a specialist provider is crucial for ongoing management and assessment of cardiovascular health.

## CHRONIC CORONARY SYNDROME

Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION ET CLASSIFICATION:

| Chronic coronary syndrome categories according to the ESC Guidelines: - Category                                                           | Chronic coronary syndrome categories according to the ESC Guidelines: - Description                                                        |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1                                                                                                                                          | Patients with suspected CAD and "stable" angina symptoms*                                                                                  |
| 2                                                                                                                                          | Patient with new onset of heart failure or left ventricular dysfunction and suspected CAD                                                  |
| 3                                                                                                                                          | Asymptomatic and symptomatic patients <1 year after an ACS or recent revascularisation                                                     |
| 4                                                                                                                                          | Patients > 1 year after initial angina diagnosis or revascularisation                                                                      |
| 5                                                                                                                                          | Patients with angina and suspected vasospastic or microvascular disease                                                                    |
| 6                                                                                                                                          | Asymptomatic patients in whom CAD is detected at screening                                                                                 |
| * including dyspnoea as angina equivalent. ACS: acute coronary syndrome, CAD: coronary artery disease, ESC European Society of Cardiology. | * including dyspnoea as angina equivalent. ACS: acute coronary syndrome, CAD: coronary artery disease, ESC European Society of Cardiology. |

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY:

- CCD is a heterogeneous group of conditions that includes obstructive and nonobstructive CAD with or without previous myocardial infarction (MI) or revascularization, ischemic heart disease diagnosed only by noninvasive testing, and chronic angina syndromes with varying underlying causes.
- Approximately 20.1 million persons (7.2%) in the United States live with CCD, 11.1 million Americans (4.1%) have chronic stable angina pectoris, and approximately one-quarter (n=200 000) of all MIs in the United States occur among the 8.8 million persons with CCD who have had a previous MI.

## III. ETIOLOGY:

Chronic coronary syndrome referred to as stable ischemic heart disease (SIHD), based on a classic history of angina pectoris in the presence of either risk factors for or known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY:

- Multiple pathophysiologic mechanisms may cause CCS.
- The most common is atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction.
- However, as many as one-third of patients may have no significant epicardial disease and often have microvascular disease as the underlying pathophysiology.

## V. DIAGNOSIS:

1. Clinic:
- Angina is the main symptom.
- Angina pectoris is characterized by substernal discomfort, heaviness, or a pressure-like feeling, which may radiate to the jaw, shoulder, back, or arm and which typically lasts several minutes.
- Physical examination is often unrevealing in patients with stable angina.
2. Investigation:

*Six steps to diagnosing CAD (adapted from ESC Guideline 2019):

Step 1 Assess symptoms and signs to distinguish between typical and atypical symptoms

Step 2 Assess quality of life and comorbidities. Apply guideline-based risk-factor modification based on commonly applied risk charts e.g. SCORE.

Step 3 Basic testing including troponin assays should be considered. 12 lead ECG and TTE is recommended. CMR may be considered in patients with strong suspicion of CAD where TTE is within normal limits.

Step 4 The clinical likelihood of obstructive CAD is estimated. A new phrase has been coined for the guideline entitled "clinical likelihood of CAD" and is underpinned by the improved PTP score. 3 PTP &lt;15% corresponds to &lt;1% annual risk of cardiovascular death or MI. 4 Therefore, routine testing in these patients can safely be deferred reducing unnecessary procedures and costs. The data on which the PTP in the previous guideline was based has since been updated based on a pooled analysis of 3 cohort studies and has highlighted that the presence of obstructive disease amongst patients with suspected CAD is lower than once thought.

Step 5 Offer diagnostic testing to selected patients screened via steps 1-4 to establish the diagnosis of CAD. This includes the options of invasive and non-invasive imaging depending on the risk. The choice of test also depends on the PTP of CAD with modalities such as CTCA more effective in low clinical probability situations.

Step 6 Once a diagnosis of obstructive CAD has been confirmed, patients undergo risk stratification to guide subsequent therapeutic interventions. The event risk is determined by clinician judgement and depends on the investigation modality used to determine CAD.

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS:

The differential diagnosis includes myocardial infarction, valvular disease (especially aortic valve stenosis), aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, inflammatory myocardial and/or pericardial conditions, chest wall syndrome, psychogenic causes, respiratory tract infections, and esophageal conditions.

## VII. MANAGEMENT:

1. Objective:

To reduce angina symptom and exercised-induced ischemia and prevent cardiovascular events.

2. Critical Sign:

Signs related to the complication of CCS (see complications section).

3. Mortality Risk Factors: no consensus data.
4. Outpatient Management:

Most of CCS patients do not require hospitalization.

5. First-line Treatment: (see algorithm)
6. Treatment Adjustment: (see algorithm)

7. Algorithm:
- Lifestyle Management:

Smoking cessation, healthy diet (fruits and vegetables), Physical activities (3060min a day), Healthy weight (Keep BMI&lt;25kg/m2), influenza vaccination

## · Pharmacological Management

## i. Anti - i sc he mi c dr ugs:

- 1st line drugs: Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol, Metoprolol…), Calcium channel blockers.
- 2nd line drugs: Ranolazine (Rancard), Trimetazidine (Vastarel), Ivabradine, Nicorandil.
- Respond to anti-ischemic therapy should be reassessed after 2-4 weeks of treatment.

## ii. P re ve nti on of Car di ovasc ul ar e ve nts:

- Anti-thrombotic therapy (Aspirin, clopidogrel): low dose aspirin 75-100mg 1tab/day.
- Statins and other lipid-lowering drugs (rosuvastatin, atorvastatin, ezetimibe...)
- ACE inhibitor/ARBs: if patients have hypertension, heart failure.

## · Revascularization:

Revascularization with either coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), as opposed to continuing medical therapy without revascularization, is indicated in two groups of stable patients:

- Patients with specific high-risk anatomy for which revascularization has a proven survival benefit.

- Patients who want revascularization for improved quality of life compared with medical therapy, such as those who are not tolerating medical therapy well or who want to increase their activity level.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES:

- Individuals over the age of 65 years represent a growing proportion of patients with CSS, however, recognition of disease can be more challenging in this population due to a higher prevalence of atypical symptoms, including exertional dyspnea or silent myocardial ischemia.
- The approach to the management of angina in older adults is essentially the same as for younger patients.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PRONOSIS:

According to CLARIFY registry, in patient with CSS, resolution of angina within 1 year with conservative management predicted outcomes similar to lack of angina, whereas persistence or occurrence was associated with worse outcomes.

## X. COMPLICATION:

- Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or MI),
- Congestive heart failure,
- Cardiac arrhythmias, or sudden death.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION:

We recommend that all patients with CCS receive education and counseling about issues such as medication compliance, control of risk factors, and regular exercise. In addition, there are several medical therapies which can reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and disease progression.

## EMERGENCY TACHY-ARRHYTHMIA

Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, Asst. Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Asst. Prof. Chan Sokha, Ass Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour

## I. INTRODUCTION

Arrhythmias (cardiac arrhythmias or dysrhythmias) are irregularities in the heartbeat and the electrical impulses may be too fast, too slow or erratic, spans from a relatively benign condition to life-threatening emergencies.

2 types: Tachy-arrhythmia: HR &gt; 100bpm (at resting) and Brady-arrhythmia: HR &lt; 60bpm (at resting)

## II. DEFINITION

Tachycardia is when the heart beats too fast, at a rate of more than 100 beats per minute, when at rest. This can depend on age, health status and physical condition.

## III. CLASSIFICATION

Tachycardia
├── Narrow complex
│   ├── Regular
│   │   ├── Atrial tachycardia
│   │   ├── Atrial flutter
│   │   ├── AVRT
│   │   ├── AVNRT
│   │   └── Junctional tachycardia
│   └── Irregular
│       ├── AF with RVR
│       ├── Multifocal atrial tachycardia
│       └── Atrial flutter with variable AV block
└── Broad complex
    ├── Monomorphic
    │   ├── Regular
    │   │   ├── Monomorphic VT
    │   │   ├── SVT* with aberrancy
    │   │   └── Sinus tachycardia with aberrancy**
    │   └── Irregular
    │       ├── AF with aberrancy
    │       └── Multifocal atrial tachycardia with aberrancy
    └── Polymorphic
        ├── Polymorphic VT
        └── Torsades de pointes
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

AF: atrial fibrillation, AV: atrioventricular, AVNRT: atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia, AVRT: atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia, SVT: supraventricular tachycardia, VT: ventricular tachycardia, SVT*: any cause of regular tachycardia originating from above the ventricle, Aberrancy**: any form of abnormal conduction of the electrical impulse (i.e., left bundle branch block)

## IV. PIDERMIOLOGY

For SVT: prevalence is 2.25/1000 persons, incidence is 35/100 000 person-years. Women have a risk of developing SVT that is two times greater than that of men, and persons aged &gt;\_65 years or have more than five times the risk of developing SVT than younger individuals. [1]

For SCD by ventricular arrhythmia: low incidence during infancy and childhood (1 per 100 000 person years), 25-27 the incidence is approximately 50 per 100 000 person years in middle-aged individuals (in the fifth to sixth decades of life). [2]

## IV. TIOLOGIES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Causes of tachyarrhythmia: [6]

| Cardiac                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Extra-cardiac                                                                                                                                                                    | Drug-induced                                                                                                        |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Coronary artery disease Acute myocardial ischemia Chronic myocardial ischemia Cardiomyopathy (dilative, hypertrophic-obstructive, restrictive) Inflammatory heart disease Myocarditis Pericarditis Congenital heart disease in adult Aquired valvular disease Cardiac neoplasm Hypertrophy (arterial hypertension) Channelopathies | Electrolyte disturbances Toxic (alcohol) Hemochromatosis Renal diseases Hypo- and hyperthyroidism Autoimmune diseases Neoplasm Inflammatory diseases (sarcoidosis, amyoloidosis) | Antiarrhythmic (Ex.: Digitalis) Antidepressives Bronchodilatators Antineoplastic agents Inotropes Stimulants Opoids |

## 3 Mechanisms of tachyarrhythmia: [1,2]

- Abnormal automaticity: When cells outside the normal conduction system generate spontaneous impulse.
- Triggered activity: high levels of intracellular calcium, which can lead to spontaneous calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
- Re-entry: A conduction disturbance.

## V. DIAGNOSTIC

- 1- Clinical signs and symptoms
- [Palpitations +++](https://mindthebleep.com/palpitations/)
- Chest pain (and if relieved with GTN)
- Shortness of breath/dyspnoea
- Dizziness/syncope/light-headedness

## VI. IFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Differential diagnosis for tachycardia depends on the type of tachycardia, such as wide QRS complex tachycardia or regular, narrow-QRS tachycardias.

Figure 1. Differential diagnosis for tachycardia

<!-- image -->

- 1- Narrow QRS tachycardia [1]
- A. Haemodynamically unstable patients: Synchronized DC cardioversion
- B. Haemodynamically stable patients:
- Vagal manoeuvres in the supine position with leg elevation
- Medications:
- Adenosine (6-18 mg i.v. bolus with normal saline flush) if vagal manoeuvre fail (Except pre-excited Atrial fibrillation)
- Verapamil (0.075-0.15 mg/kg i.v. (average 5-10 mg) over 2 min) or diltiazem (i.v.) (0.25 mg/kg (average 20 mg) over 2 mi) or Beta-blockers (i.v. esmolol (0.5 mg/kg i.v. bolus or 0.05-0.3 mg/kg/min infusion) or metoprolol (2.5-15 mg given i.v. in 2.5 mg boluses) if vagal maneuvers and adenosine fail
- Synchronized direct-current cardioversion if drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia)
- Catheter Ablation

## 2- Wide QRS tachycardia [2,3]

## A. Treatment of reversible conditions

- Withdrawal of offending agents is recommended whenever drug-induced arrhythmias
- Investigation for reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte imbalances, ischemia, hypoxemia, fever)

- B. Hemodynamically unstable patients: Synchronized DC cardioversion
- C. Hemodynamically stable patients: Medication therapy or Synchronized DC cardioversion if drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia
- Medications therapy:
4. ■ Acebutolol PO 200-1200 mg daily or up to 600 mg bid
5. ■ Amiodarone IV: 300 mg bolus for VF/pulseless VT arrest; 150-mg bolus for stable VT; 1 mg/min x 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min x 18 h, PO: 400 mg q8 to 12 h for 1-2 wk, then 300-400 mg daily; reduce dose to 200 mg daily if possible
6. ■ Atenolol PO: 25-100 mg qd or bid,
7. ■ Bisoprolol PO: 2.5-10 mg once daily
8. ■ Carvedilol PO: 3.125-25 mg q 12 h
9. ■ Diltiazem IV: 5-10 mg qd: 15-30 min Extended release: PO: 120-360 mg/day
10. ■ Esmolol IV: 0.5 mg/kg bolus, 0.05mg/kg/min
11. ■ Flecainide PO: 50-200 mg q 12 h
12. ■ Lidocaine IV: 1 mg/kg bolus, 1-3mg/min or 1-1.5 mg/kg. Repeat 0.5-0.75 mg/kg bolus every 5-10 min (max cumulative dose 3 mg/kg). Maintenance infusion is 1-4 mg/min although one could start at 0.5 mg/min
13. ■ Metoprolol IV: 5 mg q 5 min up to 3 doses, PO: 25-100 mg Extended release qd or q 12 h
14. ■ Sotalol IV: 75 mg q 12h, PO: 80-120 mg q 12 h, may increase dose every 3d; max 320 mg/d
15. ■ Procainamide IV: loading dose 10-17mg/kg at 20-50mg/min and Maintenance dose: 1-4mg/min, PO (SR preparation): 500-1250 mg q 6 h
16. ■ Verapamil is not recommended in wide QRS complex tachycardia of unknown etiology
- Administration of potassium and magnesium has been proposed as helpful adjuncts in the prevention of ventricular arrhythmias
- Implanted cardioverted defibrillator (ICD) (for secondary prevention)
- Catheter ablation
- Surgical ablation
- Autonomic modulation: interruption of sympathetic outflow to the heart, pharmacological beta blockade, or through stimulation of the parasympathetic pathway

Figure 4. Pediatric Tachycardia with a pulse algorithm [7]

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 311 -->
- Initial assessment and support
  - Maintain patent airway; assist breathing as necessary
  - Administer oxygen
  - Cardiac monitor to identify rhythm; monitor pulse, blood pressure, and oximetry
  - IV/IO access
  - 12-Lead ECG if available
- Evaluate rhythm with 12-lead ECG or monitor.
  - Probable sinus tachycardia if
    - P waves present/normal
    - Variable RR interval
    - Infant rate usually <220/min
    - Child rate usually <180/min
    - Search for and treat cause.
  - Cardiopulmonary compromise?
    - Yes
      - Evaluate QRS duration.
        - Narrow (≤0.09 sec)
          - Probable supraventricular tachycardia
            - P waves absent/abnormal
            - RR interval not variable
            - Infant rate usually ≥220/min
            - Child rate usually ≥180/min
            - History of abrupt rate change
            - If IV/IO access is present, give adenosine or If IV/IO access is not available, or if adenosine is ineffective, perform synchronized cardioversion
        - Wide (>0.09 sec)
          - Possible ventricular tachycardia
            - Synchronized cardioversion
              - Expert consultation is advised before additional drug therapies.
    - No
      - Evaluate QRS duration.
        - Narrow (≤0.09 sec)
          - Probable supraventricular tachycardia
            - P waves absent/abnormal
            - RR interval not variable
            - Infant rate usually ≥220/min
            - Child rate usually ≥180/min
            - History of abrupt rate change
            - Consider vagal maneuvers.
              - If IV/IO access is present, give adenosine.
        - Wide (>0.09 sec)
          - Possible ventricular tachycardia
            - If rhythm is regular and QRS monomorphic, consider adenosine.
              - Expert consultation is recommended.
- Doses/Details
  - Synchronized cardioversion
    - Begin with 0.5-1 J/kg; if not effective, increase to 2 J/kg. Sedate if needed, but don't delay cardioversion.
  - Drug Therapy
    - Adenosine IV/IO dose
      - First dose: 0.1 mg/kg rapid bolus (maximum: 6 mg)
      - Second dose: 0.2 mg/kg rapid bolus (maximum second dose: 12 mg)

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Case 1: A 48-year-old woman had a history of palpitations for 5 years. Her episodes started and stopped suddenly, lasted 1 to 2 minutes, and were associated with lightheadedness. She came to a local emergency room with a prolonged episode: ECG showed a narrow QRS tachycardia (by report; no ECG available) that was terminated with adenosine. She was treated with oral diltiazem and metoprolol but continued to have supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) episodes. She had a normal physical exam; non-invasive evaluation showed no structural heart disease. She was referred for catheter ablation of her SVT. [4]

Figure 5. Regular narrow QRS complex tachycardia with short RP'. [5]

<!-- image -->

Figure 6. After 6mg of adenosine IV, her ECG is converted to sinus rhythm and the patient was diagnosed with 'Slow-Fast AVNRT' (Atrioventricular Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia) by electrophysiological study and successfully treated by RF catheter ablation. [5]

<!-- image -->

Case 2: The patient was a 28-year-old woman referred for management of palpitations for the last 2 years. Episodes began after birth of the eighth child and often worsened when she was upset. Ambulatory recorder showed sustained ventricular tachycardia originated from right ventricular outflow tract (having a left bundle branch block (LBBB) and right-inferior axis with a precordial R-wave transition at V3 and smooth R-wave contours in inferior leads). Metoprolol was ineffective at controlling her symptoms

(palpitations and fatigue), which were increasingly bothersome. Physical examination finding was normal aside from skipped beats without signs of shock. Echocardiogram showed mild global hypokinesis (ejection fraction 45%). She was referred for a repeat EP study and ablation. [4]

Figure 7. Sustained ventricular tachycardia originated from right ventricular outflow tract [5]

<!-- image -->

Figure 8. After catheter ablation by radio-frequency, ECG showed sinus rhythm without ventricular tachycardia. [4]

<!-- image -->

## IX. OMPLICATIONS

The common complications include sudden cardiac death, syncope, stroke, heart failure, hypotension and/or shock.

## EMERGENCY BRADYCARDIA

Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, Asst. Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Asst. Prof. Chan Sokha, Asst. Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour

## I. INTRODUCTION

Bradycardia spans from a relatively benign condition to life-threatening emergencies. Bradycardia is a frequent finding in clinical practice and its significance is dependent on underlying cause and clinical presentation. The goal of initial management is stabilization by increasing the ventricular rate.

## II. DEFINITION

A normal heart rate is normally between 60 to 100 beats per minute (bpm). An emergency bradycardia is defined as a heart rate &lt; 50 bpm with one of these conditions: (1) hemodynamic compromised, (2) severe slow heart rate &lt; 35-40 bpm, (3) ventricular tachyarrhythmias, (4) acute heart failure, (5) acutely altered mental status.

## III. ETIOLOGIES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The causes of bradycardia can be separated into primary or secondary (Table 1). The primary or intrinsic etiologies are relatively rare in the acute setting and occur more often in the elderly patients. Secondary or extrinsic etiologies are more frequently seen in the acute care and are more likely to be reversible with medical therapy.

| Primary                                        | Secondary                                   |
|------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Idiopathic (ageing) degeneration               | Acute myocardial infarction                 |
| Ischemic heart disease                         | Medications: digoxin, betablocker overdose… |
| Myocarditis, Endocarditis                      | Hypokalemia, hyperkalemia                   |
| Infiltrative disease: sarcoidosis, amyloidosis | Hypothyroidism                              |
| Congenital disease                             | Hypoxia                                     |
| Surgical trauma: valve replacement             | Hypothermia                                 |
| Surgical trauma: valve replacement             | Acidosis                                    |
| Surgical trauma: valve replacement             | Physical training (athletes, sports)        |
| Surgical trauma: valve replacement             | Vagal tone                                  |

Table 1: The above causes can involve the sinus node and atrio-ventricular node (AV node) or distal His bundle-Purkinje system results in sick sinus syndrome and different degree of AV block at the nodal level or infra-nodal level, respectively.

## IV. IAGNOSTIC

- 1- Clinical signs and symptoms

Bradycardia may present as fatigue, dizziness, syncope, pre-syncope, shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, cardiac arrest. Assessment for signs of hypoperfusion or hemodynamic compromised such as cyanosis, altered mental status, pallor will help guide management.

- 2- Investigations

A 12-lead standard ECG has the most diagnostic value. Prolonged Holter monitoring is also helpful for intermittent bradycardia event. Serologic finding such as potassium, BUN, Creatinine, thyroid function test (TSH, fT4, fT3) will reveal common secondary causes of bradycardia. Serum cardiac markers, such as troponin, BNP or NT-proBNP are requested to assess myocardial ischemia or injury as a cause of bradycardia. Chest radiograph may reveal enlarged cardiac silhouette (pericardial effusion or cardiomegaly). Cardiac ultrasound can identify structural heart disease.

## V. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Premature ventricular complex bigeminy, blocked premature atrial complex.

## VI. ANAGEMENT

- 1- Objectives

The goal of initial management is stabilization by increase the ventricular rate through one of the following: (1) pharmacological intervention and/or (2) nonpharmacological intervention. 2, 5 The physicians need to assess and determine the underlying causes of bradycardia.

- 2- Critical sign

(1) hemodynamic compromised, (2) severe slow heart rate &lt; 35-40 bpm, (3) ventricular tachyarrhythmias, (4) acute heart failure, (5) acutely altered mental status.

- 3- Mortality risk factors Family history of sudden cardiac death, history of syncope, preexistent heart failure,

associated cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities.

- 4- Outpatient management Bradycardia patient with above critical signs are recommended to hospitalization for further investigation and appropriate management.
- 5- Treatment
- A. Pharmacological intervention
- Atropine: first-line drug for unstable and acute symptomatic bradycardia
- Dosage: 1 st dose 1mg IV bolus, repeat every 3 to 5 min and maximal dose is 3 mg, dose lower than 0.5 mg is not recommended
- Alternative drugs: Dopamine, Epinephrine and Isoproterenol
- Dosage of Dopamine: IV infusion 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min and titrate to patient response
- Dosage of Epinephrine: IV infusion 2 to 10 mcg/min and titrate to patient response
- Dosage of Isoproterenol: IV infusion 2 to 10 mcg/min and titrate to patient response
- Pharmacological intervention should not delay implementation of external pacing for patients with poor perfusion
- B. Non-pharmacological intervention #
- Transcutaneous cardiac pacing
- Technique: places pads on the patient chest and connects the ECG leads. Turn the pacer on with pacing rate to &gt; 30 bpm above intrinsic rhythm and set 70 mA. Start pacing, once pacing captured, set current at 5-10 mA above the threshold.
- Complication: severe discomfort and failure to pace and capture.
- Temporary transvenous cardiac pacing
- Technique: equipped with fluoroscopy (usually in Cath-Lab). The site chosen is usually on femoral, subclavian or internal jugular vein. Venous sheath is inserted by Seldinger technique. Temporary pacing lead insertion into the appropriate pacing cardiac chamber (apical RV) and ensuring accurate lead placement.
- Complication: thrombophlebitis, infection, cardiac perforation.

## VII. SPECIAL CASES

Case #1: A 74-year-old female with history of hypertension presented multiple episodes of syncope and was admitted at a referral hospital. Her blood pressure was 85/50 mm Hg, heart rate was 36 bpm and SpO2 was 96%. There, physician did a complete clinical examination and lab test which showed no findings of secondary causes. The ECG (Fig. 1) showed complete AV block with ventricular rate 37 bpm. Atropine and Dopamine IV were given based on the algorithm but there was no clinical response. The patient was transferred to a heart center in Phnom Penh where the electrophysiologist performed transvenous pacing and subsequently permanent pacemaker was successfully implanted (Fig. 2).

Figure (1). Complete AV dissociation with heart rate 37 bpm suggested complete atrioventricular block.

## Bradycardia

Case #2: A 53-year-old female with history of diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease presented fatigue, dizziness and vomiting. Blood pressure was 95/62 mm Hg, heart rate was 38 bpm and SpO2 was 92%. The ECG (Fig. 3) showed escape junctional rhythm with heart rate 39 bpm and peaked T wave and shortened QTc. She was found to have severe hyperkalemia (K + 7 mmol/L) due to her underlying CKD. Management and correction of hyperkalemia to normal potassium level (K + 4.5 mmol/L) resolved the bradycardia (Fig. 4).

Figure (3). Escape junctional rhythm, peaked T wave and shortened QTc consistent with hyperkalemia.

<!-- image -->

Figure (4). ECG normalized after potassium level correction.

<!-- image -->

## VIII. COMPLICATIONS

The common complications include sudden cardiac death, syncope, trauma secondary to fall after syncope, worsening of heart failure, hypotension and/or shock, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, death.

## PULMONARY EMBOLISM

Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Pulmonary embolism (PE) refers to obstruction of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches by thrombus.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

PE incidence varies by region, but it is typically estimated at 39 - 115 cases per 100.000 person-years. Incidence increase with age, particularly in people over 60 years old. PE is slightly more common in women, especially those on hormonal therapies, during pregnancy or in post-partum period.

## III. ETIOLOGY

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is typically caused by thrombus formation, most often originating from deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the legs. The etiology involves three primary factors - Venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad). Common triggers include prolong immobility, surgery, trauma, malignancy, hormonal influences (e.g. pregnancy, oral contraceptives), and genetic thrombophilias (e.g Factor V Leiden).

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

PE occurs when a blood clot, usually from a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the legs, travels to the lungs and blocks a pulmonary artery. This obstruction reduces blood flow to the lungs, impairing oxygen exchange, and increase pulmonary artery pressure. Large clots can cause right heart strain, reduce cardiac output, and potentially lead to shock or sudden cardiac death.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

1. Initial assessment:
- Clinical History and symptoms: assess for dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis and risk factors (e.g. recent surgery, immobilization, cancer)
- Physical examination to assess vital signs, signs of DVT and signs of right heart failure
2. Risk stratification:
- Use Modified Wells scoring system (see Annex 1) or Revised Geneva scoring system (see Annex 2) to assess pre-test probability of PE
3. D-dimer testing:
- If low/intermediate pre-test probability: Perform D-dimer blood test
- If D-dimer is negative, PE can be ruled out
- If D-dimer is positive, proceed to Imaging
4. Imaging:
- CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA): Gold standard imaging technique to visualize and confirm the presence of thrombi.

- Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) scan: used when CTPA is contraindicated (e.g. renal impairment, contrast allergy)
- Compression ultrasound of the legs: perform if DVT is suspected, especially when symptoms of DVT are present
5. Echocardiography:
- For hemodynamically unstable patients, bedside echocardiography can identify right heart strain suggestive of PE
6. Additional laboratory tests:
- Arterial blood gas (ABG): show hypoxemia, hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis.
- Cardiac markers: Elevated troponins and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) can indicate RV dysfunction and are associated with worse prognosis.

## Vl. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

The differential diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE) includes conditions with similar symptoms such as myocardial infarction, pneumonia, pleuritis, pneumothorax, congestive heart failure, and pericarditis. Theses can present with chest pain, dyspnea, or tachycardia, mimicking PE. Careful evaluation of clinical history, risk factors and diagnostic imaging is essential to differentiate PE from these conditions.

## Vll. MANAGEMENT

1. Initial assessment:
- Stabilization: assess airway, breathing and circulation (ABCs)
- Vital sign monitoring: monitor HR, BP and oxygen saturation.
2. Risk stratification:
- Classify PE as low, intermediate or high risk based on clinical presentation and hemodynamic stability
3. Anticoagulation therapy
- Immediate treatment: Start anticoagulation as soon as PE is sus pected
- Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): for high-risk patients

| Key points about UFH for PE treatment Administration IV bolus followed by   | Key points about UFH for PE treatment Administration IV bolus followed by - continuous infusion                                                                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dosing protocol                                                             | · Initial bolus: 80 units/kg (usually 5000 - 10000 units) · Continuous infusion: 18 units/kg/h, adjusted based on aPTT results (target: 1.5 - 2.5 times normal value) |
| Monitoring                                                                  | aPTT measured every 6 hours initially to ensure target level                                                                                                          |
| Reversal (antidote)                                                         | Protamine sulfate                                                                                                                                                     |

- Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH): For stable patients
- Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOACs): consider for outpatient management once PE is confirmed, based on guidelines
- VKA (Vitamin K antagonists): second-line therapy. VKA are often considered when DOACs are contra-indicated or unsuitable, such as
- In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min)
- In patients on certain medications that interact with DOACs, reducing their efficacy or increase bleeding

| Key points about LMWH for PE treatment   | Key points about LMWH for PE treatment                                                                                                                     |
|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Administration                           | Subcutaneous injection (S/C)                                                                                                                               |
| LMWH                                     | Enoxaparin (Lovenox®) 20mg, 40 mg, 60 mg                                                                                                                   |
| Dosing protocol                          | 1 mg/kg twice daily                                                                                                                                        |
| Monitoring Duration                      | Anti-factor Xa LMWH is often used for the initial phase (5 - that, patients are transitioned to oral anticoagulants warfarin or direct oral anticoagulant. |

| Key points about DOAC for PE treatment - DOAC Agents   | Key points about DOAC for PE treatment - · Apixaban · Rivaroxaban · Dabigatran · Edoxaban                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|--------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dosing protocol                                        | · Apixaban: initial dose 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily · Rivaroxaban: initial dose 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily · Dabigatran: initial treatment with parenteral anticoagulation (e.g LMWH) for 5 - 10 days, then switch to 150 mg twice daily · Edoxaban: initial treatment with parenteral anticoagulation (e.g LMWH) for 5 - 10 days, then switch to 60 mg once daily |

| PE treatment Overlap with heparin UFH or LMWH is used for at least 5 days until the INR reaches the therapeutic range ( 2 - 3) for 2 consecutive days · Wafarin (COUMADINE®)   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Acenocumarol (SINTROM®) Monitoring Frequent INR checks during initiation, (monthly) once stable then less often                                                              |
| Maintenance dose Adjusted based on INR                                                                                                                                         |
| Reversal agent Vitamin K                                                                                                                                                       |

4. Thrombolytic therapy
- Indication: for patients with massive PE or those who are hemodynamically unstable (e.g hypotension)
5. Mechanical Intervention
- Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filter: consider for patients with contraindication to anticoagulant or recurrent PE despite adequate treatment
6. Monitoring and Supportive Care
- Monitoring: complications (bleeding, recurrent PE)
- Supportive Care: administer fluids or vasopressors if necessary for hemodynamic support.
7. Long term management:
- Anticoagulation duration:
- Provoked PE: 3 - 6 months of anticoagulation
- Unprovoked PE: extended anticoagulation based on individual risk factors (e.g cancer, thrombophilia)

| Key points about thrombolytic therapy for PE   | Key points about thrombolytic therapy for PE   |
|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Agent                                          | Alteplase (tPA)                                |
| Administration                                 | IV infusion                                    |
| Dosing protocol                                | 100 mg infusion over 2 hours                   |

## Vlll. SPECIAL CASES

-  Massive PE: Hemodynamically unstable, requires immediate thrombolytics or surgical embolectomy
-  Pregnancy-Related PE: due to physiological changes and venous stasis. Use Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for treatment and avoid warfarin in pregnancy
-  Cancer-Related PE: increased risk in cancer patients, long-term anticoagulation recommended using LMWH or DOACs
-  Pediatric PE: Less common, often linked to congenital heart disease or surgery, management follow specific pediatric guidelines.

## lX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Without treatment, PE can result in severe complications and high mortality rate. Prognosis improve significantly with timely intervention, reducing mortality rates. Long-term outcomes may include chronic issues like pulmonary hypertension, but many patients recover well with appropriate management.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- Right heart failure: due to increased pulmonary pressure
- Hypoxia: from impaired oxygen change
- Pulmonary Hypertension: develop from unresolved clot
- Recurrent PE
- Post-thrombotic syndrome: in case of DVT leading to PE.
- Death: untreated or severe PE can lead to sudden cardiac death

## Xl. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

Preventing PE involves assessing risk factors and implementing strategies such as pharmacologic prophylaxis (e.g. LMWH, DOACs) and mechanical measures (e.g. compression stockings). Early mobilization post-surgery and patient education on PE symptoms are crucial.

## I. DEFINITION

Acute pulmonary edema refers to clinical syndrome of new or worsening symptoms and/or signs of heart failure, leading to an unplanned hospital admission or an emergency department visit.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- Prevalence of heart failure in the population is 2% in Europe and 4% in Southeast Asia.
- Incidence of new cases per 100,000 per year: 219 in USA, 130 in UK, 70 in china
- Main challenges of heart failure hospitalization:
- o 1-4% of total hospital admission
- o &gt; 9/10 patients hospitalized due to worsening chronic heart failure
- o Average length of hospital stay: 5-10 days
- o ¼ or 24% patients are re-hospitalized within 30-days post discharge period, 20% die within 6 months
- In-hospital mortality (+++):4.8% in Asia pacific

## III. ETIOLOGY

Table. 1 Etiology of acute heart failure

| Cardiovascular                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Non-Cardiovascular                                                                                                                                                                                           | Patient-related or iatrogenic                                                                                                         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| - Acute coronary syndromes - Tachycardia (i.e., Afib) - Bradycardia (i.e. 3 rd degree AVB) - Uncontrolled hypertension or hypertensive crisis - Myocarditis - Acute pulmonary embolism - Acute valvular regurgitation (i.e. endocarditis, MI) - Aortic dissection - Cardiac tamponade | - Infections and febrile states - COPD exacerbation or asthma - Renal dysfunction - Anemia - Hyperthyroidism - Hypothyroidism - Strenuous exercise - Emotional stress - Pregnancy (peripartum cardiomyopathy | - Poor compliance with medication - Increased salt or fluid intake - Surgery - Drugs (i.e. NSAID, Thiazolidinediones) - Alcohol abuse |

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

There are two main types of congestion:

1. Peripheral congestion: progressive increase in body weight, peripheral edema, jugular distension, hepatomegaly, ascites and renal venous stasis.
2. Pulmonary congestion: worsening dyspnea, pulmonary rales and B-line at lung ultrasound.

## 1.Clinical

- Symptom:

- o Congestion: lower extremity swelling, ankle swelling, abdominal fullness, hepatic congestion
- Physical finding:
- o Vital sings: BP, HR, SpO2, Temperature, RR
- o Heart sounds: Third heart sound (LV dysfunction), Murmur, Jugular venous distension
- o Lung: rales (heart failure)

|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| I                                                   | Cardiac disease, but no symptoms and no limitation in ordinary physical activity |
| II                                                  | Mild symptoms and slight limitation during ordinary activity                     |
| III                                                 | Significant limitation in activity due to symptoms, comfortable only at rest     |
| IV                                                  | Severe limitations. Symptoms event while at rest                                 |

## 2. Investigation: Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for the results!

- Laboratory: complete blood count, chemistries, TSH, ABG, BNP if available, D-dimer if suspicion PE
- Imaging: ECG, chest X-ray, Echocardiography&amp; lung ultrasound-if available
3. Four major Clinical hemodynamics profiles of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF):
- Acute decompensated heart failure
- Acute pulmonary edema
- Cardiogenic shock
- Isolated right ventricular failure

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objectives
- Improve symptoms, congestion and low-output symptoms
- Restore normal oxygenation
- Optimize volume status
- Identifying etiology and precipitating factors
- Initiating and optimizing oral therapy, minimizing side effects
- Educating patients and considering a disease management program
2. Critical sign
- Respiratory distress: RR &gt;35/min, SpO2 &lt; 90%, PaO2 &lt; 75mmHg, PaCO2 &gt; 45mmHg
- Hemodynamic instable: low/high BP (&lt;85/&gt;140mmHg), Severe arrhythmias, HR &lt;60/min or &gt; 130/min
3. Mortality risk factor
- Patient intubated or likely to require respiratory support/intubation, includes
13. o SpO2&lt;90% despite supplement oxygen
14. o Using accessory muscles and respiratory rate &gt;25 breaths/min
- Signs and symptoms of hypoperfusion and/or SBP &lt; 90mmHg

- Heart rate &lt; 40 or &gt; 130bpm
4. Outpatient Management:

All acute pulmonary edema patients are recommended to hospitalization.

5. First-line treatment
- i. Basic Assessment
- Positioning: head of bed elevated
- O2 10 L/min → SpO2 ≥95%
- Furosemide: 40-60mg i.v. (equal or 2 times to oral dose)
- Morphine: 2mg i.v. if severe anxiety or distress
- Digoxine: 0.25-0.5mg i.v. if rapid Afib (HR&gt;110/min)

## ii. Adequate perfusion

- Wet Cold (SBP &lt;90mmHg):
- Inotrope drug: Dobutamine= 3-5µg/kg/min
- Vasopressor: Norepinephrine= 0.2-0.5µg/kg/min
- Add Diuretic when perfusion corrected
- Wet Warm (SBP: elevated or normal): Vasodilatators:
- Nitroglycerine spray 400µg sublingual, repeat 5-10 min
- Nitroglycerine i.v. continuously 1mg/ml(10mg in 20ml)
- o Start 1mg/h, check BP after 5 and 10min
- o Increase 0.5mg/h if need (SBP &gt;100mmHg), check BP 5 and 10min after each increase in dosing
- o Check BP every 20min once drip rate is reach (max 2.5mg/h, or drop SBP ≥40mmHg from initial BP)

## iii. Reassessed∼15-30min after:

- Sufficient respiratory + Ventilation
- Release dyspnea + Symptoms
- Normalization: BP, HR, urinary output
- Goals:
- SpO2 : 94-98%
- pCO2 &lt; 45mmHg, paO2 &gt; 70mmHg
- SBP: 100-120/60,
- HR: 60-100/min + regular
- Urinary output &gt;0.5ml/kg/h

## 6.Treatment adjustment

- SBP &lt;85mmHg: Increase dose Inotropes and Add Vasopressor
- Respiratory distress (SpO2 &lt;90% with O2, RR&gt;25/min): CPAP or intubation
- Urine output &lt; 20ml/h:
- Bladder catheter
- Double dose diuretic= 80-120mg i.v bolus or 100mg/6H continuously
- Combined diuretic= Bumetanide (Burinex), 2mg i.v, repeat every 20min (max 30mg/day)
- Low-dose dopamine= 3µg/kg/min
- Dialysis/ultrafiltration
