## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- Acute right heart failure: secondary to pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction or pulmonary hypertension. Management challenges; focus on optimizing preload, reducing afterload and addressing the underlying cause (e.g., anticoagulant for PE)
- Flash Pulmonary Edema: sudden onset of severe pulmonary congestion. Management: requires rapid afterload reduction; IV nitroglycerine, diuretics and oxygenation support.
- Acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome: acute MI triggers heart failure. Management requires balancing treatment for both ACS and AHF, revascularization and careful fluid management.
- Heart failure with pregnancy: peripartum cardiomyopathy is a notable cause, management focuses on balancing maternal and fetal health.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Key predictors of poor prognosis: advanced age, low SBP, High heart rate, sings of hypoperfusion with high comorbidities (diabetes, CKD, COPD or malignancy).
- Prognosis for Acute pulmonary edema remains worse with significant mortality and morbidity risks:
- In-hospital mortality: 4-12%, higher in cardiogenic shock, sepsis or severe comorbidities
- 30-days readmission rates: 20-25%
- 1-year mortality: 20-40%

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- Hemodynamic: cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia
- Respiratory: Acute respiratory failure
- Renal: Acute kidney injury (AKI), worsening renal function (Cardiorenal Syndrome)
- Neurological: stroke, delirium
- Metabolic and electrolyte: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- Primary prevention: manage risk factor of heart disease; blood pressure, lipid levels, treat diabetes, lifestyle changed &amp; screening for asymptomatic HF.
- Secondary prevention: optimized guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), prevent decompensation, regular follow-up and patient education.

## HYPERTENSION

Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

High blood pressure is actually a leading risk factor for heart disease and early death. It's sometimes called the &lt;silent killer&gt;.

High blood pressure is also called hypertension, when the systolic blood pressure is ≥140 mmHg and/or the diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg.

| Thresholds for diagnosing HTN based on clinic and out-of-clinic BP   | Asia   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------|
| Clinic                                                               | 140/90 |
| Home                                                                 | 135/85 |
| ABPM (ambulatory BP measurements)                                    |        |
| Daytime                                                              | 135/85 |
| Nighttime                                                            | 120/70 |
| 24h average                                                          | 130/80 |

| Classification                  | SBP (mmHg)   |        | DBP (mmHg)   |
|---------------------------------|--------------|--------|--------------|
| Optimal                         | <120         | and    | <80          |
| Normal                          | 120-129      | and/or | 80-84        |
| High normal                     | 130-139      | and/or | 85-89        |
| Hypertension Grade 1 (Mild)     | 140-159      | and/or | 90-99        |
| Hypertension Grade 2 (Moderate) | 160-179      | and/or | 100-109      |
| Hypertension Grade 3 (Severe)   | >180         | and/or | >110         |
| Isolated systolic hypertension  | >140         | and    | <90          |

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Recent estimates have suggested the number of patients with hypertension in Cambodia could increase to 26% among 30-79 years in both sexes (WHO 2019).

## III. AETIOLOGY

Over 90% of all cases of hypertension are of unknown aetiology (essential hypertension). One of the described risk factors for the development of essential hypertension is:

- Age
- Family history
- Being overweight or obese
- Sedentary lifestyle (lack of exercise)
- Using tobacco of any kind
- Too much salt (sodium) in the diet
- Excessive alcohol intake

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

There are various mechanisms described for the development of hypertension, which include increased salt absorption resulting in volume expansion, an impaired response of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and increased activation of the sympathetic nervous system. These changes lead to the development of increased total peripheral resistance and increased afterload, which in turn leads to the development of hypertension.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 334 -->
- Elevated BP readings (home, office, or pharmacy)
  - Hypertension visit 1
    - History, physical examination, and diagnostic tests
      - BP ≥ 180/110 mm Hg → Hypertension
      - AOBP ≥ 135/85 mm Hg
        - OBPM ≥ 140/90 mm Hg
          - NO → No hypertension (Annual BP measurement recommended)
          - YES → OBPM
            - Visit 2-3
              - SBP ≥ 140 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 90 mm Hg
                - If possible, confirm with home or ambulatory BP monitoring → Hypertension
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

## BP Measuring Technique

- Don't smoke, exercise, drink caffeinated beverages or alcohol within 30mn of measurement
- Take at least 2 readings at 1 min interval
- Rest in a chair for at least 5mn with your left arm resting comfortably on a flat surface at heart level
- Sit calmly and don't talk
- Place the bottom of the cuff above the bend of the elbow

## Sign and symptom

What are the signs and symptoms of high blood pressure? Usually none. That's why many people don't realize they have high blood pressure.

In some cases, people with more severe high blood pressure may have:

- Severe headaches
- Vision changes
- Nausea/vomiting
- Nosebleeds
- Confusion

## Investigations

- Laboratory tests: FBC, electrolytes, renal function, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, uric acid, urines test
- ECG
- Heart ultrasound if available

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Secondary hypertension should always be sought for as the differential, especially if the patient is at extremes of age (young or older).

Adrenal tumor, coarctation of the aorta, renal artery stenosis and kidney disease should always be kept in the differential.

## Pharmacological treatment

<!-- image -->

ESSENTIAL

OPTIMAL

- a) Consider monotherapy in low-risk grade 1 hypertension or in very old (≥80 yrs) or frailer patients.
- b) Consider A+D in post-stroke very elderly, incipient HF or CCB intolerance.
- c) Consider A+C or C+D in black patients.
- d) Caution with spironolactone or other potassium sparing diuretics when estimated GFR&lt;45 ml/min/1.73𝑚2 or 𝐾+&gt;4.5mmol/L.

A= ACE-inhibitor or ARB (Angiotensin Receptor Blocker)

- C= DHP-CCB (Dihydropyridine-Calcium Channel Blocker)
- D= Thiazide-like diuretic
- *Alternatives include: Amiloride, doxazosin, eplerenone or beta-blocker.

# low-dose generally refers to halt of the maximum recommended dose

## Treatment targets:

For most patients, blood pressure is considered controlled when SBP &lt;140 mmHg and DBP &lt;90 mmHg.

However, for patients with diabetes or a high risk of CVD, recommend lower targets: SBP &lt;130 mmHg and DBP &lt;80 mmHg

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Hypertensive emergencies are a heterogeneous group of acute hypertensive disorders which require rapid recognition and treatment with the appropriate therapy to avoid progressive organ dysfunction.

A hypertensive emergency is defined by a blood pressure value above 200/120 mmHg with or without target organ damage.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Untreated high blood pressure increases a person's risk of developing heart disease, stroke or kidney failure at an early stage.

## X. COMPLICATION

Complications of hypertension account for 9.4 million deaths caused by CVD worldwide every year:

- o At least 45% of deaths due to heart disease
- o 51% of deaths due to stroke
- o It contributes to about 1000 deaths a day
- Heart: LV hypertrophy, heart failure, coronary artery disease
- Brain: ischemic or haemorrhage stroke
- Retina: haemorrhages or exudates, papilledema
- Kidney: microalbuminuria, chronic kidney disease
- Peripheral vasculature: aortic aneurysm, peripheral artery disease

## XI. PREVENTION

The best approach to the primary prevention of HTN is a combination of lifestyle changes:

- Don't smoke
- Weight reduction
- Restriction sodium intake
- Physical activity
- Alcohol consumption with moderation
- Eat a healthy diet

Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITIONS

1. Heart failure occurs "The situation when the heart is incapable of maintaining a cardiac output adequate to accommodate metabolic requirements and the venous return."
2. HF is a clinical syndrome in which patients have the following features:
+ Symptom typical of HF: Breathlessness at rest or on exercise, fatigue, tiredness, ankle swelling.
+ Signs typical of HF: Tachycardia, tachypnea, pulmonary rales, pleural effusion, raised jugular venous pressure, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly.
+ Objectif evidence of a structural or functional abnormality of the heart at rest: Cardiomegaly, third heart sound, cardiac murmurs, abnormality on the echocardiogram, raised natriuretic (BNP or NT-pro-BNP) concentration.
3. Classification of HF by ESC: LVEF may be:
+ Reduced LV ejection fraction (LVEF ≤ 40%) - Heart failure with reduced ejection function (HFrEF).
+ Preserved LV ejection fraction (LVEF ≥ 50%) - Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).
+ Mid-range LV ejection fraction (LVEF 41%-49%) - Heart Failure with the LVEF being in the mid-range (HFmrEF).

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- The prevalence of HF is around 1-2% of adult in the developing countries:
+ The prevalence increased with age, CVRF, Post MI:
- Around 1% for those age younger than 55 years,
- To &gt;10% in those age older than 70 years old.
- The prevalence of HF in Cambodia is around 3-4% in general population.

## III. ETIOLOGIES

- A. The common underlying causes of HF in adults are:
- Ischemic Heart Diseases (IHD)
- Hypertension
- Dilated cardiomyopathy-idiopathic, familial
- Valvular heart disease
- Diabetic cardiomyopathy
- B. Other causes of HF include:
- Congenital heart disease
- Cor pulmonale
- Pericardial disease: constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade
- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
- Viral myocarditis
- Acute rheumatic fever
- Toxic: Alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy e.g. doxorubicin, trastuzumab (Herceptin), cyclophosphamide.

- Endocrine and metabolic disorders: thyroid disease, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma.
- Collagen vascular disease: systemic lupus erythematosis, polymyositis, polyarteritis nodosa.
- Tachycardia induced cardiomyopathy eg uncontrolled atrial fibrillation.
- Infiltrative cardiac disease e.g. amyloid, hyper-eosinophilic syndrome.
- High output HF e.g. severe anaemia, large A-V shunts/malformations.
- Peripartum cardiomyopathy.
- Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

- A. Pathophysiology:
- a. Cardiac Output (CO): Stroke Volume (SV) x Heart Rate (HR): depend on:
- SV depend on Pre-load, After-load, Myocardial contractility,
- Neuro-hormonal activations:
+ Sympathetic nervous system (SNS): Beta-1, Beta-2, Alpha-1,
+ System renin angio-tension aldosterone system (RAAS),

## b. Cardiovascular r isk factors :

- HTN,
- Prediabetes/DM,
- Dyslipidemia
- Smoking
- Diet, Alcohol, obesity, physical inactivity,
- Age, gender, ASCVD

## V. DIAGNOSIS

- A. Clinical
- a. Past medical history of CVDs? CVRF?
- b. Symptoms:
- Breathlessness,
- Orthopnea,

- Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea,
- Cough+/-wheezing
- Reduce exercise tolerance,
- Fatigue,
- Tiredness,
- Increased time to recover after exercise,
- Leg/Ankle/foot swelling,
- c. Signs
- Tachycardia or irregular heart pulse,
- Elevated jugular venous pressure,
- Hepatojugular reflux,
- Third heart sound (gallop rhythm)
- Laterally displaced apical impulse,
- Cardiac murmur,
- Abdominal swelling,
- Rapid weight gain,

## d. York Heart Association (NYHA) classification

This system groups heart failure into four categories by number. You may see Roman numerals used for these category names.

- NYHA-I: There are no heart failure symptoms.
- NYHA-II: Everyday activities can be done without difficulty. But exertion causes shortness of breath or fatigue.
- NYHA-III: It's difficult to complete everyday activities.
- NYHA-IV: Shortness of breath occurs even at rest. This category includes the most severe heart failure.

## e. American College of Cardiology

- Stage A. risk factors for heart failure but no signs or symptoms.
- Stage B. There is heart disease but no signs or symptoms of heart failure.
- Stage C. There is heart disease and signs or symptoms of heart failure.
- Stage D. Advanced heart failure requires specialized treatments.

## f. Left-sided heart failure symptoms include:

- Paroxysmal nocturnal shortness of breath.
- Shortness of breath during exercise or when lying flat.
- Chronic coughing or wheezing.
- Difficulty concentrating.
- Fatigue.
- Fluid retention causing swelling, or edema, in the ankles, legs and/or feet.
- Lack of appetite and nausea.

## g. Right sided heart failure symptoms include:

- General or inferior limbs oedema,
- Hepatomegalia, hepatalgia
- Turgescence jugular,
- Weight gain and increase abdominal girth.

## h. Factors triggered acute HF:

Patients with Chronic HF may occasionally develop acute decompensation. The more important causes that need to be recognised and treated appropriately are:

- Acute myocardial infarction/myocardial ischaemia.
- Arrhythmias (e.g. atrial fibrillation).
- Hypertensive emergencies.
- Infections (e.g. pneumonia).
- Non-compliance to medications.
- Excessive fluid and salt intake.
- Anaemia.
- Development of renal impairment.
- Adverse effects of drug therapy (e.g. non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).

## B. In vastigations :

## a. ECG:

- To assess heart rat, rhythm, QRS morphologie, QRS duration, QRS voltage, evidence of ischemia, LV hypertrophic and arrhythmia.

<!-- image -->

## c. Chest X-ray:

- To look for pulmonary congestion, Cardiomegaly and presence of underlying lung pathology, patient with HFpEF may have a cardiac normal size. d. Blood tests:
- FBC, renal function, liver function, serum glucose, lipid profile,
- Urinalysis, to look for proteinuria, glucosuria,
- Natriuretic Peptides (NP): (. Brain natriuretic petide (BNP) or . N-terminal pro BNP (NTproBNP)): BNP and NTproBNP are a family of hormones secreted by the ventricules in response to wall stress,

They are useful in the following situations:

+ In the emergency setting:
- NB are useful as a '' rule out" test for patients presenting with acute dyspnea. A level of &lt; 100pg/ml for BNP and &lt; 300mg/ml for NTproBNT makes the diagnosis of acute HF unlikely. These levels are affected by renal function and gender.
- A high level supports the diagnosis of acute HF and very high levels correlate with the severity of HF and adverse outcome.
- e. Heart Ultrasound (Echocardiography): this will allow access of:
- LV chamber size, volume and systolic function.
- LV wall thickness, evidence of scarring and wall motion abnormalities,
- Diastolic function of the heart,
- Valvular structure and function,
- Congenital cardiac abnormalities,
- LV mechanical dyssynchrony
- Pulmonary hypertension,

<!-- image -->

## VI. IFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- Chronic pulmonary disease (COPD), Asthma, Pulmonary fibrosis, Pulmonary hypertension,
- Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pneumothorax, Aspiration foreign body

## VII. ANAGEMENT OF HF

## A. Objectives

- Prevention of recurrents: Etiologies treatement and triggered factors
- Management of asymptoms LV dysfunction.
- Improve quality of life,
- Prolongation of life expectancy.

## B. Critical signs

- Orthopnea, APO
- Persistent chest pains or chest discomfort,
- Palpitations with optimal treatment.
- Cardiac arrest. Persistence of symptom after three months of optimal treatment.

## C. Mortality risk factors

- Ventricular arrhythmia, Afib with height heart rates,
- Multi-lesion coronary artery disease
- CKD, HTA, T2D
- Anemia,
- Hyponatremia and hypokalemia.

## D. Out patient management

- Patient educations, lifestyle management, call 119 in case emergency.
- Regular follow up

## E. Medical treatment

- To reduce volume overload: Lube diuretic +/- MRA
- First line medicine to reduce morbid mortalities: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, BB, MRA, SGLT2i

## Chronic Heart Failures treatment

- Classic: Digoxin + Diuretics,
- Modern: Base on the randomized studies: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI + Beta-blocker +/- Diuretics +/- Digoxin.

NB: HF treatment: Treatment of activation neuro-hormones.

## + New Guideline HF treatment with LV dysfunction:

- Stage 1: ACEI /ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- SGLT2i
- Stage 2: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA, Betablocker +/- SGLT2i,
- Stage 3: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- Betablocker +/- SGLT-2 Inhibitors +/- Digoxin
- Stage 4: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- Betablocker +/- SGLT-2 Inhibitors +/- Digoxin

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- HF with CHD,
- Diabetes and HF,
- HF in pregnancy,
- HF in adult congenital heart disease (ACHD),
- Arrhythmia-induced HF,
- Cardio-oncology and HF,
- HF and kidney dysfunction,
- HF with desynchronization
- Advanced HF/Refractory Hf/Heart transplant,
- HF with Mechanical circulatory support,
- Palliative and end of life care.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- The prognostic of HF depends on its comorbid-mortality.
- Latest studies have shown that the survival rates of people with chronic HF were:
- o 80% to 90% for one year,
- o 50% to 60% for year five,
- o Most people with end-stage HF have a life expectancy of less than one year.

## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

- Lifestyle change, patience education,
- Vaccination, flux, pneumonias, typhoïde, etc.,
- Optimal management of LV dysfunction asymptomatic.
- Optimal management of HF base on new guideline.
- Optimized all causes, IHD, VHD, CHD etc.
- Optimized treatment of comorbid-mortality of HF,
- Optimized medical treatment of cardiovascular risk factors.
- Vaccinations,

## XI. URGERIES AND DEVICES

- Heart surgeries and Intervention cardiology for heart disease that causes HF.
- Devices
- o Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT): biventricular pacing, is used to help improve the heart's rhythm and the symptoms associated with the arrhythmia. In effect, it is "resynchronizing'' the heart.
- o Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD): If an abnormal of heart rhythm is detected, the device will deliver an electric shock to restore a normal heartbeat.
- o Heart transplantation: remains de gold standard for the treatment of advanced HF in the absence of contraindication.

## KEYS MESSAGES

- o Patients with HF are classified based on their LVEF. Those with a LVEF between 41% and 49% are defined as 'mildly reduced LVEF (HFmrEF).
- o Measurement of NPs and echocardiography have key roles in the diagnosis of HF.
- o ACE-I or ARNI, beta-blockers, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended as cornerstone therapies for patients with HFrEF.
- o ICDs are recommended in selected patients with HFrEF of an ischaemic aetiology and should be considered in those with a nonischaemic aetiology.
- o CRT-P/D is recommended in those patients with HFrEF, in sinus rhythm, with a LBBB &gt;\_150 ms and should be considered in those with a LBBB &gt;130-149 ms or non-LBBB &gt;\_150 ms.
- o Advanced HF strategies (heart transplantation/MCS) may be appropriate in selected patients.
- o ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blockers, and MRA may be considered in patients with HFmrEF.
- o The diagnosis of HFpEF requires objective evidence of cardiac structural, or functional abnormalities as well as elevated plasma NP concentrations consistent with the presence of LV diastolic dysfunction and raised LV filling pressures. A diastolic stress test is recommended when these markers are equivocal.
- o To date, no treatment has been shown to reduce mortality and morbidity in patients with HFpEF.
- o Exercise is recommended for all patients who are able, to improve exercise capacity andQOL, and reduce HF hospitalization.
- o Patients with advanced HF refractory to medical/device therapy and who do not have absolute contraindications should be referred for consideration of heart transplantation. MCS should also be considered as BTT or DT in selected patients.
- o Patients hospitalized for HF should be carefully evaluated to exclude persistent signs of congestion. Oral treatment should be optimized before discharge.
- o It is recommended that patients with type II diabetes are treated with SGLT2 inhibitors.

## AORTIC REGURGITATION (AR)

Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Failure of the aortic valve to close tightly causes back flow of blood into the left ventricle in diastolic.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

The prevalence of rheumatic valvular heart disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence 41millions in world wide. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Rheumatic fever more than 95%,
- Degenerative,
- Infective endocarditis
- Congenitally bicuspid,
- Prolapse from VSD
- Systemic hypertension,
- Marfan or Marfan-like syndrome
- Malignant carcinoid syndrome,
- Silence Syphilis
- Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoide arthristis.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

## A. Acute Aortic insufficiency:

In acute aortic insufficiency, the retrograde backflow of blood results in a quick rise in the LVEDV. The acute increase in preload and afterload does not allow the time for the LV to adapt to the rapid increase in volume during diastole, and this also results in a sharp rise inf LV diastolic pressure. When the LV diastolic pressure rises above the level of LA pressure, premature mitral valve closure and MR can be seen. Additionally, there will be increases in LA pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure that cause pulmonary edema. Compensatory tachycardia may occur to blunt the decline in anterograde stroke volume, and concentric hypertrophy with increased wall thickness can occur.

## B. Chronic Aortic Insufficiency:

In chronic aortic insufficiency, the LV compensates for the diastolic regurgitation of blood from the aorta into the LV by remodeling of the LV via eccentric hypertrophy of the cardiomyocytes and LV dilatation to allow for an increase in LV stroke volume and a lesser increase in wall thickness than that which would be seen in acute aortic insufficiency. However, the left end-diastolic volume and pressure rise to a high degree such that the sarcomeres can become maximally stretched, LV remodeling and compensation mechanisms fail, and interstitial fibrosis and a drop in LV compliance occur. The composite result of these changes is a decline in the initially compensated and elevated LV stroke volume.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

- A. Discovered diagnostic: Systemic examination, heart auscultation, ECG, heart ultrasound, chest x-ray.
- B. Clinical presentation:
1. Symptoms: Aortic Regurgitation are long time tolerance, 20 to 40 years after an episode of rheumatic fever
- The most common symptoms are shortness of breath, dyspnea on exertion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea.
- Palpitations, chest discomfort, chest pain.
2. Signs:
- Heart Auscultation: Diastolic murmur
- Austin Flint murmur: This is believed to occur due to the regurgitant jet of the aortic regurgitation causing premature closing of the mitral valve. This mimics functional mitral stenosis and is described as a low-pitched and rumbling mid to late diastolic or presystolic mitral murmur best heard at the apex.
- Pulsus bisferiens: A biphasic pulse with two systolic peaks seen on pressure tracings.
- Corrigan sign: A bounding pulse in large arteries such as the carotids that expands and suddenly collapses and empties between beats.
- De Musset sign: Head nodding with every heartbeat.
- Muller sign: Systolic pulsation of the uvula.
- Quincke sign: Repeatedly alternating blushing and blanching of capillaries in the nail folds upon palpation.
- Traube sign: Pistol shot sounds heard on the femoral artery upon compression of the artery.
- Waterhammer Pulse: Peripheral arterial pulses are rapidly dissipated or "bounding". This finding can be accentuated by raising the extremities.

## C. Test:

- a. ECG: Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,
- b. Heart ultrasound: key diagnosis of AR
- Positive diagnosis base on ultrasound doppler,
- Diagnosis mechanism and etiology bas on 2D echocardiography,

- Selection patient for surgery indications

## VII. MANGEMENT

1. The goals of aortic valve regurgitation treatment are ease symptoms and prevent complications.
- If your symptoms are mild or you don't have symptoms, you may only need regular health checkups. You may need regular echocardiograms to check the health of the aortic valve. Heart-healthy lifestyle changes also are usually recommended.
2. Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis (See ARF and Endocarditis)
3. Medical treatment:
- Treat symptoms
- Reduce the risk of complications
- Lower blood pressure
8. o Volume overload: Loop diuretic with or without MRA, ACEi, ARB (see HF treatment)
9. o Prevention LV remodelling: ACEi, ARB, BB, MRA
10. o Thrombo-embolic prevention: if sinus rhythm undergone ASP-75-81mg/day, if Afib or Fluter: AVK (INR: 2-3) or NOAC,

- Surgery indications: May be needed especially if the condition and symptoms are severe. Asymptom patient and echocardiography showed sever aortic regurgitations (see algorhythm)
- Mechanical AVR: undergone AVK (INR: 2-3),
- Biological AVR: Sinus rhythm undergone anti-agregant platelats, if Afib undergone anti-coagulation.
4. Algorhythm

Management of patients with aortic regurgitation

- Significant enlargement of ascending aorta
  - Y → Surgery
  - N → Severe aortic regurgitation
    - Y → Symptoms
      - Y → Surgery
      - N → LVEF ≤ 50% or LVEDS > 50 mm (or > 25 mm/m² BSA)
        - Y → Surgery
        - N → Follow-up
    - N → Follow-up

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- AR associated with others VHD: reevaluated may need to operate together.
- AR associate with CAD, CAG help to make diagnosis to do P
- Pregnancy:
- o Mild to moderated AR closely followed up small dose of diuretic if volume overload.
- o Severe symptomatic AR with advanced HF, need to do cesarean or abortion
- Stroke: Stroke treatment and HF management.

## IX. COMPLICATIONS

- Heart failures: First left HF and the right HF,
- Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death,

- Arrhythmia: Atrial flutter, Afib need undergone systemic thrombo-embolic prevention.
- Strokes
- Infectious endocarditis,

## X. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Good prognosis if early good management, bad prognosis if presence severe LV dysfunction.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION:

- Prevention: Acute rheumatism and endocarditis, closely followed up for moderated and severe AR.
- o Severe AR with symptoms or a symptom AR and echocardiography showed important LV dilated or LV dysfunction: AVR.

- Recommendation: (see Algorhythme)
- o Mild to moderated MS: followed up

## AORTIC STENOSIS (AS)

Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Uncompleted opened aortic valves less than 2cm2 during LV telesystolic (normal Aortic Surface Area: 2,5 to 3,5cm 2 . Severe AS &lt;0,75cm 2 or &lt;0,50cm 2 /m 2. Moderated AS: 0,75 to 1,5cm 2 or 0,5 to 1cm 2 /m 2 . Mild AS: 1,5 to 2cm 2 ).

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

The prevalence of rheumatic disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence of 41 million worldwide. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.

There are large differences in the epidemiology of aortic valve disease between highincome and low-income countries. Rheumatic valvulopathy is most commonly seen in low-income countries. The incidences of aortic stenosis in the developing countries with the population age older than 75 years is high (374 cases per 100,000).

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Rheumatic fever more than 90% (in Cambodia)
- Calcification (in developing countries)
- Congenitally bicuspid,
- Monkeberg disease
- Malignant carcinoid syndrome,
- Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoid arthritis.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY:

Left ventricular (LV) obstruction caused by the stenosis of the valve increases LV systolic pressure. It also results in increased LV ejection time (LVET), decreased aortic pressure, and increased LV end-diastolic pressure. The increased afterload, in addition, to an increase in LV volume overload, leads to an increase in LV mass, ultimately leading to LV dysfunction and failure. Myocardial oxygen consumption increases with increased LV systolic pressure, LV mass, and LVET, while myocardial perfusion time decreases with increased LVET. Hence, LV function further deteriorates with increased myocardial oxygen consumption and decreased myocardial oxygen supply.

(From Boudouias H, Gravanis MB: Valvular heart disease. In Gravanis MB [ed): Cardiovascular Disorders: Pathogenesis and Pathophysiology. St. Louis, CV Mosby, 1993, p 64.)

<!-- image -->

## V. DIAGNOSIS

Many people with aortic stenosis, or AS, don't experience noticeable symptoms until the amount of restricted blood flow becomes greatly reduced or Aortic surface less than 1cm2

- A. Discovered diagnostic: Systemic examination, heart auscultation, ECG, heart ultrasound, chest x-ray.
- B. Clinical presentation:
- a. Symptoms:
- Angina, chest discomfort on exertion
- Syncope
- Shortness of breath, dyspnea, Symptom
- Acute pulmonary oedema.
- Palpitations,

In severe aortic stenosis with these symptoms indicated the time to surgery, if patients delay surgery will have mortality approximately 100% in five years in coming.

- b. Signs:
- Heart Auscultation:
3. . Systolic murmur: Maximal at left sternum, 2 nd space of intercostal (ribs), radiation to jaw, apec. The second heart sound may lack a split and can be heard as a single sound during inspiration.
4. . Palpation: Carotid upstroke can be observed. A slow-rising, late-peaking, and a lowamplitude carotid impulse, pulsus parvus et tardus, is an expected finding in severe aortic stenosis and, when present, is specific to aortic stenosis.
- C. Test:
- a. ECG: Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- a. Pulmonary stenosis,
- b. VSD
- c. Mitral regurgitation,

## VII. MANAGEMENT

- A. The goals of aortic valve stenosis treatment are to prevent sudden cardiac death and prevent complications.
2. If patients symptoms are mild or asymptoms, they may only need regular health checkups. They may need regular echocardiograms to check the health of the aortic valve. Heart-healthy lifestyle changes also are usually recommended.
- B. Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis (See ARF and Endocarditis)
- C. Medical treatment:
- Treat symptoms
- Reduce the risk of complications,
7. . Volume overload: Loop diuretic with or without MRA. ( see HF treatment)
8. . Prevention LV remodelling,
9. . Thrombo-embolic prevention: if sinus rhythm undergone ASP-75-81mg/day, if Afib or Fluter: AVK (INR: 2-3) or NOAC,
- D. Surgery indications: when patients have symptoms (Angina, syncope, shortness of breath or HF, Acute pulmonary oedema.
11. . Mechanical AVR: undergone AVK (INR: 2-3),

- . Biological AVR: Sinus rhythm undergone anti-agregant platelate, if Afib or Flutter undergone anti-coagulation, AVK or NOAC.

## E. Algorithm:

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 370 -->
- Management of patients with severe aortic stenosisᵃ
  - LVEF < 50%
    - N → Symptoms
      - Y → Intervention likely to be of benefitᵇ (after assessment of comorbidity and frailty)
        - N → Medical therapy
      - Y → Physically active
        - Y → Exercise test
          - Y → Symptoms or sustained fall in BP below baseline
            - Y → Heart Team evaluationᶜ
              - Y → Indicators of adverse prognosisᵈ and low procedural risk
                - N → Educate patient and reassess in 6 months (or as soon as possible if symptoms occur)
                - Y → Patients < 75 years at low-risk for SAVR (STS-PROM/ EuroSCORE II < 4%)ᵉ OR Unsuitable for TF TAVI and operable
                  - → SAVRᶠ
                - Y → All other patients
                  - → SAVRᶠ or TAVIᶠ
                - Y → Patients ≥ 75 years OR Unsuitable/High risk for SAVR (STS-PROM/ EuroSCORE II > 8%)ᵉ AND Suitable for TF TAVI
                  - → TAVIᶠ
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- Pregnancy:
- o Mild to moderated AS closely followed, no special medical management.
- o Severe symptoms, angina, syncope, HF symptoms, acute pulmonary oedema:
- Closely followed up, HF treatments, cesarean or obortion if need,
- Associated with others VHD: need surgery same time.
- Coronary artery diseases: need PCI, or CABG with AVR.
- Stroke: Stroke treatment and HF management.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND COMPLICATIONS

- Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death,
- Heart failures: First left HF and then right HF,

- Arrhythmia: Atrial flutter, Afib need undergone systemic thrombo-embolic prevention.
- Strokes
- Infectious endocarditis,

## X. PROGNOSIS

Good prognosis if early management before complications,

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- a. Prevention: Acute rheumatism and endocarditis, closely followed up for moderated and severe AS

- b. Recommendation: (see Algorithm)
- Mild to moderate AS: followed up
- Severe AS with symptoms: need surgery, AVR.

## MANAGEMENT OF AORTIC ANEURYSM

Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Aortic dilatation, in clinical practice, aortic root dilatation can be suspected in male adults when aortic diameter is &gt;40 mm and in females at &gt;36 mm or with an indexed diameter/BSA (aortic size index [ASI]) &gt;22 mm/m2.

Arterial aneurysm is defined as a diameter &gt;1.5 times (&gt;50%) larger than the predicted one.

Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of a blood vessel, affecting all three layers of the vessel wall. An aneurysm is a permanent, localized arterial dilation to more than 50% of the normal diameter. True aneurysms involve all three layers, while pseudoaneurysms disrupt intimal and medial layers.

Aneurysms can be classified by appearance, fusiform or saccular aneurysm.

- [ ]  Fusiform: Circumferential widening of the artery

- [ ]  Saccular: Localized, typically asymmetric, outpouchings of the artery wall.

Ectasia is an arterial dilatation &lt;150% of normal arterial diameter.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)

Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA) have an estimated incidence of at least 5 to 10 per 100,000 person-years. Aortic root or ascending aortic aneurysms are most common (approximately 60%), followed by aneurysms of the descending aorta (approximately 35%) and aortic arch (&lt;10%).

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)

AAAs occur in 3% to 9% of men older than 50 years and are the most common form of aortic aneurysms. Most AAAs (&gt;80%) arise in the infrarenal aorta.

- [ ]  90% of all abdominal aortic aneurysms &gt;4.0 cm is related to atherosclerotic disease.

- [ ]  Risk of rupture increases with size: the 5-years risk of aneurysms &lt; 5cm is 1-2%; whereas it is 20-40% for aneurysms &gt; 5 cm in diameter.

## III. PATHOGENESIS AND ETIOLOGY

Aortic aneurysms result from conditions that cause degradation or abnormal production of the structural components of the aortic wall: elastin and collagen.

The causes of aortic aneurysms may be broadly categorized as degenerative disorders, genetic or developmental diseases, vasculitis, infections, and trauma.

## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)

*Aortic root or ascending aorta:

- [ ]  Syndromic: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Turner syndrome.

- [ ]  Non-Syndromic: Bicuspid aortic valve, Sporadic TAA, Familial TAA.

*Descending aorta:

- [ ]  Atherosclerosis

- [ ]  Aortitis (non-infectious): vasculitis disorders (eg, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

- [ ]  Aortitis (infectious): Syphilis, Infected (mycotic) TAA cause by systemic or local infections (eg, sepsis, pneumonia), lymphangitic spread (eg, tuberculosis).

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)

- [ ]  Atherosclerosis (majority cause): risk factor: Smoking, age, HTN, Hyperlipidemia, Male sex; Family history of AAA, other cardiovascular disease

- [ ]  Inflammatory aneurysm

- [ ]  Infectious aneurysm

- [ ]  Inherited connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome).

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

A wide variety of pathological factors are associated with aortic aneurysms. These include degenerative diseases, inherited disorders, infections, inflammatory conditions (i.e., vasculitis), and trauma.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## 1. Clinic

## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):

Most TAAs are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally. Less frequently revealed by clinical symptoms:

- [ ]  Pain - tearing, radiating to back

- [ ]  Heart failure - due to AR

- [ ]  Thromboembolic (stroke, painful/parenthesis of limbs)

- [ ]  Hoarseness of voice (compression of recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, plethora and edema from superior vena cava compression

- [ ]  Aorto-esophageal fistula and hemoptysis can also be seen.

- [ ]  Can mimic other acute disorders (AMI, renal colic, pancreatitis)

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):

- [ ]  Asymptomatic

- [ ]  Incidental finding on abdominal imaging examination: as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, and nontender mass, frank ecchymosis.

- [ ]  Acute abdominal pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation or endovascular repair.

## 2. Investigation

## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):

- [ ]  Chest x-ray: widening of the mediastinal shadow and displacement or compression of the trachea or left main stem bronchus

- [ ]  Echocardiogram or transesophageal echocardiography, can be used to assess the proximal ascending aorta and descending thoracic aorta

- [ ]  Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI are sensitive and specific tests for assessment of aneurysms of the thoracic aorta and involvement of branch.

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):

- [ ]  Abdomen x-ray: demonstrate the calcified outline of the aneurysm; 25% not calcified.

- [ ]  Ultrasonography: screening and surveillance.

- [ ]  CT or MRI: gold standard's in the pre-operative and post-operative evaluation of AAA.

- [ ]  Since the presence of mural thrombi may reduce the luminal size, aortography may underestimate the diameter of an aneurysm.

## VI. DIFFERENCIAL DIAGNOSIS

- [ ]  Chest pain

- [ ] o Acute myocardial infarction

- o Pulmonary embolism
- o Spontaneous pneumothorax
- o Esophageal rupture

- [ ]  Abdominal pain

- o Renal/biliary colic
- o Bowel obstruction/perforation
- o Non-dissection-related mesenteric ischemia

- [ ]  Back pain

- o Renal colic
- o Musculoskeletal pain
- o Intervertebral disc herniation

- [ ]  Focal neurologic deficit

- o Primary ischemic cerebrovascular accident
- o Cauda equina syndrome

## VII. MANAGEMENT

1. Objective

The goal is to slow the growth of the aneurysm and prevent the rupture or dissection.

2. Critical signs

*Risk of dissection:

- [ ]  Diameter &gt; 60mm of ascending aorta

- [ ]  Diameter &gt; 70mm of descending aorta.

## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA):

- a. Medical therapy:
2. o Control blood pressure: (target BP&lt; 130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP &lt; 140/90mmHg for diabetic; target HR: 60bpm.)
- Beta blocker (Atenolol; Bisoprolol, Metoprolol…)
- ACEi or ARB
5. o Statin for dyslipidemia target LDL cholesterol &lt;70 mg/dL.
6. o Screening 6 months after initial scan then every 12 months unless symptomatic or increased rate of expansion or if size is 4.5cm - 5.5cm.
7. o Smoking Cessation

## b. Percutaneous or surgical intervention:

Indication for surgery:

- o Instable Hemodynamic
- o Symptomatic

- o Diameter ≥ 55mm or rate of growth ≥ 1.0cm per year.
- o Causing bronchial compression, aortobronchial or aortoesophageal fistulas
- o Traumatic, Mycotic
- *Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR) or Open surgery repair.

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA):

- [ ]  AAA diameter of 25-29 mm, Ultrasound imaging should be considered 4 years later.

- [ ]  Patient with small diameter (30-55mm), The interval for imaging should be considered:

- o Every 3 years for AAA of 30-39mm.

- [ ] o Every 2 years for AAA of 40-44mm diameter.

- o Every year for AAA of &gt; 45mm diameter.
- a. Medical Therapy:

- [ ]  Control blood pressure: (target BP&lt; 130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP &lt; 140/90mmHg for diabetic or CKD; target HR: 60bpm.). Beta blocker is 1st line in HTA drug with AAA. ACEi, ARB and other Antihypertension is drug of choice.

- [ ]  Statins: reduce the risk of cardiovascular events related to atherosclerosis

- o cardiovascular disease and rupture.

- [ ]  Antiplatelet to reduce intraluminal mural thrombus is controversial but usually use in o others indication of CVD.

- [ ]  Smoking Cessation

## b. Surgical Therapy Indication:

- [ ]  Asymptomatic AAA:

- o Diameter &gt;55mm.
- o Aneurysm growth &gt;10mm per year.

- [ ]  Symptomatic AAA

- o In case of ruptured AAA, emergency repair is indicated.
- o In case of symptomatic but non ruptured AAA, urgent repair is indicated.

## AAA repair methods:

- [ ]  Open aortic aneurysm repair

- [ ]  Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EAVR)

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiac abnormality. A thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is present ≈ 50% of BAV patients, who also have an 8-fold higher risk of aortic dissection than the general population.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- [ ]  Thoracic abdominal aneurysms (TAA) enlarge an average of 3 to 5 mm/year.

- [ ]  Risk factors for rapid enlargement include larger size of aneurysm, location in the descending aorta, and presence of mural thrombi.

- [ ]  The risk of rupture appears to rise abruptly as TAAs reach 6 cm in diameter.

- [ ]  Survival rate of patients with untreated large TAAs is 54% at 5 years.

- [ ]  TAA rupture has a mortality of 97%.

- [ ]  Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) typically enlarge at a rate of 10%/year, but some

enlarge exponentially; about 20% remain the same size indefinitely.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- [ ]  Rupture or Dissection

- [ ]  Thrombus embolism.

- [ ]  Lower Limb ischemia.

- [ ]  Infected (mycotic) aneurysms

- [ ]  Aorto-enteric fistulas, Aorto-caval fistulas

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- [ ]  Stringent control of hypertension

- [ ]  Lipid profile optimization

- [ ]  Smoking cessation

- [ ]  Other atherosclerosis risk reduction measures.

- [ ]  Avoid isometric exercises

## MITRAL REGURGITATION (MR)

Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Is the heart valve condition in which the flaps of the mitral valve do not close properly, causing a backward flow of blood back to the left atrium.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

MR is the most common valvular abnormality worldwide, affecting over 2 to 3% of the total population and has a prevalence that increases with age.

## III. ETIOLOGY

## A. Primary MR:

- a. Infectious/Rheumatic:
- Rheumatism valvular heart disease is most common cause of VHD, more than 95% of total VHD in the developing country,
- Endocarditis
- b. Degenerative:
- Mitral valve prolapses,
- Myxomatous degenerative,
- Maorfanc syndrome
- c. Congenital:
- Congenital malformations of the mitral valve,
- B. Secondary MR:
- a. Papillary Muscle Rupture:
- Papillary muscle rupture is a very rare condition seen in 1% to 2% of patients after myocardial infarction (MI)
- or infective endocarditis. It leads to severe mitral regurgitation due to dysfunction of the papillary muscles,
- b. Ischemic MR (IMR):
- IMR results from prior MI associated with normal mitral valve leaflets and chordae. Ischemia of the segments underlying the papillary muscles results in remodeling. This phenomenon causes papillary muscle displacement, which results in a more apical position of the leaflets known as a "seagull sign".
- c. Congestive heart failure (CHF) Associated:
- Cause by annulus dilation
- Remodeling of left LV
- d. Chronic Atrial Fibrillation,
- e. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
- f. Other rare causes of MR such as prolonged use of certain medications can cause MR,

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

## A. Pathophysiology mechanism:

- The definition of mitral regurgitation is a retrograde flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
- Mitral regurgitation leads to left ventricular volume overload due to increased stroke volume, caused by an increase in blood volume within the left atrium and hence an increased preload delivered to the left ventricle during diastole.
- In chronic progressive MR, ventricular remodeling occurs, allowing maintenance of cardiac output, and an initial increase in ejection fraction (EF) is usually observed. - --
- However, depending on the regurgitant fraction, the effective EF can be considerably lower. Over time, there is a positive feedback loop by which volume overload from MR causes ventricular dilatation, widening of the mitral annulus, and diminished coaptation of leaflets, leading to further worsening of MR.
- Eventually, volume overload becomes so severe that excitation-contraction coupling becomes impaired and wall stress-related afterload on the left ventricle leading to dilatation and decreased contractility, resulting in a reduction of EF.

## B. Anatomy pathology: Any disease affection these anatomies can cause MR, - Mitral leaflets (anterior and posterior)

- Mitral valve annulus,
- Chordae teninease
- Papillary muscle
- LV remodeling,

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## C. Carpentier classification:

- Type I: Normal leaflet motion
+ annular dilation, leaflet perforation
+ regurgitation jet directed centrally
- Type II: Excessive leaflet motion
+ papillary muscle rupture, chordal rupture, redundant chordae,
+ eccentric jet, directed away from involved leaflet.
- Type III: restricted leaflet motion,
+ IIIa: leaflet motion restricted in both systole and diastole,
- . rheumatic heart disease,
- . jet may be centrally or eccentrically directed,
+ IIIb: leaflet motion restricted in diastole
- . papillary muscle dysfunction, LV dilation,
- . jet may be centrally or eccentrically directed.

| Carpentier's   | Functional Classification                      | Example(s)                                             |
|----------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Type I         | Normal leaflet motion                          | Annular dilation (secondary MR) or leaflet perforation |
| Type II        | Excessive leaflet motion                       | Mitral prolapse or flail                               |
| Type III       | Restricted leaflet motion                      | LV dilatation                                          |
| Illa           | Restricted opening (during systole & diastole) | Rheumatic disease                                      |
| IIIb           | Restricted closure (during systole)            | Ischemic MR, functional MR                             |

## V. DIAGNOSIS

- A. Clinical presentation: normally patients asymptom for long decade for mild or moderated chronic MR (inferior than grad III)
- B. Symptoms:
1. Acute severe MR:
- Palpitation, chest discomfort,
- Dyspnea NYHA III, IV,
- Orthopnea, Acute pulmonary embolism,
2. Chronic Rheumatic severe MR:
- Long term compensated
- For severe chronic Rheumatic MR superior than grade III,
+ Fatigue,
+ Shortness of breaths (dyspnea) on exertion, grade by NYHA
+ Orthopnea, Acute pulmonary embolism.
+ Palpitations,
+ Chest discomforts,

## C. Signes:

+ Heart Auscultation: Holosystolic murmur, maximum apex, radiated to axillary,

+ Galop of S3 or Galops,
+ Tachycardia: regular (sinus rhythm) or irregular (Atrial Fibrillation)
+ Enlarge of chock point to the left apex due to LV dilations,
+ Lung auscultation: Crackle if APO or acute bronchitis.

1. ECG: Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,
2. Echocardiolgraphie: (Key exman to diagnose MR)
- Quantification of severity of MR by PISA
- Certified etiologie of MR
- Evaluation of LV function and LV dilation,
- Estimatate PAP,
- Selected patient for indications interventional surgery and opened heart surgery.

## VII. MANAGEMENT: MR IS LONG TERM TOLERANCE

- Mild to Moderate: Follow up and prevention of endocarditis and RAA.
- Sever chronic MR symptomatic:
- Medical treatment:
- o Prevention of endocarditis and RAA.
- Sinus rhythm:
+ Volume overload: Loupe diuretic (Furosemide) +/- MRA (Spironolactone or Eplenone)
+ LV remodeling and LV dysfunction or LV dilated: HF management,
+ Thrombo-embolic prevention: Antiplatelet: ASP-81/day
- Afib or Flutter: Antithrombotic:
+ Heparin standart or henoxaparin, Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, or NOAC. etc.
+ Heart rate controle: Digoxine, Betablocker etc.
+ Volume overload: Loupe diuretic (Furosemide) +/- MRA (Spironolactone or Eplenone),
+ LV remodeling, LV dysfunction, LV dilated: HV management.

## · Surgery:

- The first choice is conservative surgery: mitral valves repair if feasible, Mitral Valve Annuloplasthies:

- MVR (Biologic or Mechanical) (see Algorithm),
+ Biologic MVR:
- . Optimal management of HF,

- . Sinus rhythm: Antiplatelet, ASP-81/day
- . AFib or Flutter: Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, etc

## + Mechacnical MVR:

- . Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, etc.
- . Optimal management of HF,
+ Interventional repair (Mitral valve clip) if contra-indication for opened heart surgery.

- MR long term tolerance

- Supraventriculaer arrhythmia: Afib, Flutter,

- Prevention of endocarditis, RAA by good management pharyngitis and other infectious diseases,

## MITRAL STENOSIS (MS)

Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Mitral stenosis (MS) is a form of valvular heart disease, characterized by narrowing of mitral valve orifice in diastole. Today, the most common cause of MS is rheumatic fever, but the stenosis usually appears clinically relevant only after several decades.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

The prevalence of rheumatic disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 100000. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Rheumatic fever more than 95%,
- Calcification of mitral valve leaflets,
- Congenital heart disease,
- Mitral annular calcification,
- Endomyocardial fibroelastosis,
- Malignant carcinoid syndrome,
- Myxom of mitral valves
- Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoid arthritis.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

- The normal mitral valve orifice area is 4 to 6cm2. If mitral valve areas less then 2cm2 cause and impediment to the blood flow from the LA int LV. This creates a presser gradient across the MV. As the gradient across the MV increases, the LV requires the atrial kick to fill with blood.
- MS causes an increase int LA pressure. The normal LV diastolic pressure is 5 mmHg. A pressure gradient across the MV of 20 mmHg due to severe MS will cause a LA pressure of about 25 mmHg. This LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature resulting in pulmonary hypertension.
- A LA pressure remains elevated, the LA will increase in size. As the LA increases in size, there is a greater chance of developing Afib. If Afib develops, the atrial kick is lost.
- Thus, the LV filling depends on the atrial kick in severe MS. With the loss of the atrial kick, there is a decrease in cardiac output and sudden development of CHF.
- MS progresses slowly from initial signs of mitral stenosis to NYHA functional class II symptoms to Afib to NYHA functional class III or IV symptoms.

## C. Anatomy pathology:

## Mitral Valve Anatomy According to the Wilkins Score

## Grade 1

- Mobility: Highly mobile valve with only leaflet tips restricted
- Thickening: Leaflet near normal in thickness (4 mm to 5 mm)
- Calcification: A single area of increased echo brightness
- Subvalvular Thickening: Minimal thickening just below the mitral leaflets

## Grade 2

- Mobility: Leaflet mid to base portions have normal mobility
- Thickening: Mid leaflets normal, considerable thickening of margins (5 to 8 mm)
- Calcification: Scattered areas of brightness confirmed to leaflet margins
- Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening of chordal structures extending to one of the chordal lengths

## Grade 3

- Mobility: Valve continues to move forward in diastole, mainly from the base
- Thickening: Thickening extending through the entire leaflet (5 mm to 8 mm)
- Calcification: Brightness extending into the mid portions of the leaflets
- Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening extended to the distal third of the chords

## Grade 4

- Mobility: No or minimal forward movement of the leaflets in diastole
- Thickening: Considerable thickening of all leaflet tissue (more than 8 mm to 10 mm)
- Calcification: Extensive brightness throughout much of the leaflet tissue
- Subvalvular Thickening: Extensive thickening and shortening of all chordal structures extending down to the papillary muscles.

- The most common symptoms are orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea,

- Ascites, edema and hepatomegaly if right side HF develops.
- There is also an increase in symptoms of fatigue and weakness with exercise and pregnancy.
- b. Signs:
- Heart Auscultation:
9. . Normal sinus rhythm: diastolic murmur, Eclat zB1 and B2

- Palpitation, cat shacking,
- Lung auscultation: crackle, sibilente,
- Right heart failure signs,

## MANAGEMENT AND SURVEILLANCE OF PROSTHETIC VALVES

Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Prosthetic heart valves are designed to replicate the function of native valves by maintaining unidirectional blood flow and can be separated into two broad categories, mechanical and bioprosthetic (also called tissue) valves, each with different advantages and disadvantages.

Mechanical heart valves (MHV) are made entirely from non-biological (artificial) materials including metals (titanium, cobalt), pyrolytic carbon, and polymers in order to provide mechanical stability and durability.

Bioprosthetic valves (BPV) are, at least in part, made from animal (e.g., porcine, bovine or equine) (heterograft or xenograft) or human (homograft or allograft) tissue mounted onto a metal or polymer supporting structure with three pillars (also called struts or posts) and have a trileaflet configuration that resembles the geometry of a native aortic valve.

## II. SELECTION OF PROSTHETIC VALVES

The choice between a mechanical and a bioprosthetic valve is a complex decision based on prosthetic valve characteristics, patient-related factors (e.g., comorbidities) and patient preferences such as wishes and expectations.

Table 1. Factors to be considered for the choice of prosthetic heart valve

| In favor of a bioprosthesis                                                | In favor of a mechanical valve                                                                                                |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| For AVR: age >65 years                                                     | For AVR: age <60/50 years                                                                                                     |
| For MVR: age >70/65 years                                                  | For MVR: age <65 years                                                                                                        |
| Anticoagulation contraindicated, not desired, or cannot be monitored       | Other indication for anticoagulation (e.g., atrial fibrillation)                                                              |
| Desired pregnancy Limited life expectancy                                  | Small aortic root size (preclusion of future transcatheter valve-in-valve [VIV] implantation for failed aortic bioprosthesis) |
| Patient preference (avoidance of risk or inconvenience of anticoagulation) | Patient preference (avoidance of risk of reintervention)                                                                      |

## III. BASELINE ASSESSMENT AND FOLLOW-UP

All patients with prosthetic valves require lifelong follow-up to detect early deterioration in prosthetic function or ventricular function, or progressive disease of another heart valve. Clinical assessment should be performed yearly or as soon as possible if new cardiac symptoms occur. TTE should be performed if any new symptoms occur or if complications are suspected. After transcatheter, as well as surgical implantation of a BHV, echocardiography, including measurement of transprosthetic gradients, should be performed within 30 days after valve implantation (i.e. baseline), at 1 year, and annually thereafter.

Many clinicians in the United States use 4-6-week INR follow-up intervals for these patients. However, the 2012 American College of Chest Physicians' guidelines suggested a 12week INR follow-up interval may be appropriate.

## IV. ANTITHROMBOTIC THERAPY

## 1. Mechanical heart valves

The term antithrombotic therapy refers to anticoagulant, antiplatelet therapy or both. All mechanical valves require lifelong oral anticoagulation using a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) (Class I). It is preferable to specify a single international normalised ratio (INR) target median value for each patient and to concede that the acceptable range includes 0.5 INR units either side of this target. There are no data to support the use of non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in patients with MHVs.

Table 2 Target international normalized ratio for mechanical prostheses

| Prosthesis thrombogenicity   |   Patient-related risk factors a - None |   Patient-related risk factors a - ≥1 risk factor |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Low b                        |                                     2.5 |                                               3.0 |
| Medium c                     |                                     3.0 |                                               3.5 |
| High d                       |                                     3.5 |                                               4.0 |

AF = atrial fibrillation; LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction.

- a Mitral or tricuspid valve replacement; previous thromboembolism; AF; mitral stenosis of any degree; LVEF &lt;35%.
- b Carbomedics, Medtronic Hall, ATS, Medtronic Open-Pivot, St Jude Medical, Sorin Bicarbon.
- c Other bileaflet valves with insufficient data.
- d Lillehei-Kaster, Omniscience, Starr-Edwards (ball-cage), Bjork-Shiley and other tilting-disc valves.

## 2. Adjunctive antithrombotic pharmacotherapy in bioprosthetic valves

- VKA for 3 months should be considered in all patients with a mitral or tricuspid BHV and ASA or VKA should be considered for 3 months after surgical implantation of an aortic bioprosthesis.
- OAC is recommended lifelong for patients with surgical BHVs who have other indications for anticoagulation. The evidence supporting the use of NOACs in preference to VKA has increased.

## V. SPECIAL CASES

- Combination of oral anticoagulant (OAC) with antiplatelet drugs: this combination may be considered in patients with coexistent atherosclerotic (e.g., peripheral artery, coronary artery or cerebrovascular) disease (Class IIb)
- Interruption of anticoagulant therapy for planned invasive procedure: bridging therapy during interruption of oral anticoagulation for planned invasive procedures is a complex issue (discussed in "Vitamin K antagonism in surgery" section)
- Management of vitamin K antagonist (VKA) overdose and bleeding (Table 3)

| INR >4.5 with bleeding         | ▪ The VKA should be discontinued ▪ 10 mg vitamin K should be administrated by slow i.v, infusion and repeated every 12 h if needed ▪ Until the anticoagulation effect is reversed, administration of prothrombin complex concentration (PCC) and/or fresh frozen plasma (FFP) therapy should be initiated according to body weight and pre-treatment INR. ▪ Monitored by re-check of INR at 30 min and every 4-6 h until normalization. ▪ The optimal time to restart anticoagulation should be discussed in relation to location of the bleeding event and interventions performed to stop bleeding and/or to treat an underlying cause.   |
|--------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| INR > 10 without bleeding      | ▪ The use of PCC and/or FFP therapy is not recommended ▪ The VKA must be stopped ▪ oral vitamin K (2.5-5 mg) prescribed, while the INR must be monitored on a daily base for 2 weeks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding | ▪ The VKA should be stopped temporarily, and a small dose of oral vitamin K (1-2 mg) can be considered on an individual basis balancing between the risks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| INR <4.5 and asymptomatic      | ▪ Requiring careful down-titration and/or skipping one or more doses. ▪ In all patients with MHVs, VKAs must be resumed once the INR achieves the therapeutic range or is slightly elevated                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

## - Mechanic heart valves (MHV) in pregnancy:

- o The need for anticoagulation increases maternal and foetal mortality and morbidity due to the risk of MHV thrombosis and high risk of bleeding during pregnancy and delivery.
- o The potentially teratogenic VKAs cross the placenta and have a dosedependent relationship with adverse outcomes, including foetal wastage and embryopathy.
- o It is very challenging to manage the anticoagulant during pregnancy for the safety of mother and child as well as avoiding the complications.

## VI. COMPLICATIONS

- Structural failure (bioprosthetic valves): resulting in thickening, calcification, tearing, or disruption of the prosthetic valve (PV) with eventual haemodynamic dysfunction, manifesting as stenosis, regurgitation or a combination of both.
- Thrombosis and thromboembolism: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction and embolism.
- Pannus formation: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction
- Paraprosthetic regurgitation
- Bleeding related to antithrombotic therapy
- Intravascular haemolysis
- Infectious endocarditis
- Heart failure

## VII. PATIENT EDUCATION

Patients should be educated about

- Prosthetic valve outcomes,
- The need for proper care (including optimal dental care, the need for antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, and when required, appropriate antithrombotic therapy)
- Seeking prompt medical attention for any new sign or symptom that might be related to a valve complication such as a significant change in the audible click of a mechanical prosthesis, persistent or recurrent fever, decrease in exercise tolerance, ischemic cerebral events, or palpitations.
- The relation of VKA and diet
- Follow-up and checking PT and INR regularly with his/her doctor.
- Not to start, stop, or change the dose of any medicine or supplement without checking with his/her doctor.
- Telling his/her doctor, nurse, and pharmacist about all medicines he/she takes. This includes prescription or over-the-counter medicines, natural products, and vitamins. (As in Cambodia, prescribed-VKA patient should not take other medication without consulting his/her doctor due to medication interaction).
- Birth control and if she has an accidental pregnancy, should inform her follow-up doctor and not to stop taking VKA without consultation.

## DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS

Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil,

Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap,

Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha,

Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of blood clot (thrombus) in a deep vein, typically in the legs.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

DVT is a significant global health issue, affecting around 1 in 1000 people annually. The incidence increases with age and risk factors include immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, and genetic clotting disorders. DVT is more common in women due to risk factors like pregnancy and oral contraceptive use.

## III. ETIOLOGY

The etiology of DVT involves a combination of factors that promote blood clotting in the veins. These include immobility (e.g after surgery or long flights), trauma to the vein, hypercoagulability (due to genetic disorders like Factor V Leiden), and vascular injury. Additional risk factors include cancer, use of oral contraceptives, pregnancy and obesity.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The pathophysiology of DVT involves Virchow's triad, which consists of three key mechanisms: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Venous stasis, often caused by prolonged immobility, reduces blood flow, promoting clot formation. Endothelial injury from trauma or surgery triggers clotting at the injury site, while hypercoagulability - whether from genetic disorders, cancer or hormonal changes - increases the blood's tendency to clot. Together, these factors lead to thrombus formation in deep veins, usually in the legs.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

1. Clinical assessment:
- Assess symptoms (leg pain, swelling) and use a clinical prediction tool like the two-level modified Well's Score (Annex 1) to determine the likelihood of DVT
2. D-dimer Test:
- For patients with DVT unlikely, a D-dimer blood test is performed. If the D-dimer is negative, DVT is ruled out. If positive, further imaging is required.
3. Imaging with Venous Ultrasound:
- For patients with DVT likely or positive D-dimer, compression venous ultrasound is the first-line imaging test.
4. Further Imaging:
- If the ultrasound results are unclear or DVT involves unusual locations (e.g. pelvic veins), advanced imaging like CT venography or MR venography may be used.

5. Follow-up:
- In patients where initial tests are inconclusive but suspicion remains, repeat ultrasound after 5 - 7 days may be performed to confirm or exclude DVT.

## Vl. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

Several conditions that present with similar symptoms such as leg pain and swelling:

1. Cellulitis: a bacterial skin infection that cause redness and swelling
2. Muscle strain or tear: injury to muscle can lead to localized pain and swelling
3. Baker's cyst: a fluid-filled cyst behind the knee that can rupture, causing pain and swelling
4. Lymphedema: swelling due to lymphatic obstruction can mimic DVT
5. Chronic venous insufficiency: persist swelling and skin changes due to poor vein function, often confused with acute DVT

## Vll. MANAGEMENT

1. Initial assessment: risk stratification is crucial. Categorize patients as low, intermediate or high risk based on clinical presentation and underlying conditions
2. Initial treatment (first 5 - 21 days)
- Initiate anticoagulation in most patients unless contraindicated
- Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban are preferred for most non-cancer patients
- LMWH (Low molecular weight heparin) or unfractionated heparin (UFH) is used for certain patients (e.g. cancer, renal impairment, high bleeding risk).
- VKA (Vitamin K antagonists): second-line therapy. VKA are often considered when DOACs are contra-indicated or unsuitable, such as
- In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min)
- In patients on certain medications that interact with DOACs, reducing their efficacy or increase bleeding
- Compression stockings are recommended to reduce symptoms like swelling and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.

|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|

3. Long-term management (first 3 - 6 months)
- Continue anticoagulant to prevent clot extension and recurrence. The choice of anticoagulant is based on patient's characteristic
- DOACs are first-line for non-cancer patients
- LMWH is preferred in cancer patients
- Monitor for bleeding risks
4. Extended treatment (&gt; 6 months)
- For patients at high - risk of recurrence (e.g. those with active cancer, recurrent DVT, or persistent risk factors), anticoagulation may be extended indefinitely, balancing the risk of bleeding
- For patients with lower recurrence risk, anticoagulation may be stopped after 3 - 6 months, with follow-up imaging to assess for clot resolution.

          - Low risk patient
            - Short term LMWH (full or lower dose)
            - Or venous US surveillance

## Vlll. SPECIAL CASES

-  Pregnancy-Related DVT: due to physiological changes and compression of pelvic veins. Use Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for treatment.
-  Cancer-Related DVT: due to increased coagulability associated with malignancy, treatment (chemotherapy) and immobility. Management often involves long-term anticoagulation with LMWH or DOACs.
-  Post-surgical DVT: Common in orthopedic and abdominal surgeries. Prophylactic measures (e.g. early mobilization, compression stockings) and anticoagulation may be initiated perioperatively.
-  Upper extremity DVT: often associated with central venous catheters or repetitive trauma. Management focus on catheter removal and anticoagulation.
-  May-Thurner Syndrome: compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery leading to DVT. Management includes stenting or surgical intervention alongside anticoagulation.

## lX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Immediate risk: DVT can lead to serious complications such as pulmonary embolism (PE) especially in acute phase
- Long-term outcomes: many patients may experience resolution of symptoms, but some develop post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), characterized by chronic pain and swelling
- Recurrence: the risk of recurrent DVT varies based on individual risk factors (e.g. cancer, history of thrombosis), with rates ranging from 10 - 30% in 10 years
- Appropriate anticoagulation and monitoring improve outcomes, reducing the risk of complications and recurrences.

## X. COMPLICATIONS

- Pulmonary embolism (PE)
- Post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS): resulting from damage to veins and valves
- Recurrent DVT
- Chronic venous insufficiency: long-term damage to veins lead to varicoses veins and skin ulcer
- Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: a rare, severe condition where extensive thrombosis causes blue discoloration of the limb, leading to tissue ischemia and necrosis.
- Venous gangrene: a rare but critical complication (death of tissue due to compromised blood flow)

## Xl. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

- Identify individuals at high risk (e.g. surgery patients, those with cancer, or prolonged immobilization) to tailor prevention strategies
- Use compression stocking to promote venous return during hospitalization or surgery
- Pharmacological prophylaxis: administer anticoagulant (LMWH or DOACs) for highrisk patients
- Early mobilization: encourage early mobilization after surgery or during prolonged hospitalization
- Patient education: inform patients about DVT symptoms and the important of prevention measures particularly after surgery or during long travel.

## PREVENTION OF DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS

Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. INTRODUCTION

The prevention of deep venous thrombosis (DVT), a common and potentially serious condition, is a critical component of clinical care.

Effective DVT prevention begins with identifying patients at risk:

## 1. Risk factors:

- Medical conditions: Cancer, heart failure, stroke, acute infection
- Immobilization: Prolong bed rest, paralysis, or travel
- Surgery: orthopedic (hip and knee) or major abdominal/pelvic surgeries
- Previous DVT or pulmonary embolism (PE)
- Thrombophilias: inherited or acquired conditions (e.g. Factor V leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome)
- Others: obesity (BMI &gt; 30), pregnancy, hormonal therapy (oral contraceptives, or hormonal replacement)

## 2. Assessment tools

- Padua Prediciton Score (for hospitalized medical patients)
- Caprini Risk Score (for surgical patients)
- IMPROVE Bleeding Risk Score (risk assessment for bleeding)

## II. RISK ASSESSMENT AND PROPHYLACTIC RECOMMENDATION FOR MEDICAL PATIENTS

| High Risk (PPS ≥ 4)                                              | Pharmacological prophylaxis (e.g : LMWH, UFH)                          |
