## IV. ISK ASSESSMENT FOR BLEEDING

1. Improve Bleeding Risk Score

The IMPROVE bleeding risk score is a validated tool for assessing the risk of bleeding in hospitalized patients who may require pharmacological prophylaxis for DVT / PE

| Risk Factor                               |   Points |
|-------------------------------------------|----------|
| Active gastroduodenal ulcer               |        4 |
| Bleeding within 3 months before admission |        4 |
| Platelet count < 50 x 10 9 /L             |        4 |
| Age ≥ 85 years                            |        3 |
| Hepatic failure (INR > 1.5)               |        2 |
| Severe renal failure (eGFR < 30 ml/min)   |        2 |
| ICU or critical care unit stay            |        2 |
| Central venous catheter                   |        1 |
| Rheumatic disease                         |        1 |
| Current cancer                            |        1 |
| Male sex                                  |        1 |

## 2. Scoring and Risk category

- Score ≥ 7 : High risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis should be used cautiously or avoided). Mechanical prophylaxis may be alternative.
- Score &lt; 7: Low risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis is safe and recommended)

## V. METHOD OF PROPHYLAXIS

1. Mechanical Prophylaxis:

Mechanical methods promote venous blood flow and are primarily used for patients at high bleeding risk or as an adjunct to pharmacological prophylaxis

- Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC): inflatable sleeve applied to the legs to promote venous return and useful in surgical and ICU patients with high bleeding risk
- Graduated Compression Stocking (GCS): Elastic stockings that apply pressure to the legs, reducing venous stasis.
2. Pharmacological prophylaxis
- Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH):
- Enoxaparin 40 mg (SC) daily
- Enoxaparin 20 mg (SC) daily (for renal impairment with eGFR 15 - 30 ml/min)
- Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): 5000 units (SC) every 8 - 12 h, preferred in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR&lt; 30 ml/min)
- Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOA):
- Rivaroxaban: 10 mg orally once daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 15 ml/min)
- Apixaban: 2.5 mg orally twice daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 15 ml/min)
- Dabigatran: 110 mg orally on the first day, then 220 mg once daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min).

## Vl. TIMING AND INITIATION OF PROPHYLAXIS

## 1. Medical patients

- Indication: prophylaxis is indicated for hospitalized medical patients with a Padua Prediction Score ≥ 4
- Timing:
- Initiate on admission and continue throughout hospitalization
- Avoid prophylaxis in patients with active bleeding or high bleeding risk

- Option: LMWH is preferred (Enoxaparin)

## 2. Surgical patients

| Clinical situation                | Prophylactic agents       | Timing of initiation   |
|-----------------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| General Surgery                   | LMWH: Enoxaparin 40 mg OD | 12 - 24 h post-op      |
| Orthopedics                       | LMWH: Enoxaparin 40 mg OD | 12 - 24 h post-op      |
| Hip/Knee replacement Hip Fracture | Rivaroxaban 10 mg OD      | 6 - 10 h post-op       |

## Vll. DURATION OF PROPHYLAXIS

## 1. Medical patients

- Duration: Until the patient is fully ambulatory or discharged from hospital
- Extended prophylaxis: not routinely recommended after hospital discharge unless they are at very high risk of venous thromboembolism and low risk of bleeding

## 2. Surgical patients

| Indication                               | Duration                                                         |
|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Major General Surgery                    | Until hospital discharge (7 - 10 days)                           |
| Orthopedic Surgery                       | Minimum duration: 10 - 14 days                                   |
| Hip/Knee Replacement Hip Fracture repair | Extended duration: up to 35 days post-operatively is recommended |

## I. DEFINITION

Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.
- Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.
- Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.

## III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS

- Risk factors for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac factors or non-cardiac risk factors.
- It is most often from bacteria and more rarely a fungus from

| Bacteria                  | Source of Infection                                |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Staphylococcus aureus     | Skin                                               |
| Oral Streptococcus, HACEK | Oral, dental                                       |
| Group D Streptococcus     | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy)                |
| Enterococcus              | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy), Urinary tract |

| Cardiac risk factors                                                         | Non-cardiac risk factors               |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| · Previous infective endocarditis                                            | · Central venous catheter              |
| · Valvular heart disease                                                     | · People who inject drugs              |
| · Prosthetic heart valve                                                     | · Immunosuppression                    |
| · Central venous or arterial catheter                                        | · Recent dental or surgical procedures |
| · Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device Congenital heart disease | · Recent hospitalization Haemodialysis |

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

<!-- image -->

## V. DIAGNOSIS

1. Clinical Manifestations
- Symptoms: Fever is the most common symptom of IE
- It is often associated with chills, anorexia, and weight loss.
- Other common symptoms: Malaise, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, night sweats, abdominal pain, tooth pain and dyspnea.
- Signs: A new or changing cardiac
- Supportive signs: splenomegaly, petechiae or splinter hemorrhages.
- Relatively uncommon manifestations highly suggestive of IE:
- Janeway lesions
- Osler nodes
- Roth spots
2. Investigation for Endocarditis
- Blood cultures: At least two sets of blood cultures should be obtained from separate venipuncture sites prior to initiation of antibiotic therapy.
- Cardiac imaging:
- Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first diagnostic test for patients with suspected IE.
- Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has higher sensitivity than TTE and is better for detection of cardiac complications.
- Cardiac CT: May be helpful for cases in which definitive evidence of IE and its complications cannot be demonstrated with TEE, and/or for planning surgery in patients with extra valvular complications.
- Additional evaluation for IE source or complications: ECG, chest radiography, other radiographic imaging tailored to clinical manifestations, and dental evaluation.
3. Definitions of the 2023 European Society of Cardiology modified diagnostic criteria of infective endocarditis

- Haematogenous osteoarticular septic complications (i.e. spondylodiscitis).

## IE Classification (at admission and during follow-up)

## Definite:

- 2 major criteria.
- 1 major criterion and at least 3 minor criteria.
- 5 minor criteria.

## Possible:

- 1 major criterion and 1 or 2 minor criteria.
- 3-4 minor criteria.

## Rejected:

- Does not meet criteria for definite or possible at admission with or without a firm alternative diagnosis.
1. Blood cultures positive for IE
- (a) Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from two separate blood cultures: Oral streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis), HACEK group, S. aureus, E. faecalis.
- (b) Microorganisms consistent with IE from continuously positive blood cultures:
- ≥ 2 positive blood cultures of blood samples drawn &gt;12 h apart.
- All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate cultures of blood (with first and last samples drawn ≥1 h apart).
- (c) Single positive blood culture for C. burnetii or phase I IgG antibody titre &gt;1:800.
2. Imaging positive for IE:

Valvular, perivalvular/periprosthetic and foreign material anatomic and metabolic lesions characteristic of IE detected by any of the following imaging techniques:

- Echocardiography (TTE and TOE)
- Cardiac CT
- [18F]-FDG-PET/CT(A)
- WBC SPECT/CT

## Major criteria

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

The differential diagnosis for endocarditis is broad and should be considered based on two clinical categories: presence of bacteremia in the absence of valvular vegetation and presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteremia.

| Presence of bacteremia in the absence of valvular vegetation                                                                                                                   | Presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteremia                                                                                                             |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Intravascular catheter infection · Cardiac device infection · Prosthetic joint infection · Hematogenous osteomyelitis · Septic thrombophlebitis · Infected arterial aneurysm | · Culture-negative endocarditis or sterile vegetation(s) (marantic endocarditis or Libman-Sachs endocarditis) due to a noninfectious etiology or antiphospholipid syndrome. |

2. Indications and timing of surgery in the presence of heart failure in infective endocarditis:

Timing of surgical intervention in patients with IE complicated by HF should be decided by the Endocarditis Team, although surgery should not be delayed by Endocarditis Team discussions in patients requiring emergency operations. The presence of HF leads to recommendation for surgery in the majority of patients and is the principal indication for urgent surgery in IE patients.

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 425 -->
- Surgical timing for patient with left-sided infective endocarditis
  - Heart failure
    - Cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema
      - Y → Emergency surgery (Class I)
      - N → Poor haemodynamic tolerance
        - Y → Urgent surgery (Class I)
        - N → Non-urgent surgery (Class I)
  - Uncontrolled infection
    - Local complications (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation)
      - Y → Urgent surgery (Class I)
      - N → Persistent positive blood culturesᵃ
        - Y → Urgent surgery (Class IIa)
        - N → Resistant bacteriaᶜ or fungi
          - Y → Urgent or non-urgent surgery (Class I)ᵈ
          - N → PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli
            - Y → Urgent surgery (Class IIa)
            - N → Non-urgent surgery (Class I)
  - High risk of embolism or established embolism
    - Vegetation ≥10 mm and emboli despite appropriate antibiotic therapy
      - Y → Urgent surgery (Class I)
      - N → Vegetation ≥10 mm and other reason for surgeryᵇ
        - Y → Urgent surgery (Class I)
        - N → Vegetation ≥10 mm and no evidence of embolus
          - Y → Urgent surgery (Class IIb)
          - N → Antibiotic therapy and continued observation

## VIII. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.
- Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.
- Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.

- Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.

## IX. COMPLICATIONS

Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.

|    | Cardiac complications                                         | Metastatic infection                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|----|---------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -  | Heart failure -                                               | Forms of metastatic infection include Septic embolization, metastatic                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -  | Perivalvular abscess                                          | abscess, and mycotic aneurysm.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -  | Pericarditis (suppurative or nonsuppurative) -                | Emboli can occlude or damage virtually any vessel in the systemic or pulmonary arterial circulation:                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -  | Intracardiac fistula (eg, aorta- atrial or aorta-ventricular) | · Stroke · Paralysis (due to embolic infarction of either the brain or spinal cord) · Blindness (due to embolism or due to endophthalmitis as a result of bacteremic seeding) · Ischemia of the extremities · Splenic or renal infarction · Pulmonary embolism · Acute myocardial infarction |

## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

Measures for prevention of IE include:

- Maintenance of oral hygiene
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures
- Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.
- Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.

## I. DEFINITION

Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.
- Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.
- Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.

## III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS

- Risk factors for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac factors or noncardiac risk factors.
- It is most often from bacteria and more rarely a fungus from

| Bacteria                  | Source of Infection                                |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Staphylococcus aureus     | Skin                                               |
| Oral Streptococcus, HACEK | Oral, dental                                       |
| Group D Streptococcus     | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy)                |
| Enterococcus              | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy), Urinary tract |

| Cardiac risk factors                                                         | Non-cardiac risk factors               |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| · Previous infective endocarditis                                            | · Central venous catheter              |
| · Valvular heart disease                                                     | · People who inject drugs              |
| · Prosthetic heart valve                                                     | · Immunosuppression                    |
| · Central venous or arterial catheter                                        | · Recent dental or surgical procedures |
| · Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device Congenital heart disease | · Recent hospitalization Haemodialysis |

## V. DIAGNOSIS

1. Clinical Manifestations
- Symptoms: Fever is the most common symptom of IE
- It is often associated with chills, anorexia, and weight loss.
- Other common symptoms: Malaise, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, night sweats, abdominal pain, tooth pain and dyspnea.
- Signs: A new or changing cardiac
- Supportive signs: splenomegaly, petechiae or splinter hemorrhages.
- Relatively uncommon manifestations highly suggestive of IE:
- Janeway lesions
- Osler nodes
- Roth spots
2. Investigation for Endocarditis
- Blood cultures: At least two sets of blood cultures should be obtained from separate venipuncture sites prior to initiation of antibiotic therapy.
- Cardiac imaging:
- Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first diagnostic test for patients with suspected IE.
- Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has higher sensitivity than TTE and is better for detection of cardiac complications.
- Cardiac CT: May be helpful for cases in which definitive evidence of IE and its complications cannot be demonstrated with TEE, and/or for planning surgery in patients with extra valvular complications.
- Additional evaluation for IE source or complications: ECG, chest radiography, other radiographic imaging tailored to clinical manifestations, and dental evaluation.

3. Definitions of the 2023 European Society of Cardiology modified diagnostic criteria of infective endocarditis

## Major criteria

1. Blood cultures positive for IE

(a) Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from two separate blood cultures: Oral streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis), HACEK group, S. aureus, E. faecalis.

- (b) Microorganisms consistent with IE from continuously positive blood cultures:
- ≥ 2 positive blood cultures of blood samples drawn &gt;12 h apart.
- 3 j ≥4 apart).

w

w ≥1

- (c) Single positive blood culture for C. burnetii or phase I IgG antibody titre &gt;1:800.
2. Imaging positive for IE:

Valvular, perivalvular/periprosthetic and foreign material anatomic and metabolic lesions characteristic of IE detected by any of the following imaging techniques:

- Echocardiography (TTE and TOE)
- Cardiac CT
- [18F]-FDG-PET/CT(A)
- WBC SPECT/CT

## Minor criteria

Predisposing conditions (i.e. predisposing heart condition at high or intermediate risk of IE or PWIDs)

Fever defined as temperature &gt;38°C

Embolic vascular dissemination (including those asymptomatic detected by imaging only):

- Major systemic and pulmonary emboli/infarcts and abscesses.
- Haematogenous osteoarticular septic complications (i.e. spondylodiscitis).
- Mycotic aneurysms
- Intracranial ischaemic/haemorrhagic lesions
- Conjunctival haemorrhages
- J w '

Immunological phenomena:

- Glomerulonephritis
- Osler nodes and Roth spots
- Rheumatoid factor

## Microbiological evidence:

- Positive blood culture but does not meet a major criterion as noted above.
- Serological evidence of active infection with organism consistent with IE.

## IE Classification (at admission and during follow-up)

## Definite:

- 2 major criteria.
- 1 major criterion and at least 3 minor criteria.
- 5 minor criteria.

## Possible:

- 1 major criterion and 1 or 2 minor criteria.
- 3-4 minor criteria.

## Rejected:

- Does not meet criteria for definite or possible at admission with or without a firm alternative diagnosis.

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

The differential diagnosis for endocarditis is broad and should be considered based on two clinical categories: presence of bacteremia in the absence of valvular vegetation and presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteremia.

| Presence of bacteremia in the absence of valvular vegetation                                                                                                                   | Presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteremia                                                                                                             |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Intravascular catheter infection · Cardiac device infection · Prosthetic joint infection · Hematogenous osteomyelitis · Septic thrombophlebitis · Infected arterial aneurysm | · Culture-negative endocarditis or sterile vegetation(s) (marantic endocarditis or Libman-Sachs endocarditis) due to a noninfectious etiology or antiphospholipid syndrome. |

2. Indications and timing of surgery in the presence of heart failure in infective endocarditis:

Timing of surgical intervention in patients with IE complicated by HF should be decided by the Endocarditis Team, although surgery should not be delayed by Endocarditis Team discussions in patients requiring emergency operations. The presence of HF leads to recommendation for surgery in the majority of patients and is the principal indication for urgent surgery in IE patients.

## VIII. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.
- Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.
- Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.
- Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.

## IX. COMPLICATIONS

Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.

|    | Cardiac complications                                         | Metastatic infection                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|----|---------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -  | Heart failure -                                               | Forms of metastatic infection include Septic embolization, metastatic                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| -  | Perivalvular abscess                                          | abscess, and mycotic aneurysm.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -  | Pericarditis (suppurative or nonsuppurative) -                | Emboli can occlude or damage virtually any vessel in the systemic or pulmonary arterial circulation:                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -  | Intracardiac fistula (eg, aorta- atrial or aorta-ventricular) | · Stroke · Paralysis (due to embolic infarction of either the brain or spinal cord) · Blindness (due to embolism or due to endophthalmitis as a result of bacteremic seeding) · Ischemia of the extremities · Splenic or renal infarction · Pulmonary embolism · Acute myocardial infarction |

## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

Measures for prevention of IE include:

- Maintenance of oral hygiene
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures
- Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.
- Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.

## PERICARDITIS

Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Pericarditis refers to the inflammation of the pericardial layers with or without pericardial effusion.

## Type of pericarditis

|                      | Definition of Pericarditis According to the Time of Presentation                                     |
|----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Acute                | Even lasting <4 weeks                                                                                |
| Incessant            | Even lasting >4 to 6 weeks without remission But <3 months                                           |
| Recurrent (20-30%)   | Symptoms occur about 4 to 6 weeks after an episode of acute pericarditis with no symptoms in between |
| Chronic constrictive | Lasting >3 months                                                                                    |

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Acute pericarditis is diagnosed in 0.2% of all cardiovascular in-hospital admissions and is responsible for 5% of emergency room admissions for chest pain.

## III. ETIOLOGY

- Idiopathic is most common: presumed to be viral
- Infectious
- o Tuberculosis
- o Viral: Coxsackie virus A, B (most common), echovirus
- o Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus
- Post-MI: acute (direct extension of myocardial inflammation, 1-7 d post-MI), Dressler's syndrome (autoimmune reaction, 2-8 weeks post-MI)
- Post-cardiac surgery (e.g. CABG), other trauma
- Metabolic: uraemia/CKD, hypothyroidism
- Neoplasm: Hodgkin's, breast, lung, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma
- Collagen vascular disease: SLE, polyarteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma
- Other: drugs (e.g. hydralazine), radiation, infiltrative disease (sarcoid)

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Due to the parietal layer's rich innervation, any inflammatory process mediated by an infectious, autoimmune or traumatic insult can result in severe retrosternal chest pain, as is commonly seen in acute pericarditis. This explains why the vast majority of presentations (&gt;90%) have chest discomfort. In cases of pericardial effusion, the pericardial compliance can increase in response to slowly accumulating fluid, allowing the pericardial sac to dilate over time without compressing the cardiac chambers. This means that the rate of fluid accumulation (and resulting pressure changes, as in pericardial compliance) is often more important than the volume in determining the hemodynamic sequela affecting the heart.

## V. DIAGNOSIS

## Symptoms

Chest pain is the most common symptom of pericarditis (&gt;95%). It usually feels sharp or stabbing, and some patients having achy or pressure-like chest pain.

## The pain:

- Usually occurs behind the breastbone or on the left side of the chest
- Spread to the left shoulder and neck
- Get worse when coughing, lying down or taking a deep breath
- Get better when sitting up or leaning forward

Other signs and symptoms of pericarditis may include:

- Cough
- Fatigue or general feeling of weakness or being sick
- Leg swelling
- Low-grade fever
- Palpitation
- Shortness of breath when lying down
- Swelling of the belly (abdomen)

## Investigations

- ECG: initially diffuse elevated ST segments ± depressed PR segment, the elevation in the ST segment is concave upwards → 2-5 d later ST isoelectric with T wave flattening and inversion
- Chest X-ray
- Heart ultrasound: performed to assess for pericardial effusion
- CT or MRI: when located pericardial effusion, pericardial thickening or masses, constrictive pericarditis

<!-- image -->

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES

| Common                                                                                    | Less common                                      | Rare                                 |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Myocardial infarction Acute gastritis Gastroesophageal reflux disease Pleuritis Pneumonia | Esophageal spasm Pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax | Aortic dissection Esophageal rupture |

## VII. TREATMENT

- Anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs/ASA, steroids)
- Colchicine
- Treat the underlying disease

| Drug       | Dose                               | Duration   |
|------------|------------------------------------|------------|
| Aspirin*   | 750-1,000 mg every 8 h             | 1-2 weeks  |
| Ibuprofen* | 600-800 mg every 8 h               | 1-2 weeks  |
| Colchicine | 0.5-1.2 mg in one or divided doses | 3 months   |

* Tapering once inflammatory markers have normalized

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- Inpatient investigation and more intensive evaluation for a non-viral etiology should be considered where there is:
- o Any fever &gt;38°C
- o Gradual onset
- o Large effusion (&gt;20 mm) or tamponade
- o Lack of response to 1 week of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
- o Any history of trauma, immunosuppression/deficiency or oral anticoagulant use
- If pericarditis is caused by a bacterial infection, treatment may include antibiotics and drainage, if necessary.
- If pericarditis causes fluid buildup around the heart, a surgery or other procedure may be needed to drain the fluid (pericardiocentesis).

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

The prognosis of acute pericarditis largely depends on the underlying aetiology. It is excellent in cases of idiopathic pericarditis. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment of acute pericarditis may reduce the risk of acute complications and recurrences.

## X. COMPLICATION

- Pericardial effusion
- Constrictive pericarditis
- Cardiac tamponade (this life-threatening condition requires emergency treatment)

## XI. PREVENTION

Acute pericarditis can't be prevented. We can take steps to reduce your chance of having another acute episode, complications or chronic pericarditis. These steps include getting prompt treatment, following your treatment plan and getting ongoing medical care as needed.

## CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS

Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap,Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha,Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. DEFINITION

Constrictive pericarditis (CP) is a chronic inflammatory process, often characterized by chronic scarring, fibrosis and calcification of the pericardium associated with diastolic dysfunction, eventually leading to low cardiac output and heart failure.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Complication of acute CP is a relatively rare complication of viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis (&lt;0.5%) but, in contrast, is relatively frequent for specific etiologies, especially bacterial. In Asian series, TB pericarditis is reported to be the underlying etiology in 20-80% of cases

## III. ETIOLOGY

## 1. Common causes:

- Complication of acute idiopathic pericarditis
- Post cardiac surgery or post chest radiotherapy
- Infection (viral or bacterial)
- Tuberculosis
- Bacterial infections that lead to purulent pericarditis

## 2. Less common causes:

- Infection (fungal)
- Neoplasms
- Uremia
- Connective tissue disorders
- Drugs (e.g: procainamide and hydralazine)
- Trauma
- Myocardial infarction (with past medical history of Dressler syndrome and hemopericardium)

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Pericardial non-compliance creates a stiff ventricular-pericardial unit,

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 433 -->
- Pericardial non-compliance creates a stiff ventricular-pericardial unit,
  - limiting ventricular relaxation and determines ventricular diastolic pressure, resulting in elevated, equalized diastolic pressures in all chambers
    - decreasing the LV end diastolic volume (LV preload) and therefore left-sided stroke volume.
      - Clinically, predominantly as right-sided congestion (jugular venous distention, edema, and ascites) as well as elevation in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and a decreased cardiac output response to exercise (given inadequate ventricular filling) results in dyspnea and effort intolerance
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

      - Clinically, predominantly as right-sided congestion (jugular venous distention, edema, and ascites) as well as elevation in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and a decreased cardiac output response to exercise (given inadequate ventricular filling) results in dyspnea and effort intolerance

decreasing the LV end diastolic volume (LV preload) and therefore left-sided stroke volume.

Clinically, predominantly as right-sided congestion (jugular venous distention, edema, and ascites) as well as elevation in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and a decreased cardiac output response to exercise (given inadequate ventricular filling) results in dyspnea and effort intolerance

## IV. DIAGNOSIS

1. Initial assessment:
- The low prevalence of CP makes identifying key physical examination and historical features an important initial step in the diagnostic process.
- History of cardiac surgery, radiation or tuberculosis should heighten clinical suspicion in the presence of edema, abdominal distention and exertional dyspnea.
- In early stage: symptoms secondary to a reduction in cardiac output including fatigue and exertional dyspnea
- In late stage, the filling pressures become significantly elevated, and systemic venous pressure rises, signs of overt RHF develop such as jugular venous distention, edema, ascites, pleural effusion.
- Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) is present in virtually all patients:
- Kussmaul's sign
- Rapid x- and y-descents seen in the JVP of a patient with constrictive pericarditis. These are appreciated as rapid inward "flicking"/collapsing deflections in the presence of an elevated JVP.
- Other findings: diastolic apex beat or diastolic precordial impulse, highpitched early diastolic pericardial knock in heart auscultation.
2. Investigations:
- a. Laboratory testing: nonspecific in constrictive pericarditis.
- b. Echocardiography: As an initial diagnostic test, echocardiography can confirm the diagnosis of CP in most cases if pre-test probability is sufficiently high.
- The pathognomonic finding is respirophasic septal shifting, detected by either M mode or 2D imaging and abnormal beat-to-beat septal motion, or "shudder," due to differential rapid early diastolic filling of the right and then left ventricle.

- The inferior vena cava is universally plethoric in the absence of hypovolemia; a sensitive but nonspecific feature of CP.
- The exaggerated respiratory preload changes are also exemplified by an inspiratory decrease in mitral valve inflow Doppler and an increase in tricuspid valve inflow Doppler.

## c. Cardiac radiology:

- In CP, chest x-rays can demonstrate pericardial calcification, a pathognomonic finding in the presence of clinical heart failure and elevated JVP. Chest CT is more sensitive for pericardial calcification than chest x-ray.
- Chest CT and MRI allow for precise measurement of pericardial thickness, with MRI in particular demonstrating excellent accuracy (93%) in detection of pericardial thickening &gt;4 mm.

## Vl. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

The differential diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis (CP) includes conditions with similar symptoms such as restrictive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tamponade, systolic or diastolic congestive heart failure (CHF), Right-sided valvular abnormalities, Right-sided atrial tumors, and Superior vena cava syndrome and nephrotic syndrome. Theses can present with dyspnea, edema, ascites, pleural effusion, jugular vein distention mimicking CP. Careful evaluation of clinical history, laboratory finding and diagnostic imaging (echocardiography, cardiac CT or MRI) is essential to differentiate CP from these conditions.

## Vll. MANAGEMENT

## 1. Objective:

- Improving cardiac function, reducing inflammation and congestion.
- The primary etiology be identified and managed accordingly
- The definitive cure for CP is primarily surgical in the form of complete pericardiectomy, where feasible.

## 2. Critical signs:

End-stage disease can include cachexia, markedly reduced resting cardiac output (cardiac index ≤1.2 L/m2 per min), hypoalbuminemia due to protein-losing enteropathy, and/or congestive hepatopathy including cardiac cirrhosis.

## 3. Outpatient management

Outpatient care may be appropriate during the early stages of the disease, particularly when the diagnosis is still uncertain and symptoms are relatively stable. It is important to emphasize and encourage a low salt and fluid-restricted diet as these are probably beneficial in order to avoid congestion and exacerbations of heart failure symptoms. Although no specific restrictions are needed, activity can often be severely limited by symptoms. However, decreased daily activities may be recommended in some patients.

## 4. Pharmacologic therapy:

Medical treatment may be considered as a trial of two to three months as conservative treatment if it is transient CP. The following specific treatment modalities should be considered for each of the special situations highlighted.

- Subacute CP may respond to steroids if treated before pericardial fibrosis develops.
- Diuretics, particularly loop diuretics, are the mainstay to relieve congestion and to optimise clinical volume status; however, they may decrease preload to the point of reducing cardiac output and thus require closer monitoring.
- Any other medications used to treat patients with CP should be specifically directed to the underlying aetiology of the pericardial disease.

- Any therapy directed towards the causative disease, e.g., antituberculosis therapy, is appropriate.
- CP-related complications require their own specific therapy as appropriate, e.g., atrial arrhythmias.
- In general, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers should be avoided.
- Patients with advanced cardiac symptoms related to constriction may derive little benefit from surgery, as these are often the high surgical risk group.

## 5. Pericardiectomy

Pericardiectomy: a pericardiectomy remains the definitive therapy and a potential cure in most CP patients

Indication - We suggest pericardiectomy for patients with chronic constrictive pericarditis who meet all of the following criteria:

- Symptoms and signs have persisted despite at least 4 to 12 months of IL-1 inhibitor therapy.
- Symptoms are moderate to severe (New York Heart Association [NYHA] functional class III or IV (table 2).
- Constrictive pericarditis has not progressed to "end-stage." (See 'Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy' below.)
- There is no concomitant restrictive cardiomyopathy

Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy: Due to the complex nature of the surgery and the associated operative mortality, surgery should be carefully considered in patients who may not benefit from the procedure.

- Mild disease
- End-stage disease
- Mixed constrictive-restrictive disease
- Other high-risk groups - Mortality after pericardiectomy is also high in individuals with end-stage kidney disease or ventricular systolic dysfunction.

## 6. Mortality risk factors of pericardiectomy

Detrimental outcomes of pericardiectomy include progressive heart failure or advanced heart failure symptoms (NYHA III-IV), sepsis, renal failure, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, prior mediastinal radiotherapy as the primary cause of constriction, and other concomitant severe comorbidities.

Preoperative myocardial atrophy or fibrosis is as well one of the causes of peri-operative mortality due to reduced ventricular mobility, particularly the RV free wall, are associated with acute RV dilatation related to subsequent increased preload to the RV, to increased venous return which then leads to acute RV failure and decreased cardiac output, function and subsequent death. Extensive pericardial calcification might have prognostic implications, which make pericardiectomy more extensive and complex.

## Approach to treatment of subacute constrictive pericarditis in adults

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 439 -->
- Initial treatment: NSAID plus colchicine
  - Good
    - Continue treatment for 2 to 3 months
    - Then slowly taper NSAID as
      - Patient tolerates NSAID taper
        - Discontinue colchicine once NSAID is tapered off
      - Symptoms or signs Recur during taper
        - Switch to a Glucocorticoid plus Colchicine
          - Good response
            - Continue treatment for 2 to 3 months
            - Then slowly taper glucocorticoid as
              - Patient tolerates Glucocorticoid taper
                - Discontinue colchicine once glucocorticoid is tapered off
              - Symptoms or signs Recur during taper
                - Switch to an IL-1 inhibitor
                  - Good response
                    - Continue treatment for at least 4 to 12 months
                    - Then slowly taper IL-1 inhibitor as tolerated
                    - If symptoms or signs recur during taper, restart IL-1 inhibitor
                    - If response to a second course of IL-1 inhibitor
                  - Inadequate response
                    - Refer for pericardiectomy
  - Inadequate
    - Switch to a Glucocorticoid plus Colchicine
      - Inadequate response
        - Refer for pericardiectomy
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

Due to high prevalence of Tuberculosis in Cambodia (WHO's estimated TB incidence in Cambodia is 302 per 100,000 population in 2018), in a case of constrictive pericarditis, Tuberculosis should be investigated as one of potential causes.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

Long-term survival after pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis is inferior to that of an age- and sex-matched population, although in many patients this is likely related to comorbid conditions. In one series, the 5- and 10-year survival rates were 78 and 57 percent, respectively.

## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION

The conditions which are primarily the leading causes of CP should be adequately managed to prevent the occurrence of CP as listing in Etiology Section above.

## XI. COMPLICATIONS

Constrictive pericarditis if left untreated will lead to heart failure due to myocardial atrophy or fibrosis (diastolic et systolic dysfunction), Abnormal heart rhythm, liver and kidney dysfunction, which result in severe congestion in limbs, ascites, pleural effusion and dyspnea.

## MANAGEMENT OF CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES DURING PREGNANCY

Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour

## I. INTRODUCTION

Today the number of pregnancy woman complicated by cardiovascular disease (CVD) is increasing worldwide. In western industrialized countries such patients represent 0.2-4% of all pregnancies. Counselling and management of women of childbearing age with suspected cardiac disease should start before pregnancy occurs; they should be managed by interdisciplinary teams; high risk patients should be treated in specialized centers; and diagnostic procedures and interventions should be performed by specialists with great expertise in the individual technique and experiences in treating pregnant patients.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

Hypertensive disorder are the most frequent cardiovascular events during pregnancy, occurring in 6-8% of all pregnancies.

In the western world, congenital heart disease is the most frequent cardiovascular disease present during pregnancy (75-82%). Congenital heart disease represents just 9-19% outside Europe and North America.

Rheumatic valvular disease dominates in non-western countries, including our country, Cambodia, comprising 56-89% of all cardiovascular disease in pregnancy.

Cardiomyopathies are rare, but represent sever causes of cardiovascular complication in pregnancy. Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is the most common cause of severe complications.

## III. HEMODYNAMIC, HEMOSTATIC AND METABOLIC ALTERATIONS DURING PREGNANCY

Pregnancy induces changes in the cardiovascular system to meet the increased metabolic demands of the mother and fetus: increases in blood volume and cardiac output (CO), and reductions in systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure (BP):

- Plasma volume reaches a maximum of 40% above baseline at 24 weeks gestations.
- A 30-35% increase in CO in normal pregnancy
- Heart rate starts to rise at 20 weeks and increases until 32 weeks
- Systemic BP (SBP) typically falls early in gestation and diastolic BP (DBP) is usually 10mmHg below baseline in the second trimester: caused by active vasodilation. In the 3 rd trimester, the DBP gradually increases and may normalized to non-pregnant values by term.
- The heart can increase its size by up to 30%

Figure 1. Hemodynamic changes in pregnancy

<!-- qwen3 fill: image, page 442 -->
[Image: graph showing usual haemodynamic changes associated with pregnancy, plotting increase (%) against pregnancy duration (weeks) for CO (cardiac output), SV (stroke volume), HR (heart rate), and TPVR (total peripheral vascular resistance)]
<!-- /qwen3 fill -->

Hemostatic changes: tend to hypercoagulability and increase risk of thromboembolic due to increases in concentration of coagulation factors, fibrinogen, and platelet adhesiveness, as well as diminished fibrinolysis.

Maternal glucose and homeostasis may change and cholesterol levels increase in adaptation to fetal-maternal needs.

These changes can affect absorption, excretion, and bioavailability of all drugs.

Uterine contractions, positioning (left lateral vs. supine), pain, anxiety, exertion, bleeding and uterine involution cause significant hemodynamic changes during labor and post-partum.

## IV. ARDIOVASCULAR DIAGNOSIS IN PREGNANCY

- History and clinical investigation
- o Family history:
- Asking about possible sudden deaths in the family can identified some disease such as: Marfan syndrome, congenital heart disease, juvenile sudden death, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic VT or Brugada syndrome.
- Asking for the history or family history of hypertension or pre-eclampsia

## o Clinical assessment:

- dyspnea: important for diagnosis a prognosis of valve lesions and for heart failure.
- Auscultation: to detect ne murmur, changes in murmur
- Oximetry: should be performed in patients with congenital heart disease

## ▪ Paraclinical investigation:

- ECG, Heart Ultrasound, proteinuria
- Holter ECG (should be performed with known previous paroxysmal or persistent documented arrhythmia (VT, Afib or atrial flutter) or those reporting symptoms of palpitations.
- TEE, Exercise testing may be indication in some special circumstances.
- Radiation exposure: if possible, procedures should be delayed at least the completion of the period of major organogenesis (&gt; 12 weeks after menses). There is no evidence of an increased fetal risk of congenital malformations, intellectual disability, growth restriction, or pregnancy lose at doses of radiation to the pregnant woman of &lt; 50mGy.

## 5.1. Percutaneous therapy

- the best time to intervene is considered to be after the fourth month in the second trimester: organogenesis is complete, the fetal thyroid is still inactive, and the volume of the uterus is still small (greater distance between the fetus and the chest).
- Fluoroscopy and cineangiography times should be short and the gravid uterus should be shielded from the radiation.
- Heparin should be given 40-70 U/Kg, keep ACT between 200-300s.

## 5.2. Cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass

- Cardiac surgery is recommended only when medical therapy or interventional procedures ail and the mother's life threatened.
- The best period for surgery is between the 13 th and 28 th week (surgery during the first trimester carries a higher risk of fetal malformations and during the third trimester is a higher incidence of pre-term delivery and maternal complication)
- Cesarean delivery may be considered before cardiopulmonary bypass if gestational age is &gt; 26 weeks.
- Before surgery a full course (at least 24h) of corticosteroids should be administered to the mother, whenever possible.

- During cardiopulmonary bypass, fetal heart rate and uterine tone should be monitored in addition to standard patient monitoring.
- Keep pump flow &gt; 2.5L/min/m2 and perfusion pressure &gt; 70mmHg, maternal hematocrit &gt; 28% is recommended to optimize the oxygen delivery.

## VI. IMING AND MODE OF DELIVERY: RISK FOR MOTHER AND CHILD

## 6.1. Labor induction

- Oxytocin and artificial rupture of the membrane are indicated when the Bishop score is favorable (avoiding long induction time)
- Dinoprostone is contraindicated in active CVD (has profound effect on BP and risk of arrythmia)
- Mechanical methods such as a Foley catheter would be preferable to pharmacological agents, particularly in the patient with cyanosis where a drop in systemic vascular resistance and/or BP would be detrimental.

## 6.2. Vaginal or caesarean delivery?

- The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal and should be take place in a tertiary center with specialist multidisciplinary team care: less blood loses and infection risk, lower risk of venous thrombosis and thrombo-embolism.
- Caesarean delivery is reserved for obstetric indications: no consensus regarding absolute contraindications to vaginal delivery as this is very much dependent on maternal status and the time of delivery and the anticipated cardiopulmonary tolerance of the patient.
- Caesarean delivery should be considered:
- For the patient on oral anticoagulants
- Marfan syndrome and an aortic diameter &gt; 45mm or between 40-45mm
- Patients with acute or chronic aortic dissection
- Patients in acute intractable heart failure
- Women with sever aortic stenosis
- Women with severe form of pulmonary hypertension (including Eisenmenger syndrome), or acute heart failure
- Patient with mechanical heart valve prothesis

## 6.3. Anesthesia/analgesia and labor

- Lumbar epidural analgesia is often recommendable: it reduces pain related elevation of sympathetic activity, reduces the urge to push and provides anesthesia for surgery.
- However, it can cause systemic hypotension and must be used with caution in patients with obstructive valve lesion.
- Labor position: the woman should be placed in a lateral decubitus position to attenuate the hemodynamic impact of uterine contractions.
- Delivery should be assisted by low forceps or vacuum extraction, without maternal pushing to avoid the unwanted effects of the Valsava manoeuvre.

## VII. ISK ESTIMATION: CONTRAINDICATION FOR PREGNANCY

- Pre-pregnancy counselling: a risk assessment should be performed prior to pregnancy and drugs reviewed so that those which are contra indicated in pregnancy can be stopped or changed to alternatives where possible
- All women with heart disease should be assessed at least once before pregnancy and during pregnancy and hospital delivery should be advised.

## mWHO I

- Uncomplicated, small or mild pulmonary stenosis, PDA, mitral valve prolapses
- Successfully repaired simple lesion (ASD, VSD, PDA, anomalous pulmonary venous drainage)
- Atrial or ventricular ectopic beats, isolated.
-  Risk is very low, cardiology follows up during pregnancy may be limited one or two visits.

## mWHO II (if otherwise well and uncomplicated)

- Unoperated ASD or VSD
- Repaired tetralogy of Fallot
- Most arrhythmias

## mWHO II-III (depending on individual)

- Mild left ventricular impairment
- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
- Native or tissue VHD not considered WHO I or IV
- Marfan syndrome without aortic dilatation.
- Aorta &lt; 45mm in aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valve
- Repaired coarctation
-  Follow up every trimester is recommended.

## mWHO III

- Mechanical valve
- Systemic right ventricle
- Fontan circulation
- Cyanotic heart disease (unrepaired)
- Other complex congenital heart disease
- Aortic dilatation 40-45mm in Marfan syndrome

- Aortic dilatation 45-50mm in aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valve
-  High risk of complications, follow up monthly or bi monthly during pregnancy with cardiologist and obstetrician is recommended.

## mWHO IV (pregnancy contraindicated)

- Pulmonary arterial hypertension of any cause
- Sever systemic ventricular dysfunction (LVEF &lt; 30%, NYHA III - IV)
- Previous peripartum cardiomyopathy with any residual impairments of left ventricular function
- Sever mitral stenosis, sever symptomatic aortic stenosis
- Marfan syndrome with aorta dilated &gt; 45mm.
- Aortic dilatation &gt; 50mm in aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valve
- Native sever coarctation
-  Advised against pregnancy, if pregnancy occurred consider termination of pregnancy. If they will not consider termination, monthly or bi-monthly review is recommended.

## VIII. ETHODS OF CONTRACEPTION

Monthly injectable that contain medroxyprogesterone acetate: not recommended in patient with heart failure because of risk of fluid retention.

Oral contraceptive containing 20mcg of ethinyl estradiol are safe in women with a low thrombogenic potential but not in women with complexes vascular disease.

Barrier method (condom) and IUD is the safest and most effective method in women with cyanotic congenital heart disease and pulmonary vascular disease (caution with this method: 5% of patients experience vasovagal reactions at the time of implant). It is contraindicated in cyanotic women with Ht &gt; 55% (risk of intrinsic hemostatic defects that will cause excessive menstrual bleeding)

## II. CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE AND PULMONARY HYPERTENSION

## 1. Maternal high-risk conditions (mWHO III-IV)

## 1.1. Pulmonary hypertension

Pulmonary hypertension defined as mean PAP ≥ 25mmHg at rest. It encompasses a group of disease with different pathophysiologies which include PAH, pulmonary hypertension related to left heart disease, to lung disease and/or hypoxia, chronic tromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, idiopathic, heritable forms of the disease as well as pulmonary hypertension associated with congenital heart disease, with or without previous corrective surgery.

## Management:

- If pregnancy occurs, termination should be offered.
- If patients choose to continue pregnancy despite the risk, they should be managed in a center with expertise in PAH with all therapeutic options available.
- Goal is to maintain circulating volume, avoid systemic hypotension, hypoxia and acidosis which may precipitate refractory heart failure.

- Supplemental oxygen therapy, IV prostacyclin or aerosolized iloprost are occasionally used antenatally and peripartum to improve hemodynamic during delivery.
- In patients who are already taking drug therapy for PAH before becoming pregnant, continuation of this therapy should be considered, but patients should be informed about the teratogenic effects of some therapies, such as bosentan.
- In the patients where the indication of anticoagulation outsides pregnancy is established, anticoagulation should be maintained during pregnancy.
- Type of the anticoagulation that can be used during pregnancy: UFH, LMWH, VKA need to be decided on an individual basis.
- In PAH associated with portal hypertension, anticoagulation is not recommended.

## Delivery:

- The mode of delivery should be individualized.
- Planned caesarean delivery and vaginal delivery are favored over emergency caesarean delivery.

## 1.2. Eisenmenger syndrome

## Management:

- If pregnancy occurs, termination should be offered (to be noted, termination also carries a risk)
- If patients choose to continue pregnancy despite the risk, care should be based in a specialist unit.
- Bed rest may be beneficial.
- Anticoagulant: prevention for thrombo-embolism should be considered after hematology review and investigations for blood hemostasis (anticoagulation should be use with caution, as patients with Eisenmenger syndrome are also prone to hemoptysis and thrombocytopenia).
- Diuretic should be used in patients with heart failure at the lowest effective dose (to avoid hemoconcentration and intravascular volume depletion)
- Supplement oral or IV iron: use in case of microcytosis and iron deficiency.

## Delivery:

- An early caesarean delivery should be planned if the maternal or fetal condition deteriorates.
- Incremental regional anesthesia may improve maternal outcome.

## 1.3. Cyanotic heart disease without pulmonary hypertension

## Management:

- Women with an oxygen saturation below 85% at rest should be advised against pregnancy.
- Restriction of physical activity and supplemental oxygen (monitoring oxygen are recommended)
- Use of compression stocking and avoiding the supine position to prevent venous stasis.

- Prophylactic heparin administration should be considered (after hematology review and investigations for blood hemostasis.
- Diuretic and iron therapy are indicated and manage in the same way as in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome.

## Delivery:

- Vaginal delivery is advised in most cases.
- If the maternal or fetal condition deteriorates, an early caesarean delivery should be planned.
- Incremental regional anesthesia may improve maternal outcome.

## 2. Maternal low and moderate risk conditions (mWHO I, II and III)

## 2.1. Atrial septal defect (ASD)

- Pregnancy is well tolerated by most women with an ASD
- The only contraindication is the presence of PAH or Eisenmenger syndrome
- Maternal risk includes: trombo-embolic complications ~ 5%, arrythmia especially in unrepair ASD, ASD closed at older age and the pregnant woman is &gt; 30 years old.

## Management:

- Follow up twice during pregnancy is sufficient
- Catheter device closure can be performed during pregnancy but is only indicated when the condition of the mother is deteriorating
- Prevent of venous stasis with using of compression stockings and avoiding the supine position to reduce the risk of paradoxical embolism.
- Early ambulation after delivery, in case of prolonged bed rest, prophylactic heparin administration should be considered.

## Delivery:

- Spontaneous vaginal delivery is in most case appropriate.

## 2.2. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

- For large VSD with pulmonary hypertension, manage as pulmonary hypertension
- Small peri membranous VSDs without left heart dilatation have a low risk of complications during pregnancy
- Follow up twice during pregnancy is sufficient and spontaneous vaginal delivery is appropriate.

## 2.3. Atrioventicular septal defect (AVSD)

- After correction, pregnancy is usually well tolerated when residual valve regurgitation is not severe and ventricular function is normal.
- Patients with severe (residual) left atrioventricular (AV) valve regurgitation with symptoms and/or impaired ventricular function should be treated surgically prepregnancy.

- AVSD with pulmonary hypertension =&gt; manage as pulmonary hypertension in above section.

## Management

- Follow up during pregnancy at least once each trimester.
- Clinical and echocardiographic follow up is indicated monthly or bimonthly in patients with moderate or severe valve regurgitation or impaired ventricular function.
- Prevention the risk of paradoxical thrombo-embolism.

## Delivery:

- Spontaneous vaginal delivery is in most case appropriate.

## 2.4. Coarctation of the Aorta (CoA)

- After repair, the pregnancy is often well tolerated.
- Those women with unrepaired native CoA and those repaired who have residual hypertension, residual CoA, or aortic aneurysms have an increased risk of aortic rupture and rupture of a cerebral aneurysm during pregnancy and delivery.

## Management:

- Close surveillance of BP is warranted, and regular follow up at lease every trimester is indicated.
- Hypertension: should be treated but avoid an aggressive treatment to avoid placental hypoperfusion.
- PCI for re-CoA is possible during pregnancy but it carries higher risk of aortic dissection than outside pregnancy. It should be performed if sever hypertension persists despite medical therapy and there is maternal or fetal compromise (the use of cover stent may lower the risk of dissection).

## Delivery:

- Spontaneous vaginal delivery is preferred with use of epidural anesthesia particularly in hypertensive patients.

## 2.5. Pulmonary valve stenosis and regurgitation

## Management:

- Mild and moderated PS are regarded low-risk lesions and follow up once every trimester is sufficient.
- In patient with sever PS, cardiac evaluation by echocardiography should be performed monthly or bi-monthly to determine clinical status and for surveillance of RV function.
- Percutaneous valvuloplasty can be undertaken in severely symptomatic PS not responding to medical therapy and bed rest during pregnancy or in severe pulmonary stenosis (peak Doopler gradient &gt; 64m) Hg) pre-pregnancy.

## Delivery:

- Vaginal delivery is favored in patients with non-severe PS or sever PS in NYHA class I/II
- Caesarean section is considered in patients with severe PS and in NYHA class III/IV despite medical therapy and bed rest, in whom percutaneous pulmonary valvulotomy cannot be performed or has failed.

## 2.6 Tetralogy of Fallot

## Management:

- Follow up every trimester is sufficient in the majority of women
- In women with sever PR, monthly or bi-monthly cardiac evaluation with echocardiography is indicated.
- Diuretic and bed rest: if RV failure occurs during pregnancy
- Transcatheter valve implantation or early delivery should be considered in those who do not respond to conservative treatment.

## Delivery:

- The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal in almost all cases.

## 2.7 Ebstein's anomaly

- In women with Ebstein's anomaly without cyanosis and heart failure, pregnancy is often tolerated well.
- Symptomatic patients with cyanosis and/or heart failure should be treated before pregnancy or counselled against pregnancy.
- In severe symptomatic TR, repair should be considered pre-pregnancy.

## Management:

- Follow up
- Even sever TR with heart failure can usually be managed medically during pregnancy
- Prevention of paradoxical emboli (in case of interatrial shunting that can be develop shunt reversal and cyanosis)

## Delivery:

- The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal in almost all cases.

## III. AORTIC DISEASE

Several heritable disorders affect the thoracic aorta, pre-disposing patients to both aneurysm formation and aortic dissection:

- Marfan syndrome
- Bicuspid aortic valve
- Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
- Turner syndrome

All women with genetically proven Marfan syndrome or other familial aortic pathology should have counselling on the risk of dissection and the recurrence risk, and have a complete evaluation including imaging of the entire aorta before pregnancy.

## Management

- Follow up: aortic diameter should be monitored by echocardiography at 4-12 weeks intervals throughout pregnancy and 6 months post-partum
- ß-blockers is recommended to use in patients with Marfan syndrome during pregnancy to prevent dissection.
- * Celiprolol is recommended in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV
- Fetal growth should be monitored when the mother is taking B-blockers.
- Intervention before pregnancy is recommended if ascending aorta ≥ 45mm in patients with Marfan syndrome or other syndromes with high risk of dissection, otherwise intervention should be done pre-pregnancy when the ascending aorta ≥ 50mm or &gt; 27mm/m 2 for small woman.
- When progressive dilatation occurs during pregnancy, before the fetus is viable, aortic repair with the fetus in utero should be considered.
- When the fetus is viable, caesarean delivery followed directly by aortic surgery is recommended.

## Delivery

- If the woman is taking ß-blockers during pregnancy they should be continue in the peripartum periods
- If the ascending aorta diameter is 40-45mm, vaginal delivery with expedited second stage and regional anesthesia is advised to prevent BP peaks or Caesarean delivery could be considered based on the individual situations.
- Caesarean section should be considered when the aortic diameter exceeds 45mm and should be performed early especially in women with Ehlers- Danlos syndrome type IV.

## IV. ALVULAR HEART DISEASE

Rheumatic heart disease remains a major problem in developing countries. Stenotic valve disease carries a higher pregnancy risk than regurgitant lesion, and left sided valve disease have a higher complications rate than right sided valve lesions.

Specific problems, mainly related to anticoagulant therapy, are present in women with mechanical valve prostheses.

## 1. Mitral stenosis

- The risk of decompensation depends on the severity of MS.
- Heart failure occurs frequently in pregnant women with moderate to server MS (valve area &lt; 1.5cm2), particularly during the second and third trimesters, even in previously asymptomatic women.
- AF carries the additional risk of thrombo-embolic events.

## Management

- All patients with moderate to severe MS even when asymptomatic should be counselled against pregnancy.
- Intervention should be performed pre-pregnancy, favoring percutaneous interventions.
- Clinical and echocardiographic follow up is indicated monthly or bi-monthly depending on hemodynamic tolerance for moderate to server MS. For mild MS, evaluation is recommended every trimester and prior to delivery.
- In patients with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension (estimated systolic PAP &gt; 50mmHg), restricted activities and B1-selective blockers are recommended.
- Diuretics are recommended (avoiding high dose) when congestive symptoms persist despite B-blockers
- Therapeutic anticoagulation is recommended in the case of paroxysmal or permanent AF, left atrial thrombosis, or prior embolism or spontaneous echocardiographic contrast in the LA, large left atrium (≥ 40mL/m2), low CO or congestive heart failure.

## Intervention

- Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is preferable performed after 20 weeks gestations.
- It is indicated in women with NYHA class III/IV and/or estimated systolic PAP &gt; 50mmHg despite optimal medical treatment, in the absence of contraindications and if patient characteristics are suitable.

## Delivery

- Vaginal delivery: in patient with mild MS and in patients with moderate to server MS in NYHA class I/II without pulmonary hypertension.
- Caesarean section: in patients with moderate or severe MS who are in NYHA class III/IV or have pulmonary hypertension despite medical therapy.

## 2. Valvular aortic stenosis

Cardiac morbidity during pregnancy is related to severity of AS and symptoms. Asymptomatic mild or moderate AS, pregnancy is well tolerated. Also, patients with severe AS, may sustain pregnancy well, as long as they remain asymptomatic during exercise testing and have a normal BP response during exercise.

## Management

- All symptomatic patients with severe AS or asymptomatic patients with impaired LV function (LVEF &lt; 50%) or a pathological exercise test should be counselled against pregnancy.
- Valvuloplasty or surgery should be performed pre-pregnancy.

`

- Regardless of symptoms, pre-pregnancy surgery should be considered in patients with ascending aorta &gt; 50mm (27.5mm/m 2 ).
- Monthly or bimonthly cardiac evaluation including echocardiography are advised to determine symptom status, progression of AS, or other complications.
- Restricted activities are indicated for patients developing signs or symptoms of heart failure during pregnancy.
- Diuretics are indicated in case of congestive symptoms.
- ß-blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel antagonist or digoxin should be considered for rate control in AF.

## Intervention

- Percutaneous valvuloplasty is indicated in severely symptomatic patients not responding to medical therapy in non-calcified valves with minimal regurgitation.
- If this is not possible and patients have life-threatening symptoms, valve replacement should be considered after early delivery by caesarean section.

## Delivery

- In severe AS=&gt; caesarean delivery should be preferred with endotracheal intubation and general anesthesia.
- In non-sever AS=&gt; vaginal delivery is favored, avoiding a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance during regional anesthesia and analgesia.

## 3. Mitral and aortic regurgitation

Left sided regurgitant valve lesions carry a lower pregnancy risk than stenotic valve lesion because the decreased systemic vascular resistance reduces regurgitant volume.

Sever regurgitation with LV dysfunction is poorly tolerated, as is acute severe regurgitation.

## Management

- Pre-pregnancy valve repair surgery should be done in patients with severe regurgitation and symptoms or compromised LV function or LV dilatation.
- Follow up every trimester in mild/moderate regurgitation and more often in sever regurgitation (needed to be individualized)
- Symptoms of fluid overload can usually be managed medically
- In acute sever regurgitation with therapy-refractory heart failure, surgery sometimes is unavoidable.

## Delivery

- Vaginal delivery is preferable, in symptomatic patients, epidural anesthesia and shortened second stage is advisable.

## 4. Valvular atrial fibrillation

Prevention of thrombo-embolic risk is important. UFH / LMWH can be used in the first and last trimester.

LMWH should be given in weigh adjusted therapeutic dose (twice daily) until 36h prior to delivery.

OACs (VKA) or LMWH can be used in the 2 nd trimester.

INR should be kept between 2.0 and 2.5 (to minimize the risk for the fetus).

## 5. Bio prothesis

Pregnancy is generally well tolerated in women with a fell functioning bio prothesis. Pre-pregnancy assessment and counselling as well as follow up, medical treatment, and indications for intervention are comparable with those for pregnancies with native valve dysfunction.

## 6. Mechanical prosthesis and anticoagulation

Concerning of women with mechanical prothesis include increased risk of valve thrombosis, of hemorrhage complications and of offspring complications (miscarriage and hemorrhagic complications).

For the management of anticoagulant in mechanical valve during pregnancy, please see following schema (Figure 3, Figure 4 and Table 4).

## Delivery

- Planned vaginal delivery is usually preferred with prior switch to heparin.
- A planned cesarean section may be considered in patient with high risk of valve thrombosis (aim to keep the time without OACs as short as possible).
- Caesarean delivery should be performed if labor onset occurs while the patient is still on OACs.

## V. CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE AND ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME

ECG and measurements of troponin level are recommended when a pregnant woman has a chest pain.

Primary coronary angioplasty is recommended as the preferred reperfusion therapy for STEMI during pregnancy. The safety of DES in pregnant woman is still unknow and they should be avoided because it requires prolonged DAPT.

In non-ST-elevation ACS / NSTEMI, an invasive management should be considered in only patient with risk criteria, otherwise a conservative management should be considered.

The use of ACEi / ARBs and renin inhibitor is contraindicated during pregnancy.

ß-blockers and low dose aspirin are considered to be relatively safe.

Clopidogrel should only be used when strictly needed (after stenting) and for the shortest duration possible.

Breastfeeding is not recommended in mother who take antiplatelet agents other than low dose aspirin due to lack of data.

## VI. ARDIOMYOPATHIES AND HEART FAILURE

It is recommended to treat women with HF during pregnancy according to current guideline for non-pregnant patients, respecting contraindications for some drugs in pregnancy In patients with PPCM and DCM, subsequent pregnancy is not recommended if LVEF does not normalize, counselling for recurrent risk during subsequent pregnancy is recommended in all cases, even after recovery of LV function.

Figure 5. Rapid interdisciplinary workup and treatment of mother and foetus

<!-- image -->

In this case bromocriptine treatment may be considered to stop lactation and enhance recovery (LV function).

Due to the high metabolic demands of lactation and breastfeeding, preventing lactation may be considered in patients with severe heart failure.

ß-blocker is recommended to continue in women who used theme before pregnancy or install them with caution in heart failure, in HCM or in arrythmia.

Cardioversion should be considered for persistent atrial fibrillation.

Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH or VKA according to stage of pregnancy is recommended for patients with atrial fibrillation or with intracardiac thrombus detected by imaging or with evidence of systemic embolism.

## VII. RRTHMIAS

1. SVT and AF
- Acute management
- Stable hemodynamic =&gt; vagal maneuvers followed by adenosine if these fail (other drugs: beta -1- selective blockers should be considered if adenosine fail or not available)
- Instable hemodynamic =&gt; immediate electrical cardioversion
- Long term management
- SVT without pre-excitation: ß1 selective blockers or verapamil
- SVT in patients with WPW syndrome: flecainide or propafenone
- Digoxin and verapamil should be considered for rate control of AT or AF if beta blocker fails
- Catheter ablation with electroanatomical system should be considered in experiences centers in case of drug-refractory and poorly tolerated SVT.

PS: Atenolol should not be used for any arrhythmias

2. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias
- Acute management

- Immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended for sustained both unstable and stable VT.
- For acute conversion of sustained, hemodynamically stable, monomorphic VT, a beta blocker, sotalol, flecainide, procainamide or overdrive ventricular pacing should be considered.

## ▪ Long term management

- In patients with long QT syndrome or catecholaminergic polymorphic VT or idiopathic VT: ß-Blockers are recommended.
- VERAPAMIL also can be used for the prevention of idiopathic sustained VT if associated with severe symptoms or hemodynamic compromise. Sotalol and Flecainide could be use if other drugs fail.
- ICD (preferable one chamber) is recommended prior to pregnancy if clinically indicated but also during pregnancy, especially if the foetus is beyond 8 weeks of gestation, if indication emerges.
