## 3. Bradyarrhythmias

## ▪ Sinus node dysfunction:

- sinus bradycardia may appear as a reflex cardiac slowing (Valsava maneuver) during delivery.

- Rare case of bradycardia cause symptoms of hypotension, if occur =&gt; change the position of the mother to a left lateral decubitus position.
- For persistent symptoms, a temporary pacemaker maybe necessary.

## ▪ AV blocks

- 1 st degree AV block can be observed during pregnancy in the absence of underlying heart disease
- Temporary pacing during pregnancy is recommended in selected women with complete heart block and symptoms due to the risk of bradycardia and syncope.
- Implantation of permanent pacemaker can be performed safely, especially if the fetus is beyond 8 weeks gestations (with echo guidance).

## VIII. HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS

Hypertension is the most common medical problem in pregnancy, complicating up to 15% of pregnancies and accounting for about a quarter of all antenatal admission.

- Diagnosis and risk assessment
- Lab test: urine analysis, blood count, hematocrit, liver enzyme, serum creatinine and serum uric acid, 24hour proteinuria, urine metanephrine and normetanephrine
- Ultrasound of the adrenals
- Doppler ultrasound of uterine arteries (to detect uteroplacental hypoperfusion), which is associated with a higher risk of pre-eclampsia and intra uterine growth retardation.

## ▪ Definition and classification of hypertension in pregnancy

- The definition of hypertension in pregnancy is based on absolute BP value (SBP ≥ 140mmHg or DBP ≥ 90mmHg).
- Mildly hypertension: 140-159/90-109mmHg
- Severely hypertension: ≥ 160/110mmHg

Pre-existing hypertension: hypertension that either precedes pregnancy or develop before 20 weeks of gestation. This is usually persists &gt; 42 days post-partum.

Gestation hypertension or pregnancy induced hypertension: develop after 20 weeks gestations and resolves in most cases within 42 days post-partum. It is characterized by poor organ perfusion.

Pre-existing hypertension plus superimposed gestational hypertension with proteinuria.

Antenatally unclassifiable hypertension: when BP is first recorded after 20 weeks gestations and hypertension is diagnosed.

Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy specific syndrome that occurs after mid-gestation: de novo appearance of hypertension with new onset of significant proteinuria &gt; 0.3g/24h.

## Signs and symptoms of pre-eclampsia

- Right upper quadrant/epigastric pain due to liver oedema +/- hepatic hemorrhage
- Headache +/- visual disturbance (cerebral edema)
- Occipital lobe blindness
- Hyperreflexia +/- clonus
- Convulsion (cerebral edema)
- HELLP syndrome
- Pharmacological Management

- Low dose aspirin (100-150mg daily) is recommended in women at high or moderate risk of pre-eclampsia from week 12 to weeks 36-37.
- Methylodopa, labetalol and calcium antagonists are recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.
- IV Nitroglycerine is recommended in case of pre-eclampsia with pulmonary edema, infusion of 5mcg/min and gradually increase every 3-5mins to a maximum dose of 100mcg/min.
- IV labetalol or oral methyldopa or nifedipine is recommended in severe hypertension.
- ACE inhibitors, ARBs or direct renin inhibitor are not recommended.
- Diuretic should be avoided because they may decrease blood flow to the placenta.

In women with gestational hypertension or pre-exiting hypertension superimposed by gestational hypertension, or with hypertension and sub clinical organ damage or symptoms, initiation of drugs treatment is recommended at SBP &gt; 140mmHg or DBP &gt; 90mmHg. In all other cases, initiation of drug treatment is recommended if SBP ≥ 150mmHg or DBP ≥ 95mmHg.

SBP ≥ 170mmHg or DBP ≥ 110mmg in a pregnant woman is an emergency and hospitalization is recommended.

## ▪ Delivery

- In women with gestational hypertension or mild pre-eclampsia, delivery is recommended at 37 weeks.
- Induction of delivery is recommended in gestational hypertension with proteinuria with adverse conditions such as visual disturbances, coagulation abnormalities, or fetal distress.

## IX. VENOUS THROMBO-EMBOLISM

1. Prevention
- Early mobilization and avoidance of dehydration.
- Using compression stoking

In case of anticoagulation is needed:

- Enoxaparin 0.5IU/KG body weight or
- Dalteparin 50IU/Kg body weight twice daily.

2. Management of acute venous thrombo-embolism
- Pulmonary embolism
- Clinical presentation (same as in non-pregnant state): dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, haemoptiysis, and collapse.
- Diagnosis:
- D-dimer levels increase physiologically in pregnant women with each trimester, thus a positive D-dimer test base on the conventional cut-off level is not necessarily indicated of VTE, but it helps to rule out VTE in the case of negative D-dimer.
- Bilateral compression ultrasonography is indicated follow by measurement of D-dimer.
- MRI may be used to rule out iliac vein thrombosis
- CT pulmonary angiography should be performed with the diagnosis cannot be confirmed or excluded with the above-discussed tool.
- Treatment:
- LMWH:
11. o Enoxaparin 1mg/kg body weight bid.
12. o Dalteparin 100iu/kg body weight bid.

- o Aiming for 4-6h peak anti Xa values of 0.6-1.2 IU/mL
- UFH (used in patients with renal failure and when urgent reversal of anticoagulation by protamine is needed, as well as in the acute treatment of massive pulmonary emboli:
- o Loading dose of 80U/Kg followed by
- o IV continuous fusion of 18U/Kg/h
- o Therapeutic target aPTT ratio 1.5-2.5 times the average laboratory control value
- o The aPTT has to be determine 4-6h after the loading dose, 6h after any dose change and then at least daily when in the therapeutic range.

When haemodynamics are improved and the patient is stabilized, UFH can be switched to LMWH in therapeutic dose and maintain during pregnancy.

- LMWH should be switched to i.v. UFH at least 36h before the induction of labour or caesarean delivery.
- UFH should be discontinued 4-6h before anticipated delivery and restarted 6h after a vaginal birth or 12h after caesarean delivery if there are no bleeding complications.
- UFH and LWMH are not contraindicated to breastfeeding.
- VKA may be started on the second day after delivery and continued for at least 3 months or for 6 months if pulmonary embolism occurred late in pregnancy.
- INR should be between 2 and 3 and needs regular monitoring, ideally once every 1-2 weeks.
- Thrombolysis: Relatively contraindicated during pregnancy and peripartum =&gt; should only be used in high-risk patients with severe hypotension or shock.
- Other anti-coagulants: Fondaparinux and Rivaroxaban are not recommended to use in pregnancy (due to transplacental passage of the drug)

## ▪ Acute deep vein thrombosis

- Clinical presentation:
- leg swelling (&gt; 85% left sided due to compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery and the gravid uterus),
- isolated pain in the buttock, groin, flank or abdomen (in case of isolated iliac vein thrombosis)

## - Diagnosis:

- D-dimer (see diagnosis in pulmonary embolism)
- Compression ultrasound leg vein imaging

In women with high pre-test probability, a positive D-dimer and a normal initial compression ultrasound =&gt; magnetic resonance venography may be considered to exclude isolated pelvic DVT.

Women with low pre-test probability and normal D-dimer should undergo serial compression ultrasonography on day3 and after 1 week without anticoagulation.

- Treatment
- LMWH:

## I. GENERAL PRINCIPLES

There are no uniform recommendations for the treatment of pregnant women yet. As drug treatment in pregnancy concerns the mother and the fetus, optimum treatment of both must be targeted. In case of emergency, drugs that are not recommended by the pharmaceutical industry during pregnancy and breastfeeding should not be withheld from the mother. The potential risk of a drug and the possible benefit of the therapy must be weighed against each other.

Before pharmacological treatment in pregnancy is started, it is recommended to check table below (Table 2) for clinical safety data.

In the absence of clinical safety data, it is recommended to check the electronic drug table (www.safefetus.com) for pre-clinical safety data.

In the absence of adequate human safety data, decision-making should be based on individual drug efficacy and safety profiles, and the available animal data, and the decision must be made together with the patient.

Decision making based on former US Food and Drug Administration (FAD) categories alone is no longer recommended.

## II. RECOMMENDATION FOR DRUGS USES

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are pregnancy category D drugs because of the risk of reduced fetal renal function and increased fetal and neonatal morbidity and death, especially with use during the 2 nd and 3 rd trimester. Women taking ACE inhibitors or ARB who desire to become pregnant should be advised to stop taking these drugs before conception to minimize the risk of fetal abnormality.

ß-Blockers have a favorable safety profile, and no teratogenic risk have been reported with their use. They have been associated with an increase in small-for-gestational-age infants and neonatal bradycardia and hypoglycemia but in practical terms are considered safe to use. Atenolol has been associated with low birth weight and therefore is not the ß-blocker of choice during pregnancy.

The routine use of diuretics is discouraged because of the potential reduction in maternal plasma volume early in gestation that is potentially harmful to the fetus. They should be used judiciously.

Amiodarone has been associated with a 9% incidence of fetal hypothyroidism and a 21% incidence of intrauterine growth retardation and should be reserved for cases of refractory ventricular arrythmia.

Drugs listed as category X include the following:

- Anticoagulants: Vitamin K antagonist cross the placenta and are potentially fetotoxic. They are commonly used in women with mechanical valves, and the risk and benefits associated with their use should be discussed with the patient before pregnancy is completed.
- Endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, and macitentan)
- Statin: although inadvertent exposure to statin during early pregnancy appears unlikely to increase the risk of adverse pregnancy outcome, theoretical considerations concerning the role of cholesterol in embryo development and the lack of demonstration benefit of treating hyperlipidemia during gestation are reasons for not recommending statin during pregnancy.

## CARDIAC EVALUATION BEFORE NON-CARDIAC SURGERY (NCS)

Ass Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, , Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Ass Prof. Chan Sokha, Ass Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour

## I. DEFINITIONS OF SRUGICAL TIMING AND RISK

| TIMING         | DEFINITION                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Emergency      | Immediate threat to life or limb without surgical intervention, where there is very limited or no time for preoperative clinical evaluation, typically <2 h.                                                                          |
| Urgent         | Threat to life or limb without surgical intervention, where there may be time for preoperative clinical evaluation to allow interventions that could reduce risk of MACE or other postoperative complications, typically ≥2 to <24 h. |
| Time-sensitive | Surgery may be delayed up to 3 months to allow for preoperative evaluation and management without negatively impacting outcomes.                                                                                                      |
| Elective       | The surgical procedure can be delayed permitting a complete preoperative evaluation and appropriate management.                                                                                                                       |

| RISK CATEGORY   | DEFINITION                                                                             |
|-----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Low risk        | Combined surgical and patient characteristics predict a low risk of MACE of <1%.       |
| Elevated risk   | Combined surgical and patient characteristics predict an elevated risk of MACE of ≥1%. |

* MACE: Major Adverse Cardiac Events (Death, Heart Attack, Heart failure, Arrhythmia, Stroke)

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY

- Each year, approximately 14.4 million inpatient and 19.2 million ambulatory surgeries are performed in the United States, with an estimated 313 million surgeries performed worldwide. Cardiovascular risk factors and disease are prevalent among adults undergoing NCS, and perioperative cardiovascular complications are an important cause of morbidity and mortality.
- In a large retrospective analysis of adults ≥45 years undergoing in-hospital surgery, perioperative death, myocardial infarction (MI), or ischemic stroke occurred in 1 of every 33 surgical admissions, corresponding to &gt;150,000 annual perioperative events in the United States. Although orthopedic

(40.0%), general (21.4%), and vascular (10.7%) surgeries were the most performed, patients undergoing vascular, thoracic, and solid organ transplantation surgeries had the highest incidence of cardiovascular events. Irrespective of the surgical subtype, perioperative cardiovascular complications are associated with prolonged inpatient hospitalizations, significantly higher medical costs, and increased mortality.

## III. PREOPERATIVE CARDIOVASCULAR DIAGNOSTIC TESTING

- ECG: For patients with known coronary heart disease, significant arrhythmia, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, other significant structural heart disease, or symptoms of CVD undergoing elevated risk surgery (COR:2a)
- ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY to assessment of ventricular function: In patients undergoing NCS with new dyspnea, physical examination findings of HF, or suspected new/worsening ventricular dysfunction (COR: 1)
- STRESS TESTING: Vasodilator pharmacological stress imaging, Exercise stress testing, Dobutamine stress echocardiography
- CARDIOPULMONARY EXERCISE TESTING: in whom objective functional capacity is reduced. Reduced cardiorespiratory fitness increases the risk of postoperative complications.
- CORONARY COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY ANGIOGRAPHY: In patients with acute chest pain and no known CAD, CCTA may be useful to exclude atherosclerotic plaque and obstructive CAD and is recommended as an alternative to invasive angiography.
- INVASIVE CORONARY ANGIOGRAPHY:

## V. CARDIOVASCULAR COMOBIDITIES AND PERIOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT

- CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE: In patients with ACS being considered for elective NCS, coronary revascularization as appropriate and deferral of surgery is recommended to reduce perioperative cardiovascular events. (COR:1C)

## ➢ HYPERTENSION:

- o Pre-operative: In most patients with hypertension planned for elective NCS, it is reasonable to continue medical therapy for hypertension throughout the perioperative period. Except, poorly controlled hypertension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] ≥180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure [DBP] ≥110 mm Hg before the day of surgery), deferring surgery may be considered to reduce the risk of perioperative complications.
- o Intraoperative Blood Pressure Management: In patients undergoing NCS, maintaining an intraoperative mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥60 to 65 mm Hg or SBP ≥90 mm Hg is recommended to reduce the risk of myocardial injury.
- o Postoperative Blood Pressure Management:
- In patients undergoing NCS, treatment of hypotension (MAP &lt;60-65 or SBP &lt;90 mm Hg) in the postoperative period is recommended to limit the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal events, and mortality.
- In patients with hypertension undergoing NCS, it is recommended that preoperative antihypertensive medications be restarted as soon as clinically reasonable to avoid complications from postoperative hypertension.

## ➢ HEART FAILURE:

- o In patients with HF undergoing elective NCS, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) should be withheld for 3 to 4 days before surgery when feasible to reduce the risk of perioperative metabolic acidosis.

- o it is reasonable to continue GDMT (Guideline Direct Medical Therapy) (excluding SGLT2i) in the perioperative period, unless contraindicated, to reduce the risk of worsening HF.

## ➢ HYPERTROPHY CARDIOMYOPATHY:

- o For patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) undergoing NCS, factors that aggravate or trigger dynamic outflow obstructions (Ex, positive inotropic agents, tachycardia, or reduced preload) are harmful and should be avoided to reduce the risk of hemodynamic instability.

## o If hypotension develops:

- Prioritize intravenous fluid administration to correct hypovolemia.
- Use alpha-agonists, such as phenylephrine or vasopressin, 7 rather than beta-agonists, which can worsen LVOT obstruction.
- Consider intraoperative echocardiography to evaluate LVOT obstruction in the setting of hypotension.
- In selected cases, intravenous beta-blockade may be necessary to reduce LV myocardial contractility and relieve LVOT obstruction.

## ➢ PULMONARY HYPERTENSION:

- o In patients receiving stable doses of targeted medical therapies, continue these agents.
- o In patients with severe † PH undergoing elevated-risk NCS, Referral to or consultation with a specialized PH center and invasive hemodynamic monitoring.

## ➢ ADULT CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE

- o Preoperative consultation with an adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) specialist is recommended before the surgery.

## ➢ VALVULAR HEART DISEASE

- o Patients with severe valvular heart disease should be evaluated for the need for valve intervention before elective NCS.
- o In asymptomatic patients with moderate or severe AS and normal LV systolic function as assessed by echocardiography within the past year, it is reasonable to proceed with elective low-risk NCS.

## ➢ ATRIAL FIBRILLATION

- o Treat potential underlying triggers contributing to AF and rapid ventricular response (Ex, sepsis, anemia, pain).
- o Initiation of postoperative anticoagulation therapy can be beneficial after considering the competing risks associated with thromboembolism and perioperative bleeding.

## ➢ PREVIOUS STROKE OR TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC STROKE

- o it is reasonable to delay elective NCS for ≥3 months after the most recent cerebrovascular event to reduce the incidence of recurrent stroke, MACE, or both.

## VI. PERIOPERATIVE MEDCIAL THERAPY

- STATTINE: Continuation of statin therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.
- RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN-ALDOSTERONE SYSTEM INHIBITORS: Omission 24 hours before surgery may be beneficial to limit intraoperative hypotension.
- ANTIPLATELET THERAPY AND TIMING OF NCS IN PATIENT WITH CAD
- o Timing of N CS after PCI :
- In patients with recent coronary artery balloon angioplasty without stent placement, elective NCS should be delayed for a minimum of 14 days to minimize perioperative MACE.
- In patients with DES-PCI placed for ACS who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, surgery should ideally be delayed ≥12 months to minimize perioperative MACE.
- In patients with DES-PCI placed for CCD who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, it is reasonable to delay surgery for ≥6 months after PCI to minimize perioperative MACE.
- o Perioperativ e Antip la tele t Managem ent Po st PCI
- In patients with prior PCI undergoing NCS, it is recommended to continue aspirin∗ (75-100 mg), if possible, to reduce the risk of cardiac events.
- In patients with CAD who require time sensitive NCS within 30 days of PCI with BMS or &lt;3 months of PCI with DES, DAPT should be continued unless the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit of the prevention of stent thrombosis.
- In patients with prior PCI in whom OAC monotherapy must be discontinued before NCS, aspirin should be substituted when feasible in the perioperative period until OAC can be safely reinitiated.
- o P erioperativ e Antip la tele t Managem ent in Patients Without Pri or PCI
- In patients with CCD without prior PCI undergoing elective NCS, it may be reasonable to continue aspirin in selected patients when the risk of cardiac events outweighs the risk of bleeding.
- ORAL ANTICOAGULANT: multidisciplinary team-based approach to time-based interruption is recommended to balance the competing risks of thromboembolism and perioperative bleeding.

- BETA BLOCKER: beta blockers should be continued through the perioperative period as appropriate based on the clinical circumstances.

## VII. MANAGEMENT OF POSTOPERATIVE STEMI/NSTEMI

- Patients who develop STEMI after NCS should be considered for GDMT, including consideration of ICA, balancing bleeding, and thrombotic risks with the severity of the clinical presentation.
- Patients who develop NSTEMI after NCS should receive medical therapy as recommended for patients with spontaneous MI but after consideration of postoperative bleeding risks and hemodynamic status.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES

- Preoperative evalu ati on before liver and k idney transplan tat ion : Data from the
- U.S. Renal Data System and Medicare claims reported that more frequent invasive or noninvasive CAD testing in the year before kidney transplantation was not associated with lower rates of 30-day posttransplant death or acute MI.
- Obes ity and baria tric surgery: careful attention to history and risk factors

during preoperative assessments is essential, because:

- o patients who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy, prior cardiac history was associated with greater risks of perioperative cardiac arrest and 30-day mortality.
- o patients with obesity undergoing bariatric surgery reported that a history of ACS or HF was associated with increased risks of perioperative cardiovascular complications.
